days.intro: A riddle of two eagles and a vine describes Judah’s broken loyalty, and God promises to plant a tender cedar shoot himself. Chapter 18 rejects the proverb that children pay for their parents’ sins: each person answers for their own life, and God desires no one’s death.
days.question: What would it mean for you to turn and live today?

days.title: For the Sake of His Name
days.intro: When elders come to consult him, God retells Israel’s history of rebellion in Egypt and the desert. Again and again he spared them for the sake of his name. Then comes a song of a sharpened sword, and Babylon’s king choosing his road by divination.
days.question: Looking at your own history, where has God been patient with you?

days.title: Someone to Stand in the Gap
days.intro: God lists Jerusalem’s crimes: bloodshed, contempt for parents, abuse of the stranger, orphan and widow. He will melt the city like metal to remove its dross. He sought one person to stand in the gap and found none. Two sisters, Oholah and Oholibah, picture Samaria and Jerusalem.
days.question: For whom could you stand in the gap through prayer this week?

days.title: The Death of Ezekiel’s Wife
days.intro: As Babylon lays siege to Jerusalem, Ezekiel’s wife, the delight of his eyes, dies, and he is told not to mourn openly, a sign to the exiles. Oracles follow against Ammon, Moab, Edom and Philistia, then a lament for Tyre, pictured as a splendid ship that sinks.
days.question: How do you bring your sorrow to God when life leaves no time to grieve?

days.title: The King Who Called Himself God
days.intro: The king of Tyre says, “I am a god,” and will fall. A lament pictures him once in Eden, perfect until pride corrupted him. Sidon is judged, Israel is promised a safe return, and Egypt, whose king boasts that the Nile is his own, will be laid waste.
days.question: Where are you tempted to act as though your gifts were your own making?

days.title: The Watchman’s Duty
days.intro: Egypt is warned by the fate of Assyria, a great cedar felled for its pride. Ezekiel laments Pharaoh’s descent among the dead. Then he is again made a watchman. News comes that Jerusalem has fallen, yet people treat his words like a pleasant love song and do nothing.
days.question: What word from God have you enjoyed hearing but not yet put into practice?

days.title: I Will Shepherd My Sheep
days.intro: God condemns shepherds who feed themselves and neglect the flock. He will seek the lost himself and set over them one shepherd, his servant David. Edom is judged. Then comes a great promise: clean water, a new heart, and a new spirit within his people.
days.question: When has God come looking for you after you strayed?

days.title: Dry Bones Live
days.intro: In a valley of dry bones Ezekiel prophesies, and breath enters them: Israel will rise from the grave of exile. Two sticks joined in his hand show one people under one king. Gog of Magog attacks God’s restored people and is utterly defeated.
days.question: What seems dead in your life that you could entrust to God’s Spirit?

days.title: A Vision of the New Temple
days.intro: Twenty-five years into exile, Ezekiel is brought in vision to a very high mountain. A man with a measuring reed leads him through a new temple, gate by gate and room by room. The careful measurements show that God’s dwelling is holy and set apart.
days.question: What would it look like to set apart a holy time and space for God?

days.title: The Glory Returns
days.intro: The glory of the Lord that left the temple now returns through the east gate and fills the house. That gate must stay shut because the Lord entered by it; many Church Fathers saw here an image of Mary. Rules follow for the altar, priests, and land.
days.question: How do you prepare to welcome the Lord when you come to Mass?

days.title: The River from the Temple
days.intro: After rules for the prince and the offerings, Ezekiel sees water flowing from the temple, rising from ankle-deep to a river. It makes salt waters fresh, and trees along it bear fruit every month. The land is divided among the tribes, and the city is named “The Lord Is There.”
days.question: Where do you need God’s life to flow into what feels barren?

days.title: Daniel and the King’s Dream
days.intro: Daniel and his three friends, young exiles at Babylon’s court, refuse the king’s rich food and thrive on vegetables and water. When King Nebuchadnezzar demands that his wise men tell him his own dream, God reveals it to Daniel: a great statue shattered by a stone.
days.question: Where might faithfulness ask you to quietly refuse what everyone else accepts?

days.title: The Fiery Furnace
days.intro: Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego refuse to worship the king’s golden statue and are thrown into a blazing furnace. Walking unharmed in the flames, they pray and sing a great hymn calling all creation to bless the Lord. The psalm mocks idols with ears that cannot hear.
days.question: What would you refuse to bow down to, even under pressure?

days.title: The Writing on the Wall
days.intro: Nebuchadnezzar is humbled for his pride, living like a beast until he acknowledges God. Belshazzar drinks from the temple’s sacred vessels and sees a hand writing on the wall. Under Darius, Daniel keeps praying three times a day, is thrown to the lions, and comes out unharmed.
days.question: What daily habit of prayer would you keep even if it cost you?

days.title: One Like a Son of Man
days.intro: Daniel sees four beasts rise from the sea, then the Ancient of Days on his throne, and one like a son of man receiving an everlasting kingdom. Jesus will take this title for himself. Daniel confesses his people’s sins, and Gabriel explains the seventy weeks.
days.question: When the world seems ruled by beasts, how do you hold on to Christ’s kingship?

days.title: Those Who Sleep Shall Wake
days.intro: After three weeks of fasting, Daniel sees a man clothed in linen and is strengthened by an angel. A long vision traces wars between the kings of the north and south. At the end, Michael arises, and many who sleep in the dust will awake, the wise shining like stars.
days.question: How does hope in the resurrection change the way you live today?

days.title: Susanna and Bel
days.intro: Two corrupt elders falsely accuse the virtuous Susanna, who trusts God rather than give in to them. Young Daniel questions them separately, and their stories about a tree do not match. Then Daniel exposes the priests of the idol Bel, kills a dragon, and survives the lions again.
days.question: When have you been tempted to stay silent while someone was falsely accused?

days.title: Comfort My People
days.intro: Isaiah’s tone changes to comfort for the exiles. A voice cries to prepare the Lord’s way in the desert. God, who measures the oceans in his hand, renews the strength of those who hope in him. Chapter 42 introduces the gentle Servant who will not break a bruised reed.
days.question: Where are you weary and in need of the strength God promises?

days.title: Cyrus, God’s Anointed
days.intro: God calls Israel by name: you are mine, and the waters will not overwhelm you. Isaiah mocks the craftsman who burns half a log to cook and carves an idol from the rest. God even names the Persian king Cyrus as his chosen instrument to free his people.
days.question: What does it mean to you that God calls you by name?

days.title: A Light to the Nations
days.intro: Proud Babylon will sit in the dust. God refines his stubborn people for his name’s sake. The Servant is made a light to the nations, and God will never forget Zion, any more than a mother forgets her child. The Servant offers his back to those who strike him.
days.question: Who in your life needs to hear that God has not forgotten them?

days.title: The Suffering Servant
days.intro: How beautiful are the feet of those who bring good news. Then the heart of the book: the Servant despised, wounded for our sins, led like a lamb to slaughter, whose suffering heals us. The Church reads it on Good Friday. Then God invites the thirsty to the waters.
days.question: How do you respond to the Servant who was wounded for your sins?

days.title: Good News to the Poor
days.intro: God rejects fasting that ignores the hungry and oppressed: the true fast frees and feeds. Light dawns on Zion and the nations come to it. In chapter 61 the anointed one brings good news to the poor, words Jesus reads aloud in the synagogue at Nazareth.
days.question: What kind of fasting is God inviting you to in this season?

days.title: New Heavens and New Earth
days.intro: Isaiah prays that God, our Father, will remember that we are clay in his hands. God promises new heavens and a new earth, and comforts Jerusalem as a mother comforts her child. Obadiah’s single chapter condemns Edom for gloating over Jerusalem’s fall.
days.question: Where do you need God’s comfort the way a child needs a mother’s?

days.title: The Return from Exile
days.intro: King Cyrus lets the Jews return to Jerusalem and hands back the temple vessels. A long list names the families who go home. They rebuild the altar, keep the feast of Tabernacles, and lay the temple’s foundation, while elders who remember the first temple weep aloud.
days.question: What new beginning is God offering you, even if it looks smaller than before?

days.title: Building Through Opposition
days.intro: Local enemies write to the Persian king, and work on the temple stops. The prophets Haggai and Zechariah stir the people to build again, and King Darius confirms Cyrus’s decree. The temple is finished. Then Ezra the scribe arrives, devoted to studying, living, and teaching God’s law.
days.question: What opposition discourages you from the work God has given you?

days.title: Ezra Leads a Second Return
days.intro: Ezra brings a new group home from Babylon. He is ashamed to ask the king for soldiers, so the people fast and pray for a safe journey. In Jerusalem he grieves over marriages to idol worshippers and leads the people to repent.
days.question: When have you trusted God enough to go ahead without the safety net you wanted?

days.title: Build the Lord’s House
days.intro: Haggai asks why the people live in fine houses while God’s house lies in ruins. Zerubbabel and Joshua the high priest start building. Zechariah then sees night visions: horsemen, a measuring line, and Joshua’s filthy garments replaced with clean ones.
days.question: What have you put off for God while you tended to your own house?

days.title: Not by Might but by Spirit
days.intro: Zechariah’s visions continue: a golden lampstand between two olive trees, a flying scroll, four chariots, and a crown for Joshua the high priest. The temple will be finished not by army or strength but by God’s spirit. Watch for the humble king riding a donkey.
days.question: Where are you relying on your own strength instead of on God’s Spirit?

days.title: The Pierced One and Nehemiah’s Prayer
days.intro: Zechariah’s last chapters speak of a shepherd valued at thirty pieces of silver, of one pierced and mourned, and of living waters flowing from Jerusalem. The Gospels echo these lines. Then Nehemiah, the Persian king’s cupbearer, hears of Jerusalem’s ruin and prays.
days.question: What news about others has moved you to fast and pray?

days.title: Rebuilding the Walls
days.intro: Nehemiah gets the king’s leave, inspects the broken walls by night, and rallies the people. Family by family they rebuild. When Sanballat and Tobiah mock and threaten, the builders work with one hand and hold a sword with the other.
days.question: What work has God given you that is worth guarding while you build it?

days.title: The Wall Is Finished
days.intro: Enemies try tricks, false prophets, and rumors to frighten Nehemiah into hiding. He refuses, and the wall is finished in fifty-two days. Nehemiah sets guards and finds the record of the families who first came home from Babylon.
days.question: When fear tells you to stop, what helps you keep going?

days.title: Ezra Reads the Law
days.intro: The people gather and ask Ezra to read the Law aloud. They weep as they listen, but their leaders tell them the joy of the Lord is their strength. They keep the feast of Tabernacles, confess their history, and sign a covenant.
days.question: When has hearing God’s word brought you both sorrow and joy?

days.title: Jerusalem Is Dedicated
days.intro: Lots are cast so that one family in ten will live in Jerusalem. Long lists name the residents, priests, and Levites. Then two great choirs walk along the new wall, and the joy of the city is heard far away.
days.question: What lists, names, or people in your life deserve thanks today?

days.title: Reforms and the Final Prophet
days.intro: Nehemiah returns to find old abuses back: the temple misused and the Sabbath broken. He acts firmly. Malachi then rebukes careless priests, foresees a pure offering in every place, and promises a messenger and Elijah before the day of the Lord.
days.question: What small faithful habit has slipped in your life and needs restoring?

days.title: Rend Your Hearts
days.intro: A plague of locusts strips the land, and Joel calls everyone to fast and pray. Rend your hearts, not your garments, he says. God then promises to pour out his spirit on all flesh, words Peter will quote at Pentecost.
days.question: What would it look like for you to return to God with your whole heart?

days.title: Esther Becomes Queen
days.intro: In the Persian court, Queen Vashti is deposed and the Jewish orphan Esther takes her place. Mordecai uncovers a plot against the king, then angers the proud Haman, who wins a decree to destroy all the Jews. Esther must decide whether to risk her life.
days.question: Where might God have placed you for such a time as this?

days.title: Haman’s Plot Undone
days.intro: On a sleepless night the king learns that Mordecai once saved his life. Haman is forced to honor the man he hates. At Esther’s banquet she exposes Haman, who dies on the gallows he built. The Jews are spared and Purim begins.
days.question: When have you seen a situation turned around in a way you never expected?

days.title: The Prayers of Esther
days.intro: These chapters, kept in the Greek Esther, add what the Hebrew leaves unsaid: Mordecai’s dream, his prayer, and Esther’s prayer to the Lord who alone is king. Trembling, she goes before the king, and God changes his heart. Psalm 120 (121) fits her prayer well.
days.question: What do you need courage for today, and have you asked God for it?

days.title: Holofernes Marches West
days.intro: Nebuchadnezzar sends his general Holofernes to crush the western nations, and city after city gives in. Israel alone prepares to resist and cries out to God. Achior, an Ammonite leader, warns Holofernes that Israel’s God protects his people when they are faithful.
days.question: Who has spoken a hard truth to you that you did not want to hear?

days.title: Bethulia Under Siege
days.intro: Holofernes sends Achior bound to Bethulia, where the Israelites take him in. The Assyrians cut off the town’s water, and the desperate people agree to surrender in five days. Then we meet Judith, a devout widow who scolds the elders for putting God to the test.
days.question: When have you tried to set a deadline for God to act?

days.title: Judith Goes Out
days.intro: Judith prays for strength, then dresses in her finery and walks with her maid into the enemy camp. Holofernes is charmed by her beauty and her words. Each night she goes out to pray, and on the fourth day he invites her to a banquet.
days.question: How do you prepare in prayer before a hard conversation or task?

days.title: Judith’s Victory Song
days.intro: Alone with the drunken Holofernes, Judith prays and strikes him down, then brings his head back to Bethulia. The leaderless Assyrians flee. Achior comes to believe in Israel’s God, and Judith leads the people in a song of praise before living out a long, holy life.
days.question: Where have you seen God work through someone the world overlooked?

days.title: Antiochus Profanes the Temple
days.intro: After Alexander the Great, his empire splits, and Antiochus Epiphanes comes to power. He loots the temple, sets up an idol on the altar, and outlaws the Law. Some Jews go along, but many choose death rather than break God’s covenant.
days.question: What pressure do you feel to quietly set your faith aside?

days.title: Mattathias Refuses
days.intro: In the town of Modein, the priest Mattathias refuses the king’s order to sacrifice to idols and kills the apostate who steps forward. He and his sons flee to the hills. Before he dies, he urges them to remember the faithful heroes of Israel’s past.
days.question: Whose faithful example from the past gives you strength today?

days.title: Judas Rededicates the Temple
days.intro: Judas Maccabeus takes his father’s place. With a small, outnumbered force he wins battle after battle, saying that strength comes from heaven, not from numbers. Then he cleanses the temple, builds a new altar, and begins the eight-day feast of dedication.
days.question: What in your life needs cleansing and rededication to God?

days.title: Rescue in Gilead and Galilee
days.intro: Neighboring peoples turn on the Jews living among them. Judas and Jonathan march into Gilead while Simon goes to Galilee, freeing their kin and bringing them home. Two commanders who disobey orders to seek glory for themselves are badly defeated.
days.question: Who in your life needs you to come to their aid right now?

days.title: Antiochus Dies in Grief
days.intro: In Persia, Antiochus hears of his defeats and dies in sorrow, admitting the evil he did in Jerusalem. His young son’s army returns with war elephants, and Eleazar gives his life to bring one down. In the end, the king makes peace with the Jews.
days.question: What regret would you rather face now than at the end of your life?

days.title: Nicanor Falls, Rome Is Allied
days.intro: A new king, Demetrius, backs the false high priest Alcimus, who betrays the devout with a broken oath. Judas defeats the general Nicanor, and the day is kept as a feast. Hearing of Rome’s power, Judas makes a treaty with the Romans.
days.question: Where are you tempted to put your trust in powerful people more than in God?

days.title: The Death of Judas
days.intro: Facing a huge army with only a few hundred men, Judas refuses to flee and falls in battle. All Israel mourns him. His brother Jonathan takes command, avenges their brother John, and wears down the enemy until Bacchides leaves the land.
days.question: How do you carry on when someone you relied on is gone?

days.title: Jonathan Becomes High Priest
days.intro: Two rivals for the Syrian throne, Alexander and Demetrius, both try to win Jonathan over with gifts and promises. Jonathan sides with Alexander, who names him high priest and honors him. He then defeats the general Apollonius in battle.
days.question: How do you tell the difference between real friendship and flattery?

days.title: Kings Rise and Fall
days.intro: Ptolemy turns on Alexander, and both kings soon die. The new king, Demetrius, is rescued by Jewish soldiers from his own people in Antioch, then breaks his promises. Jonathan sides with the young Antiochus and wins more victories.
days.question: When someone breaks a promise to you, how do you respond?

days.title: Jonathan Is Betrayed
days.intro: Jonathan renews ties with Rome and Sparta. But Tryphon, who wants the throne, lures him into Ptolemais with false friendship and takes him captive. Simon, the last brother, takes command. Tryphon kills Jonathan, and Simon builds a family tomb at Modein.
days.question: Who has God given you to carry on a good work someone else began?

days.title: Peace Under Simon
days.intro: Under Simon, Judea finally knows peace: everyone sits under his own vine and fig tree, with no one to fear. The people honor Simon on bronze tablets and make him leader and high priest. Then a new king, Antiochus, turns against him.
days.question: What would real peace look like in your home this week?

days.title: Simon’s Death and Two Letters
days.intro: Simon’s sons defeat the king’s army, but Simon and two sons are murdered at a feast by his own son-in-law. Second Maccabees then opens with letters urging Egyptian Jews to keep the temple’s dedication feast and tells how Jeremiah hid the ark.
days.question: How do you remember and celebrate what God has already done for you?

days.title: Heliodorus and the Temple Treasury
days.intro: An official named Heliodorus comes to seize the temple treasury, and the whole city prays. A rider and two shining young men strike him down, and he lives only through the high priest Onias’s prayer. Then ambitious men buy the high priesthood and push Greek ways.
days.question: When have the prayers of others carried you through?

days.title: Eleazar and the Seven Brothers
days.intro: Antiochus plunders the temple and outlaws the Law. The aged scribe Eleazar refuses even to pretend to eat pork, so as not to mislead the young. A mother watches her seven sons die for their faith, urging them on with hope in the resurrection.
days.question: Whose faith are you shaping by the example you set?

days.title: Judas Fights Back
days.intro: Judas gathers those who stayed faithful, and after prayer they defeat Nicanor’s army. Antiochus dies a painful death, his late vows unable to save him. The temple is purified, and in another battle five shining horsemen from heaven are seen leading the Jews.
days.question: Before you face something hard, do you turn to prayer first or last?

days.title: Prayer for the Fallen
days.intro: Judas defeats Lysias, who seeks peace. Later, fallen soldiers are found wearing idol charms. Judas leads prayer and sends money for a sin offering. The book calls it a holy thought to pray for the dead. The Church sees here a root of praying for souls in purgatory.
days.question: Who among the dead could you remember in prayer today?

days.title: Judas’s Dream and Victory
days.intro: Nicanor threatens to tear down the temple, and an elder named Razis dies rather than be captured. Before the final battle, Judas dreams of Onias and the prophet Jeremiah praying for the people. Strengthened, Judas defeats Nicanor, and the author humbly ends his account.
days.question: Which saints do you ask to pray for you, and why them?

days.title: The Souls of the Just
days.intro: Wisdom opens by urging rulers to love justice. God did not make death; it came through the devil’s envy. The wicked plot against the just man who calls himself God’s son. But the souls of the just are in God’s hand, tested like gold in a furnace.
days.question: Where is God refining you like gold right now?

days.title: Seeking Lady Wisdom
days.intro: The wicked look back with regret too late, while the just receive a crown from the Lord. Kings are urged to seek Wisdom, who is easily found by those who love her. The writer, speaking as Solomon, says he prayed for her and prized her above thrones and riches.
days.question: What do you value more than wisdom, if you are honest?

days.title: Solomon Prays for Wisdom
days.intro: Solomon tells how he sought Wisdom as a bride and asked God for her in prayer. Then he traces her hand in history, guiding Adam, Noah, Abraham, Jacob, Joseph, and Israel in the Exodus. God loves all things he has made.
days.question: How have you seen God’s guiding hand in your own story?

days.title: God’s Patience and False Gods
days.intro: God punished the Canaanites little by little, giving them room to repent. Then Wisdom turns to idolatry: people who admire the world’s beauty yet miss its Creator, and those who worship what their own hands have made. Watch for how idol worship first began.
days.question: What created thing do you sometimes treat as if it were God?

days.title: Plagues and Bread from Heaven
days.intro: The book closes by retelling the Exodus as a series of contrasts. Where Egypt suffered plagues, Israel received gifts: manna, the bread from heaven, and light while Egypt sat in darkness. God’s almighty word leaps down from heaven on Passover night.
days.question: How has something that seemed like a loss become a blessing for you?

days.title: All Wisdom Comes from God
days.intro: A grandson explains how he translated his grandfather’s book in Egypt. Then Sirach begins: all wisdom comes from the Lord, and fearing God is where it starts. Anyone who serves God should expect testing. Honor your father and mother, and stay humble.
days.question: How are you honoring your parents in this season of your life?

days.title: Mercy, Friends, and Firm Speech
days.intro: Sirach urges kindness to the poor and orphans, and patience while Wisdom tests her children. Do not put off turning to God or count on his mercy while you keep sinning. A faithful friend is a strong shelter and a treasure beyond price.
days.question: Who is a faithful friend to you, and have you told them so lately?

days.title: Remember Your Last End
days.intro: These chapters gather practical advice: do not chase high places, honor priests, help the poor, respect the elderly, and think before you lend or speak. Remember your last end and you will not sin. An old friend is like aged wine.
days.question: How might remembering your death change how you live today?

days.title: Pride and Humility
days.intro: Sirach turns to people in power and the danger of pride, which begins when the heart turns away from its Maker. Do not judge by appearances: the bee is small, but its honey is the sweetest. Be generous to the good and wary of the wicked.
days.question: Where is pride quietly steering your choices?

days.title: Choose Your Company
days.intro: Touch pitch and it sticks to you, so choose your companions well. Greed starves the soul, so do good with what you have while you live. God set fire and water before us and left us free to choose. He commands no one to sin.
days.question: Which of your friendships draws you closer to God?

days.title: God Sees and Shows Mercy
days.intro: Do not think you can hide from God. Sirach recalls how the Lord formed us from earth, gave us understanding, and made a covenant with us. Our days are like a drop in the sea, so God is patient and pours out mercy. Turn back to him.
days.question: What part of your life have you been hiding from God?

days.title: Guard Your Tongue
days.intro: If you hear something against your neighbor, let it die within you. Sirach praises timely silence and warns that a liar’s disgrace never leaves him. Flee from sin as from a snake. The wise and the foolish are known by how they speak.
days.question: What word about someone else do you need to let die within you?

days.title: A Prayer to Guard My Mouth
days.intro: Sirach offers sayings about lazy and foolish people, and about friendships wounded by insults or betrayed secrets. Then he prays to God as Father and Lord of his life, asking for a guard on his mouth and protection from careless oaths and lust.
days.question: What would you ask God to guard in you today?

days.title: Wisdom Makes Her Home
days.intro: Wisdom speaks in her own voice: she came forth from the mouth of the Most High and made her home in Israel, flourishing like a cedar and a vine. Christians hear Christ, God’s Word, in this song. Then come sayings on harmony and wise old age.
days.question: Where has God chosen to dwell in your ordinary life?

days.title: Words That Reveal the Heart
days.intro: Sirach praises a good wife as a great gift. A sieve shows what is left behind, and a person’s words reveal the heart. Forgive your neighbor and your own sins will be forgiven when you pray. Many fall by the sword, but more by the tongue.
days.question: Whom do you need to forgive before you pray tonight?

days.title: Lending, Alms, and Health
days.intro: Lend to a neighbor in need and repay on time. Store up almsgiving as a treasure, for it protects better than a shield. Sirach speaks of raising children, and says health and a glad heart are worth more than wealth. Riches can steal your sleep.
days.question: What worry about money is costing you sleep or peace?

days.title: Do Nothing Without Counsel
days.intro: At the table, leaders should serve their guests and the young should listen more than they speak. Seek advice before you act. Like clay in the potter’s hand, we are in God’s hands. Dreams deceive, but those who fear the Lord have nothing to fear.
days.question: Whose counsel do you seek before making big decisions?

days.title: The Prayer of the Humble
days.intro: Keeping the law is a pleasing sacrifice, and God cannot be bribed with gifts taken unjustly. The prayer of the humble pierces the clouds. Sirach prays for God to show mercy to his people, then praises a good wife and warns about choosing advisors.
days.question: When did you last pray with real humility, holding nothing back?

days.title: Physicians and Craftsmen
days.intro: Honor the doctor, for the Lord created medicine from the earth; yet pray and repent when sick. Mourn the dead, but not without end. Farmers, smiths, and potters keep the world running, while the scribe gives himself to study, prayer, and praise of God.
days.question: How can your daily work, whatever it is, become a form of prayer?

days.title: Death and a Good Name
days.intro: Every life has its toil and fear, from king to beggar, yet the fear of the Lord is like a garden of blessing. Death is bitter to the comfortable but welcome to the weary. A good name lasts. Sirach ends by praising God’s works.
days.question: What kind of name do you hope to leave behind?

days.title: Praise of Famous Men
days.intro: After a hymn to the sun, moon, stars, snow, and sea, Sirach admits words fail: God is all. Then he begins praising the ancestors: Enoch, Noah, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, then Moses, Aaron in his splendid vestments, and Phinehas.
days.question: Which ancestor in faith, family or saint, are you grateful for today?

days.title: Judges, Kings, and Prophets
days.intro: The roll of honor continues: Joshua and Caleb, Samuel, Nathan, and David, who sang God’s praise. Solomon’s wisdom and his fall are both remembered. Elijah rises like fire, followed by Elisha, King Hezekiah, and the prophet Isaiah.
days.question: What part of your story would you want God to remember?

days.title: Simon the High Priest
days.intro: The list ends with Josiah, the prophets, and the builders of the second temple. Then Sirach paints the high priest Simon in glory at the altar. The book closes with a hymn of thanks and an invitation to seek Wisdom freely, as he did in youth.
days.question: What first drew you to seek God, and how can you rekindle it?

days.title: The Birth of the Messiah
days.intro: Matthew opens with Jesus’ family tree from Abraham through David, then his birth of the Virgin Mary. Magi come to worship, and the family flees Herod into Egypt. John baptizes Jesus, who is tempted in the desert and calls his first disciples.
days.question: What is Jesus calling you to leave behind so you can follow him?

days.title: The Sermon on the Mount
days.intro: On a mountain Jesus teaches the Beatitudes and calls his followers salt and light. He deepens the Law, asks us to love our enemies, and teaches the Our Father. Give, pray, and fast in secret, and seek first the kingdom of God.
days.question: Which Beatitude do you most need to grow into?

days.title: Words and Works of Power
days.intro: Jesus finishes his sermon: do not judge, ask and you will receive, and build your house on rock. Then he acts, healing a leper, a centurion’s servant, and a paralytic, calming a storm, calling Matthew the tax collector, and raising a dead girl.
days.question: Is your life built on rock, or on something that could wash away?

days.title: The Twelve Are Sent
days.intro: Jesus sends the twelve apostles out to preach and heal, warning that they will face hostility but need not fear. From prison, John the Baptist asks if Jesus is the one to come. Jesus invites all who are weary and burdened to come to him for rest.
days.question: What burden do you need to bring to Jesus for rest?

days.title: Parables of the Kingdom
days.intro: The Pharisees accuse Jesus of driving out demons by Satan’s power, and he warns them. He says that whoever does God’s will is his brother, sister, and mother. Then he teaches in parables: the sower, the weeds, the mustard seed, the hidden treasure, and the pearl.
days.question: What kind of soil is your heart for God’s word this week?

days.title: You Are the Christ
days.intro: Herod beheads John. Jesus feeds five thousand, walks on the sea, and lifts up a sinking Peter. A Canaanite woman’s faith wins healing for her daughter. Peter confesses Jesus as the Christ and receives the keys, but is rebuked when he resists the cross.
days.question: Who do you say Jesus is, in the way you actually live?

days.title: Transfiguration and Forgiveness
days.intro: Jesus is transfigured in glory before Peter, James, and John. He teaches that the greatest is the one who becomes like a child, that the shepherd seeks the lost sheep, and that we must forgive seventy times seven. A rich young man walks away sad.
days.question: What would it take for you to forgive one more time?

days.title: The King Enters Jerusalem
days.intro: In a parable, late workers receive the same wage as the first. James and John seek high places, but Jesus came to serve and give his life. He heals two blind men, rides into Jerusalem on a donkey as Zechariah foretold, and clears the temple.
days.question: Where is Jesus asking you to serve rather than be served?

days.title: The Greatest Commandment
days.intro: In the temple, opponents try to trap Jesus with questions about taxes to Caesar and the resurrection. He names the greatest commandments: love God with your whole heart and your neighbor as yourself. Then he denounces hypocrisy and grieves over Jerusalem.
days.question: Where do you find it hardest to love your neighbor as yourself?

days.title: Watch and Be Ready
days.intro: Jesus foretells the temple’s destruction and his coming at the end of time, urging his disciples to stay awake. Parables of the ten virgins and the talents follow. At the judgment, he says, whatever we did for the least of his brothers we did for him.
days.question: Who is one of the least in your life you can serve this week?

days.title: The Last Supper and Gethsemane
days.intro: A woman anoints Jesus, and Judas agrees to betray him for thirty pieces of silver. At the Passover meal Jesus gives his Body and Blood. In Gethsemane he prays in anguish, is arrested, and is condemned before Caiaphas, while Peter denies him three times.
days.question: When have you, like Peter, failed Jesus, and how did you return?

days.title: Crucified and Risen
days.intro: Jesus is handed to Pilate, mocked, and crucified between two thieves. The earth quakes and a centurion confesses him as Son of God. On the third day an angel announces he is risen, and Jesus sends his disciples to teach and baptize all nations.
days.question: How will you live today knowing Jesus is with you always?

days.title: Mark’s Gospel Begins
days.intro: Mark moves fast. John baptizes Jesus, and Jesus begins preaching, calling fishermen, casting out demons, and healing many. Friends lower a paralyzed man through a roof. Jesus calls Levi, heals on the Sabbath, chooses the Twelve, and says his true family does God’s will.
days.question: Whom could you carry to Jesus through your prayer and help?

days.title: Who Is This Man?
days.intro: Jesus teaches from a boat in parables of seeds. When a storm terrifies his disciples, he calms it with a word. He frees a man possessed by a legion of demons, heals a woman who touches his cloak, and raises a synagogue leader’s daughter.
days.question: What storm in your life do you need to hand over to Jesus?

days.title: Bread in the Wilderness
days.intro: Jesus is rejected in his hometown, then sends out the Twelve. Herod has John beheaded. Jesus feeds five thousand and walks on the water. He teaches that what defiles comes from within, heals a Gentile woman’s daughter, and opens a deaf man’s ears.
days.question: What does Jesus want to open in you that has been closed?

days.title: Help My Unbelief
days.intro: Jesus feeds four thousand and heals a blind man in two stages. Peter confesses him as the Christ, and Jesus foretells his passion. After the Transfiguration, a father cries, “I believe, help my unbelief,” and Jesus heals his son.
days.question: Where do you need to pray, “I believe, help my unbelief”?

days.title: The Road Into Jerusalem
days.intro: Jesus teaches that marriage is lifelong, warns how riches can block the way to the kingdom, and tells James and John that greatness means serving. Blind Bartimaeus receives his sight. Then Jesus rides into Jerusalem, curses a fig tree, and clears the temple.
days.question: What would it look like for you to serve rather than be served this week?

days.title: Questions in the Temple
days.intro: In the temple, Jesus tells the parable of the wicked tenants and answers traps about taxes and the resurrection. He names the greatest commandment and praises a poor widow’s gift. Then he foretells the temple’s fall and urges his disciples to stay awake.
days.question: What small, hidden gift could you offer God today, like the widow’s two coins?

days.title: Gethsemane and the Arrest
days.intro: A woman anoints Jesus at Bethany, and Judas agrees to betray him. At the Passover meal Jesus gives his body and blood. He prays in agony in Gethsemane, is arrested, and stands before the high priest while Peter denies him three times.
days.question: When have you, like Peter, found it hard to stand with Jesus in front of others?

days.title: The Cross and the Empty Tomb
days.intro: Pilate hands Jesus over to be crucified. Simon of Cyrene carries the cross, and a Roman centurion confesses him the Son of God. Joseph of Arimathea buries him. On the first day of the week, the women find the tomb empty and hear that he is risen.
days.question: What does the empty tomb change about the way you face loss or fear?

days.title: Two Births Foretold
days.intro: Luke begins with two promised births. Gabriel announces John’s birth to Zechariah in the temple, then Jesus’ birth to Mary in Nazareth. Mary visits Elizabeth and sings the Magnificat. John is born, and Zechariah, his voice restored, praises God in the Benedictus.
days.question: Where is God asking for your yes, as he asked Mary?

days.title: The Birth of Jesus
days.intro: Jesus is born in Bethlehem and laid in a manger, and shepherds come to see him. Simeon and Anna recognize him in the temple. At twelve he is found among the teachers. Years later John preaches repentance and baptizes Jesus, and Luke traces his family line.
days.question: Like Mary, what do you need to ponder quietly in your heart right now?

days.title: Nazareth and the Great Catch
days.intro: After forty days of temptation in the desert, Jesus reads from Isaiah in the Nazareth synagogue, and his hometown rejects him. He heals many in Capernaum, fills Peter’s nets with fish, cleanses a leper, forgives and heals a paralyzed man, and calls Levi.
days.question: Where might Jesus be asking you to put out into deeper water?

days.title: The Sermon on the Plain
days.intro: Jesus chooses the Twelve and teaches blessings and woes, love of enemies, and mercy without measure. He heals a centurion’s servant, raises a widow’s son at Nain, answers John’s disciples, and forgives a sinful woman who weeps at his feet.
days.question: Who is the person you find hardest to love, and how could you show them mercy?

days.title: Seed, Storm, and Transfiguration
days.intro: Jesus tells the parable of the sower, calms a storm, frees a possessed man, heals a woman, and raises Jairus’ daughter. He sends out the Twelve and feeds five thousand. Peter confesses him the Christ, and Jesus is transfigured on the mountain.
days.question: What kind of soil is your heart right now for God’s word?

days.title: The Good Samaritan
days.intro: Jesus sends out seventy-two disciples, then answers a lawyer with the parable of the Good Samaritan. Martha serves while Mary sits at his feet. He teaches the Our Father and urges persistent prayer, then confronts critics who say he casts out demons by Beelzebul.
days.question: Who has God placed along your road this week who needs you to stop?

days.title: Watchful and Ready
days.intro: Jesus warns against hypocrisy, fear, and greed, telling of a rich fool who builds bigger barns. He urges servants to stay ready for their master’s return. He calls for repentance, heals a bent woman on the sabbath, and laments over Jerusalem.
days.question: What are you storing up, and is it making you rich toward God?

days.title: Lost and Found
days.intro: At dinner Jesus teaches humility and tells of a great banquet. He counts the cost of discipleship. Then come three parables of the lost: a sheep, a coin, and a son welcomed home by his father. He ends with a shrewd steward and the rich man and Lazarus.
days.question: Which character in the story of the prodigal son do you most resemble today?

days.title: Ten Lepers and a Tax Collector
days.intro: Jesus teaches forgiveness and faith. Ten lepers are healed, but only a Samaritan returns to give thanks. He speaks of the coming kingdom, the persistent widow, and the Pharisee and the tax collector. He blesses children, meets a rich ruler, and restores a blind man’s sight.
days.question: For what gift have you forgotten to return and thank God?

days.title: Zacchaeus and the King’s Arrival
days.intro: Zacchaeus climbs a tree to see Jesus and gives half his goods to the poor. Jesus tells the parable of the pounds, enters Jerusalem to shouts of praise, weeps over the city, and cleanses the temple. Leaders challenge him with questions on taxes and resurrection.
days.question: What would change if Jesus said he was coming to your house today?

days.title: The Last Supper
days.intro: A poor widow gives all she has, and Jesus warns of Jerusalem’s fall and the end of the age. At the Last Supper he gives his body and blood, prays for Peter, and agonizes on the Mount of Olives. He is arrested, and Peter denies him.
days.question: How do you prepare your heart to receive the Eucharist?

days.title: The Cross and Emmaus
days.intro: Pilate and Herod find no guilt in Jesus, yet he is crucified. He forgives his executioners and promises paradise to a repentant thief. On Easter, two disciples walk to Emmaus with a stranger and recognize the risen Jesus in the breaking of the bread.
days.question: Where have you recognized Jesus only after he had walked beside you a while?

days.title: The Word Made Flesh
days.intro: John opens with the eternal Word who becomes flesh. John the Baptist points to the Lamb of God, and the first disciples follow. At Cana Jesus turns water into wine, then clears the temple. By night Nicodemus learns he must be born of water and the Spirit.
days.question: What would it mean for you to “come and see,” as the first disciples did?

days.title: The Woman at the Well
days.intro: At a well in Samaria, Jesus offers a woman living water, and her town comes to believe. He heals an official’s son from a distance. In Jerusalem he heals a man ill for thirty-eight years, then speaks of his work as one with the Father.
days.question: What thirst in your life are you trying to satisfy apart from God?

days.title: The Bread of Life
days.intro: Jesus feeds five thousand and walks on the sea. In Capernaum he declares that he is the bread of life and that his flesh is true food. Many disciples leave, but Peter answers, “Lord, to whom shall we go?”
days.question: What keeps you coming back to Jesus when his words are hard?

days.title: Light of the World
days.intro: At the Feast of Tabernacles, Jesus teaches in the temple and promises rivers of living water while the crowds argue over who he is. He refuses to condemn a woman caught in adultery, calls himself the light of the world, and says, “Before Abraham was, I am.”
days.question: What darkness in your life do you want to bring into Christ’s light?

days.title: The Good Shepherd
days.intro: Jesus heals a man born blind, who is questioned and finally thrown out, yet comes to believe and worship. Jesus calls himself the door of the sheep and the good shepherd who lays down his life. He says, “I and the Father are one.”
days.question: How do you recognize the Good Shepherd’s voice among all the others?

days.title: Lazarus Comes Forth
days.intro: Jesus weeps at the tomb of his friend Lazarus, then calls him out alive. The council plots to kill Jesus. Mary anoints his feet at Bethany, crowds welcome him into Jerusalem, and he speaks of the grain of wheat that must die to bear fruit.
days.question: What in you needs to die like a grain of wheat so it can bear fruit?

days.title: The Washing of Feet
days.intro: At supper Jesus washes his disciples’ feet and gives the new commandment to love as he has loved. He foretells betrayal and denial. He calls himself the way, the truth, and the life, promises the Holy Spirit, and names himself the true vine.
days.question: Whose feet is Jesus asking you to wash in your daily life?

days.title: Jesus Prays for His Own
days.intro: Jesus promises the Spirit of truth and says their sorrow will turn to joy. He prays to the Father for his disciples and for all who will believe, that they may be one. Then he is arrested, questioned by Annas and Pilate, and denied by Peter.
days.question: How can you help answer Jesus’ prayer that his followers be one?

days.title: He Is Risen
days.intro: Jesus is crowned with thorns and crucified, entrusting his mother to the beloved disciple. Mary Magdalene meets the risen Lord, and Thomas confesses, “My Lord and my God.” By the sea, Jesus asks Peter three times, “Do you love me?” and tells him to feed his sheep.
days.question: If Jesus asked you, “Do you love me?”, how would you answer today?

days.title: The Spirit Comes at Pentecost
days.intro: Jesus ascends, and the apostles choose Matthias to replace Judas. At Pentecost the Holy Spirit comes like wind and fire, Peter preaches, and about three thousand are baptized. Peter and John heal a lame man at the temple gate in Jesus’ name.
days.question: Where do you need the Holy Spirit’s courage to speak or act?

days.title: Bold Witness in Jerusalem
days.intro: Peter and John refuse to stop preaching. The believers share everything, but Ananias and Sapphira lie and fall dead. The apostles are jailed, freed by an angel, and flogged, rejoicing to suffer for Jesus. Seven men are chosen to serve, among them Stephen.
days.question: What would it cost you to speak of Jesus more openly?

days.title: Stephen and Philip
days.intro: Stephen retells Israel’s history before the council and is stoned, praying for his killers while young Saul looks on. Persecution scatters the believers. Philip preaches in Samaria, Peter and John lay hands on the converts, and Philip baptizes an Ethiopian official.
days.question: Who do you need to forgive the way Stephen forgave?

days.title: Saul Meets the Risen Christ
days.intro: On the road to Damascus, Saul is blinded by the risen Christ and baptized by Ananias, then preaches Jesus boldly. Peter heals Aeneas and raises Tabitha. A vision teaches Peter that God shows no partiality, and the Spirit falls on the Gentile Cornelius and his household.
days.question: Whom have you written off that God may be calling, as he called Saul?

days.title: Peter Freed From Prison
days.intro: Peter defends baptizing Gentiles, and at Antioch believers are first called Christians. Herod kills James, the brother of John, and jails Peter, but an angel leads him out while the church prays. Then the Letter of James begins: let trials make you steadfast, and be doers of the word.
days.question: How is a trial you face now teaching you patience?

days.title: Faith That Works
days.intro: James warns against favoring the rich and insists that faith without works is dead. He shows how the tongue can bless or wound, contrasts earthly and heavenly wisdom, and calls for patience. He ends with the anointing of the sick and prayer for one another.
days.question: Where could your faith become more visible in what you do this week?

days.title: The First Missionary Journey
days.intro: The Spirit sets apart Barnabas and Saul, now called Paul. They preach in Cyprus and Pisidian Antioch, turning to the Gentiles when many reject them. At Lystra a crowd calls them gods, then stones Paul. On the way back they appoint elders in each church.
days.question: Where are you being sent, even in small ways, to share the faith?

days.title: The Council of Jerusalem
days.intro: Must Gentile believers be circumcised? The apostles and elders meet in Jerusalem, Peter and James speak, and the council sends its answer by letter. In Galatians Paul defends his gospel, recalls his call, and tells how he confronted Peter at Antioch.
days.question: How do you seek the Church’s guidance when Christians disagree?

days.title: Freedom in Christ
days.intro: Paul argues that God’s promise to Abraham comes through faith, and that the law was a guardian until Christ came. In him there is neither Jew nor Greek, slave nor free. Christ has set us free, so live by the Spirit and bear its fruit.
days.question: Which fruit of the Spirit do you most want to grow in you?

days.title: The Gospel Reaches Europe
days.intro: Paul closes Galatians: bear one another’s burdens, and glory only in the cross. In Acts, a vision calls him to Macedonia. Lydia is baptized at Philippi, and a jailer is converted after an earthquake. Paul preaches in Thessalonica, Berea, and Athens.
days.question: Whose burden could you help carry this week?

days.title: Corinth and Thessalonica
days.intro: Paul works with Priscilla and Aquila in Corinth and stays a year and a half, and Apollos begins preaching. Writing to the Thessalonians, Paul thanks God for their faith, recalls his gentle care, urges holiness, and comforts them about those who have died.
days.question: Who has nurtured your faith, and how might you thank them?

days.title: Waiting for the Lord
days.intro: The day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night, so stay awake, rejoice always, and pray without ceasing. In Second Thessalonians Paul corrects those who think that day has already come and tells idle believers to work quietly.
days.question: What would praying without ceasing look like in your ordinary day?

days.title: Riot in Ephesus
days.intro: In Ephesus Paul baptizes disciples who then receive the Spirit, and former magicians burn their books. Silversmiths who make shrines of Artemis start a riot. At Troas young Eutychus falls from a window and is restored. Paul says a tearful farewell to the Ephesian elders.
days.question: What might you need to give up, as the Ephesians burned their books?

days.title: The Wisdom of the Cross
days.intro: Paul writes to a church split into factions behind favorite preachers. The cross looks like foolishness, yet it is God’s power and wisdom. Paul and Apollos only plant and water, and God gives the growth. The community is God’s temple.
days.question: Where are you tempted to boast in yourself rather than in God?

days.title: Bodies, Marriage, and Idols
days.intro: Paul confronts a case of incest and lawsuits among believers. The body is a temple of the Holy Spirit, so flee immorality. He gives counsel on marriage and virginity, and on food offered to idols: knowledge puffs up, but love builds up.
days.question: How does treating your body as a temple of the Spirit change your choices?

days.title: The Lord’s Supper
days.intro: Paul gives up his rights for the gospel and runs to win an imperishable crown. He warns from Israel’s desert story and teaches that the cup and bread are a sharing in Christ. He hands on the Lord’s Supper and warns against receiving unworthily.
days.question: How do you examine yourself before receiving the Body and Blood of Christ?

days.title: The Greatest Is Love
days.intro: There are many gifts but one Spirit, and many members but one body. Without love, even the greatest gifts are nothing. Love is patient and kind and never ends. Paul asks that prophecy and tongues build up the whole church and be done in good order.
days.question: Which line of Paul’s hymn to love most challenges you today?

days.title: Christ Is Risen
days.intro: Paul hands on the core of the gospel: Christ died, was buried, and rose, appearing to many. If Christ is not raised, faith is in vain. But he is the firstfruits, and our bodies will be raised imperishable. Paul closes with the collection and greetings.
days.question: How does hope in the resurrection shape the way you live now?

days.title: Treasure in Clay Jars
days.intro: Paul praises the God of all comfort and explains his changed travel plans. He urges forgiveness for one who sinned. As ministers of a new covenant, believers reflect the Lord’s glory. We carry this treasure in clay jars, afflicted but not crushed.
days.question: How has God shown his strength through your weakness?

days.title: Ambassadors for Christ
days.intro: Paul longs for our heavenly dwelling and calls believers a new creation, entrusted with the ministry of reconciliation. He opens his heart to the Corinthians, rejoices that his hard letter led to repentance, and urges a generous gift for Jerusalem: God loves a cheerful giver.
days.question: Where is God asking you to be an agent of reconciliation?

days.title: Strength in Weakness
days.intro: Paul defends his ministry against rivals who boast. He lists his sufferings, tells of being caught up to the third heaven, and speaks of a thorn in the flesh. Christ tells him, “My grace is sufficient for you, for power is made perfect in weakness.”
days.question: What thorn in your life might become a place of grace?

days.title: All Have Sinned
days.intro: Paul is not ashamed of the gospel, the power of God for salvation. Gentiles who suppressed the truth and Jews who had the law alike stand in need of mercy, for all have sinned. Now God’s righteousness comes through faith in Jesus Christ.
days.question: How do you respond to the truth that you need God’s mercy?

days.title: Where Grace Abounds
days.intro: Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness. Justified by faith, we have peace with God. Where sin abounded, grace abounded more. In baptism we die and rise with Christ. Paul describes the struggle within: I do not do the good I want.
days.question: What struggle within you do you need to hand over to Christ?

days.title: Nothing Can Separate Us
days.intro: Those in Christ are not condemned. The Spirit makes us children of God who cry, “Abba, Father,” and helps us in our weakness. All things work together for good for those who love God, and nothing can separate us from his love. Then Paul grieves for Israel.
days.question: What fear would loosen its grip if you trusted that nothing can separate you from God’s love?

days.title: A Living Sacrifice
days.intro: Faith comes from hearing, and all who call on the Lord will be saved. Paul uses an olive tree to show that God has not rejected Israel. Then he urges: offer yourselves as a living sacrifice, use your gifts, love sincerely, and overcome evil with good.
days.question: What part of your life have you not yet offered to God?

days.title: Welcome One Another
days.intro: Paul asks the strong not to despise the weak over food or feast days, but to build each other up. Christ welcomed us, so we should welcome one another. Paul shares his plans to visit Rome and Spain and greets many coworkers by name, including Phoebe, Prisca, and Aquila.
days.question: Whom do you need to welcome more warmly, as Christ welcomed you?

days.title: Paul Arrested in Jerusalem
days.intro: Despite warnings, Paul goes up to Jerusalem. A mob seizes him in the temple, and Roman soldiers rescue him. He tells the story of his conversion and claims his Roman citizenship. Before the council he divides Pharisees and Sadducees, and a plot sends him to Caesarea.
days.question: When have you kept going though you knew hardship was ahead?

days.title: Paul Before Governors and King
days.intro: In Caesarea Paul defends himself before the governor Felix, who leaves him in prison for two years. Before Festus he appeals to Caesar. To King Agrippa he tells again of meeting Christ, and Agrippa says Paul has almost persuaded him to be a Christian.
days.question: Whom do you know who is almost persuaded, and how can you pray for them?

days.title: Shipwreck and Rome
days.intro: Paul sails for Rome under guard. A violent storm wrecks the ship, but Paul encourages everyone, and all reach shore on Malta. He survives a viper’s bite and heals the sick. At last in Rome, he lives under guard and preaches the kingdom of God openly.
days.question: How have you seen God bring you safely through a storm?

days.title: One Body, One Spirit
days.intro: Paul blesses God, who chose us in Christ before the foundation of the world. Saved by grace through faith, Jews and Gentiles are made one, the wall between them broken down. Paul prays they may know Christ’s love and urges unity: one Lord, one faith, one baptism.
days.question: How can you help keep the unity of the Spirit where you live and worship?

days.title: The Armor of God
days.intro: Paul urges walking as children of light and compares marriage to Christ’s love for the Church. He addresses children, parents, servants, and masters, then describes the armor of God. Philippians opens with thanks: for me to live is Christ, and to die is gain.
days.question: Which piece of God’s armor do you most need today?

days.title: The Mind of Christ
days.intro: Paul quotes a hymn to Christ, who emptied himself and became obedient unto death on a cross. He praises Timothy and Epaphroditus, counts all things loss compared to knowing Christ, and urges joy: rejoice in the Lord always, and do not be anxious.
days.question: What worries could you hand to God in prayer with thanksgiving today?

days.title: Christ Above All
days.intro: Paul presents Christ as the image of the invisible God, firstborn of all creation, and head of the body, the Church. He warns against empty philosophies and man-made rules. Raised with Christ, believers seek the things above and put on compassion, kindness, and love.
days.question: What would it mean for you to set your mind on things above?

days.title: A Brother, Not a Slave
days.intro: Paul asks Philemon to welcome back Onesimus, a slave who had left him, as a beloved brother. Then he writes to Timothy at Ephesus: guard sound teaching, pray for all people, choose worthy bishops and deacons, and let no one despise your youth.
days.question: Who do you need to see with fresh eyes, as a brother or sister?

days.title: Guidance for Pastors
days.intro: Paul counsels Timothy on caring for widows, honoring elders, and the danger of loving money: godliness with contentment is great gain. To Titus in Crete he describes good elders and urges sound teaching and good works, for the grace of God has appeared.
days.question: Where could you practice more contentment with what you have?

days.title: I Have Kept the Faith
days.intro: Writing from prison, Paul tells Timothy to stir up the gift of God, guard the truth, and endure hardship like a good soldier. All Scripture is inspired by God. Near the end, Paul says he has fought the good fight, finished the race, and kept the faith.
days.question: What gift of God in you needs stirring up again?

days.title: Jesus Our High Priest
days.intro: God once spoke through prophets but now speaks through his Son, greater than the angels and greater than Moses. Do not harden your hearts, but enter God’s rest. Jesus is a high priest who can sympathize with our weakness, tested in every way yet without sin.
days.question: What weakness can you bring to Jesus, knowing he understands it?

days.title: A Priest Like Melchizedek
days.intro: The author urges readers on to maturity and steadfast hope, an anchor for the soul. Jesus is a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek. He mediates a new covenant and enters the true sanctuary with his own blood, once for all.
days.question: Where do you need hope to be an anchor for your soul right now?

days.title: The Heroes of Faith
days.intro: Christ’s one sacrifice does what the old offerings could not. So hold fast, do not neglect meeting together, and endure. Then comes a roll call of faith: Abel, Noah, Abraham, Sarah, Moses, Rahab, and many more, who trusted God’s promises without yet seeing them fulfilled.
days.question: Which hero of faith in this chapter speaks most to your own journey?

days.title: Run the Race
days.intro: Surrounded by a cloud of witnesses, run with perseverance, eyes fixed on Jesus. God disciplines those he loves. Show hospitality and remember prisoners, for Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today, and forever. First Peter begins with a living hope and a call to holiness.
days.question: What weight do you need to lay aside to run your race well?

days.title: Living Stones
days.intro: Believers are living stones built into a spiritual house, a royal priesthood. Peter urges good conduct among unbelievers, patience under unjust suffering after Christ’s example, and readiness to explain your hope. Elders must shepherd the flock willingly. Cast your cares on God.
days.question: How would you explain the reason for your hope to someone who asked?

days.title: Guard Against False Teachers
days.intro: Peter urges growth in virtue and recalls the Transfiguration he witnessed. He warns of false teachers and scoffers who mock Christ’s return: with the Lord a day is like a thousand years. Jude likewise urges believers to contend for the faith and keep themselves in God’s love.
days.question: Which virtue from Peter’s list do you most want to grow in?

days.title: God Is Love
days.intro: John writes of what he has seen and touched: the Word of life. God is light, and if we confess our sins he forgives. Do not love the world. Test the spirits. Love one another, for love is from God, and God is love.
days.question: How has someone shown you God’s love in a concrete way?

days.title: The Vision on Patmos
days.intro: John ends his letter on the faith that overcomes the world, and his two short notes urge truth, love, and hospitality. Revelation opens on Patmos with a vision of the risen Christ among seven lampstands, then messages to Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamum, and Thyatira.
days.question: Have you, like the church at Ephesus, left the love you had at first?

days.title: The Lamb and the Seals
days.intro: Christ speaks to Sardis, Philadelphia, and lukewarm Laodicea: “I stand at the door and knock.” John sees God’s throne, worshiped day and night. Only the Lamb who was slain can open the scroll. As he breaks the seals, a great multitude stands in white robes.
days.question: Where is Christ knocking at the door of your heart?

days.title: The Woman and the Dragon
days.intro: Trumpets sound and plagues fall, yet many refuse to repent. John eats a little scroll, and two witnesses prophesy, are killed, and rise. A woman clothed with the sun bears a child, and a dragon wars against her. Two beasts rise to deceive the world.
days.question: Where do you need to stand firm against what the world worships?

days.title: The Fall of Babylon
days.intro: The Lamb stands on Mount Zion with the redeemed, and angels proclaim the eternal gospel and the harvest of the earth. Seven bowls of God’s wrath are poured out. A great harlot rides a beast, and Babylon, the proud city, falls while merchants mourn.
days.question: What in your life rests on Babylon’s values rather than God’s?

days.title: All Things New
days.intro: Heaven rejoices at the marriage supper of the Lamb. Christ rides out as Faithful and True, Satan is bound, and the dead are judged. Then John sees a new heaven and a new earth, the holy city where God wipes away every tear. Come, Lord Jesus.
days.question: What tears do you long for God to wipe away?

courses.title: Catechism in a Year
courses.summary: What the Church believes, a few paragraphs a day
courses.intro: Walk through the whole Catechism of the Catholic Church in a year: what we believe, how we celebrate it in the sacraments, how we live it, and how we pray. Each day Pax sums up a few paragraphs in plain words, shows the Scripture they rest on, and links to the full text on vatican.va. Start any day, at your own pace.

days.title: Made to Know and Love God
days.summary: The Catechism opens with the big picture. God, perfectly happy in himself, freely created us to share his own blessed life. He seeks us out, gathers scattered people into one family, the Church, and through his Son invites us in the Holy Spirit to become his adopted children. Jesus sent the apostles to teach all nations (Matthew 28:19–20), and believers have handed on that faith ever since. This handing on is called catechesis: the Church’s work of forming disciples. These paragraphs also trace how catechisms arose, from the Council of Trent to the Second Vatican Council and the 1985 synod of bishops that asked for this one.
days.question: What first drew you to want to know God better?

days.title: The Catechism’s Purpose and Plan
days.summary: Here the Catechism explains what it is for. It gathers the essentials of Catholic belief and moral life into one ordered whole, drawing on Scripture, the Church Fathers, the liturgy and the Church’s teaching, read in light of the Second Vatican Council. It is written first for bishops, the chief teachers of the faith, and through them for catechists and all the faithful. It rests on four pillars: the Creed we profess, the sacraments we celebrate, the life in Christ we live through the commandments, and the prayer we pray, above all the Our Father. Saint Paul joins believing in the heart with confessing aloud (Romans 10:9).
days.question: Which of the four pillars (belief, sacraments, moral life, prayer) feels weakest in your life right now?

days.title: How to Read the Catechism
days.summary: These paragraphs are a user’s guide. Numbers in the margin point to related passages elsewhere, so a reader can follow a theme across the whole book. Smaller print marks historical notes, explanations, and quotations from the Fathers, saints, liturgy and councils. Short In Brief sections sum up each unit in compact statements that are easy to remember. The Catechism does not try to fit its teaching to every culture, age or situation; that work belongs to local catechisms and to those who teach. It closes this introduction by naming the goal of all teaching: love, which outlasts everything else (see 1 Corinthians 13:8).
days.question: How might today’s study lead you toward love and not just knowledge?

days.title: Our Desire for God
days.summary: Faith answers a God who speaks first, but the Catechism starts with us. The longing for God is written into the human heart, because we were made by God and for him. People of every age have sought him; Paul told the Athenians that God is not far from any of us (Acts 17:27). Yet we can forget or flee him, as Adam hid and Jonah ran. Reason can still find God through the order and beauty of the world (Romans 1:20) and through the human person: conscience, freedom and a longing for the infinite. These are not lab proofs but converging arguments.
days.question: Where do you notice a restlessness in yourself that only God could satisfy?

days.title: Knowing and Naming God
days.summary: The Church teaches that human reason, by its own natural light, can know with certainty that God exists, starting from the things he made. That capacity matters, because without it we could not even receive God’s word. Still, wounded by sin and easily distracted, reason struggles, so God’s revelation helps everyone know even basic religious and moral truths clearly and without error. Because reason is shared by all, Christians can talk about God with anyone. Our words for God begin with creatures, whose goodness and beauty reflect him (Wisdom 13:5). They truly reach him, yet he always exceeds them, so our language must keep being purified.
days.question: What image of God have you held that might need purifying?

days.title: God Comes to Meet Us
days.summary: A short summary closes the first chapter: human beings are religious by nature, made for communion with God, and able to reach certainty that he exists by attending to creation and conscience. Our words for God really refer to him, though they never capture him fully. Then Chapter Two turns a corner. Reason can know that God is, but there is a whole other order of knowledge we could never reach on our own: divine Revelation, God freely making himself known. Out of love he discloses his hidden plan of goodness, prepared from all eternity in Christ and fully revealed in sending his Son and the Holy Spirit.
days.question: What is one thing about God you could never have figured out on your own?

days.title: God’s Plan of Loving Goodness
days.summary: Out of goodness and wisdom, God chose to reveal himself and his saving will (Ephesians 1:9): that through Christ, in the Holy Spirit, we might come to the Father and share in his own life. He did this gradually, through deeds and words bound together, like a teacher preparing a student step by step. From the beginning he showed himself to our first parents. Even after their sin he did not abandon them but promised redemption (Genesis 3:15, often called the first announcement of the Gospel). After the flood he made a covenant with Noah and the nations, a patient plan to save humanity part by part.
days.question: How has God been patient with you, teaching you step by step?

days.title: Abraham, Israel and the Prophets
days.summary: The covenant with Noah stands until the Gospel reaches all nations, and Scripture honors holy people outside Israel such as Abel, Melchizedek, Noah, Daniel and Job. Then God calls Abram from his homeland and makes him Abraham, father of many nations, promising that all peoples will be blessed in him (Genesis 12:1–3). His descendants carry that promise; Paul pictures them as the root onto which the Gentiles are grafted (Romans 11:17–18). Through Moses God frees Israel, gives the Law and forms a priestly people. The prophets announce a new covenant written on hearts (Jeremiah 31:31–34). Holy women like Sarah, Hannah and Esther kept hope alive, and Mary most purely.
days.question: Who in your family or parish has kept hope alive for you?

days.title: Christ, the Father’s Final Word
days.summary: God once spoke through the prophets in many ways, but now he has spoken through his Son (Hebrews 1:1–2). Jesus is the Father’s complete and final Word; in him God has said everything. So no new public revelation will come before Christ returns in glory. Revelation is complete, yet the Church keeps growing in her grasp of it over the centuries. Private revelations, such as approved apparitions, can help believers live the Gospel in a particular age, but they add nothing to it and are not part of the deposit of faith. Any claimed revelation that tries to surpass or correct Christ cannot be accepted. A summary follows.
days.question: Do you look for God’s word more in extraordinary signs or in Jesus himself?

days.title: Handing On the Gospel
days.summary: God wants everyone to be saved and to come to the truth, who is Christ (1 Timothy 2:4; John 14:6). So Christ sent the apostles to preach the Gospel to all nations (Matthew 28:19–20). They passed it on in two ways: by spoken word, example and the institutions they set up, and in writing, as they and their companions, inspired by the Holy Spirit, put the message into books. To keep the Gospel whole and alive, the apostles left bishops as their successors. This living handing on, carried out in the Holy Spirit, is called Tradition. Through it God keeps speaking with the Church, the bride of his Son.
days.question: Who handed the faith on to you, and how are you handing it on?

days.title: Scripture, Tradition, Magisterium
days.summary: Tradition and Scripture flow from one divine source and move toward the same goal. Scripture is God’s word in writing; Tradition carries the word entrusted to the apostles. So the Church does not draw her certainty from Scripture alone, and she honors both with equal reverence. Local customs and devotions, unlike apostolic Tradition, can change. The deposit of faith, everything God revealed for our salvation, was entrusted to the whole Church (2 Timothy 1:12–14). Authentic interpretation belongs to the Magisterium, the teaching office of the bishops in communion with the Pope, which serves God’s word and does not stand above it. Whoever hears the apostles hears Jesus (Luke 10:16).
days.question: How do you tend to receive the Church’s teaching: with suspicion, trust or curiosity?

days.title: Dogma and the Sense of Faith
days.summary: The Magisterium uses its full authority when it defines a dogma: a truth of Revelation, or one closely tied to it, that believers are bound to hold with faith. Dogmas are like lights on the road that keep our way safe, and an honest life opens us to receive them (John 8:31–32). Not all truths are equally central; they are ordered around the mystery of Christ. All the baptized share in understanding the faith, since the Spirit anoints and guides them (John 16:13); when the whole people agrees in belief, it does not err. Understanding grows as believers ponder, as Mary did (Luke 2:19). Scripture, Tradition and Magisterium stand together.
days.question: Which teaching of the Church has become a light for you rather than a burden?

days.title: God Speaks in Human Words
days.summary: A summary recalls the last article: the apostles handed on what Christ gave them; Scripture and Tradition form one sacred deposit of God’s word; the whole people of God keeps receiving it more deeply; and authentic interpretation belongs to the Pope and bishops. Then the Catechism turns to Scripture itself. God speaks to us in human language, much as the eternal Word took on human flesh. Through all the many words of the Bible, God is really saying one Word, his Son (Hebrews 1:1–3; John 1:1). That is why the Church reveres the Scriptures as she reveres the Lord’s Body, and finds in them food and strength.
days.question: How could you approach the Bible this week as a word spoken to you?

days.title: Inspired and True
days.summary: God is the author of Scripture because he inspired its human writers. They were real authors, yet God worked in and through them so that they wrote what he wanted. The books therefore teach faithfully and without error the truth God wished to record for our salvation (2 Timothy 3:16). Christianity is not a religion of a book but of the living Word, Jesus, who opens minds to understand the Scriptures (Luke 24:45). To read well, we look for what the human authors meant, paying attention to their times, cultures and kinds of writing, and we read in the light of the same Spirit who inspired them.
days.question: What helps you hear the living Word and not just read a text?

days.title: Reading Scripture with the Church
days.summary: The Catechism gives three guides for reading Scripture in the Spirit. First, attend to the unity of the whole Bible, whose center is Christ; the risen Jesus showed the disciples on the road to Emmaus how all the Scriptures spoke of him (Luke 24:25–27). Second, read within the living Tradition of the whole Church. Third, respect the analogy of faith, the way the truths of faith fit together. Scripture has a literal sense and a spiritual sense. The spiritual sense has three parts: allegorical (pointing to Christ), moral (guiding how we act) and anagogical (pointing to heaven). Scholars help, but the Church judges finally.
days.question: Where has a Bible passage spoken to you on more than one level?

days.title: The Canon and the Gospels
days.summary: Through the apostolic Tradition, the Church discerned which books belong in the Bible. This list is called the canon: 46 books of the Old Testament and 27 of the New. The Old Testament is truly inspired and keeps lasting value; the old covenant has never been revoked, and the Church has always rejected the idea of discarding it. The New Testament sets out the final truth of Revelation, centered on Jesus (Romans 1:16). The four Gospels are its heart, because they are our main source for his life and teaching. They took shape in three stages: Jesus’ own life and words, the apostles’ preaching, and the written Gospels.
days.question: Which Gospel do you know least, and could you spend some time with it?

days.title: One Plan in Two Testaments
days.summary: The four Gospels hold a unique place. The two Testaments form one plan. Through typology, the Church sees events of the Old Testament as foreshadowing what God fulfilled in Christ (Hebrews 10:1), much as the crossing of the sea points ahead to Baptism. The Old Testament keeps its own value; Jesus himself affirmed its great commandment of love (Mark 12:29–31). As Saint Augustine saw, the New lies hidden in the Old. Scripture is strength and food for the soul, so all the faithful should read it often. As Saint Jerome warned, not knowing Scripture means not knowing Christ.
days.question: What Old Testament story helps you understand Jesus better?

days.title: Scripture in Brief
days.summary: This summary gathers the article on Scripture. All of Scripture is really one book, because it all speaks of Christ and finds its fulfillment in him. Because God inspired the human authors, the Bible is truly his word and teaches his saving truth without error. Reading it rightly means asking what God wants to reveal through its authors, with the help of the Spirit who inspired it. The Church accepts 46 Old Testament books and 27 New Testament books, with the Gospels at the center. The two Testaments shed light on each other. Like the Eucharist, Scripture nourishes the whole Christian life, a lamp for our steps (Psalm 119:105).
days.question: What would help Scripture become a daily lamp for you rather than an occasional visitor?

days.title: The Obedience of Faith
days.summary: In Revelation the invisible God speaks to us as friends, as he did with Moses (Exodus 33:11). The fitting answer is faith, which Paul calls the obedience of faith (Romans 1:5). To obey in this sense, from a Latin word meaning to listen, is to freely accept a word because God, who is truth itself, guarantees it. Abraham is the model: he set out without knowing where he was going, trusted the promise of a son, and was ready even to offer Isaac (Hebrews 11:8–19). Mary embodies faith most perfectly. She believed nothing is impossible with God, and her faith held firm even at the cross.
days.question: Where is God asking you to set out without knowing exactly where you will go?

days.title: Faith as Gift and Free Act
days.summary: Faith is first a personal bond with God and, with it, assent to all he has revealed. We believe in God, in his Son Jesus, and in the Holy Spirit, who alone enables us to confess that Jesus is Lord (1 Corinthians 12:3). Faith is a grace, a gift God gives, as Jesus told Peter after his confession (Matthew 16:17). Yet it is also a truly human act that respects our freedom and reason. We believe on God’s authority, and he adds signs such as miracles, prophecy and the Church’s holiness so that faith is reasonable, not blind. Faith is certain, and it seeks to understand ever more (Ephesians 1:18).
days.question: What question about your faith would you most like to understand more deeply?

days.title: Faith That Lasts
