days.summary: Faith and science cannot truly conflict, since the same God gives both reason and Revelation. No one may be forced to believe; Christ invited people to the truth but never coerced them (John 18:37). Faith is necessary for salvation (Mark 16:16). It can also be lost, so we nourish it with God’s word, ask for more of it (Luke 17:5), and let it work through love (Galatians 5:6), since faith without works is dead (James 2:26). Faith already tastes the vision of heaven, though for now we walk by faith, not by sight (2 Corinthians 5:7). And faith is never solitary: each believer is a link in a long chain.
days.question: What practice helps your faith stay alive when it feels weak?

days.title: The Faith of the Church
days.summary: The Church believes first, and her faith carries and feeds ours. At Baptism we ask the Church for faith, and she gives it. That is why we call her our mother and teacher, though salvation comes from God alone. We believe not in formulas but in the realities they express; still, the Church’s words help us hold and share the faith, and she guards Christ’s words faithfully. Across many languages and cultures the Church confesses one faith, received from one Lord and sealed in one Baptism (Ephesians 4:4–6). Saint Irenaeus marveled that the Church, scattered across the world, speaks this faith as if with one voice.
days.question: When your own faith felt thin, how did the Church’s faith carry you?

days.title: Faith in Brief
days.summary: This summary gathers the teaching on faith. Faith is the whole person, mind and will, giving themselves to God who reveals himself. To believe is to trust God and accept all the truth he has made known. Faith is a supernatural gift, meaning one beyond our natural powers, yet it is also a free human act. It is necessary for salvation and is already the beginning of eternal life. We believe because God, who cannot deceive, has spoken. And we believe with the Church, whose single faith we profess together. The Catechism then prepares to unfold that faith article by article through the Creed.
days.question: Which line of this summary on faith speaks most to where you are now?

days.title: Creeds: Symbols of Faith
days.summary: To say I believe is to join what we believe together, and that needs a shared language. From the start the Church summed up her faith in short statements, such as confessing that Jesus is Lord (Romans 10:9), and later in fuller summaries for those preparing for Baptism. These are called creeds, from the Latin credo, I believe. They are also called symbols: in Greek a symbolon was half of a broken object, matched with the other half to prove identity. A creed is a sign of recognition among believers. Rooted in Baptism in the name of the Trinity (Matthew 28:19), it has three parts, traditionally counted as twelve articles.
days.question: When you recite the Creed at Mass, which line do you mean most?

days.title: The Apostles’ and Nicene Creeds
days.summary: Over the centuries the Church has produced many creeds, from councils and popes, and none of them is outdated. Two stand out. The Apostles’ Creed is a faithful summary of the apostles’ faith and the ancient baptismal creed of the Church of Rome. The Nicene Creed, more fully the Niceno-Constantinopolitan Creed, comes from the first two ecumenical councils in 325 and 381 and is still shared by East and West. The Catechism follows the Apostles’ Creed, filling it out with the Nicene. Saint Ambrose called the Creed a treasure of the soul. It begins with God the Father, because God is the beginning and end of all things.
days.question: Could you pray the Apostles’ Creed slowly today, pausing on each phrase?

days.title: I Believe in One God
days.summary: The first line of the Creed is the most basic, and every other article depends on it. God revealed himself to Israel as the only God. Moses taught the people that the Lord is one and must be loved with all their heart (Deuteronomy 6:4–5), and Jesus repeated this as the first commandment (Mark 12:29–30). Confessing Jesus as Lord does not divide this one God. God also gave his name. At the burning bush he revealed himself to Moses as the God of the patriarchs and as I AM WHO AM (Exodus 3:14). The name reveals God yet points to a mystery beyond us.
days.question: What does it mean for you that God has a name and can be called upon?

days.title: Holy, Merciful, Unchanging God
days.summary: God’s name shows he is faithful across generations. Before his holiness people sense their smallness: Moses removes his sandals, and Peter, after the great catch of fish, begs Jesus to leave him, a sinful man (Luke 5:8). Yet God’s holiness draws near to save. Out of reverence Israel did not speak the divine name and said Lord instead. After the golden calf, God revealed himself to Moses as merciful and gracious, rich in kindness and faithfulness (Exodus 34:6). Jesus showed that he too bears the divine name (John 8:28). God alone simply is, without beginning or end, and he does not change (James 1:17).
days.question: When have you felt both your own smallness and God’s mercy at the same time?

days.title: God Is Truth and Love
days.summary: God is truth itself. His words can be trusted completely (2 Samuel 7:28), and the order of creation reflects his wisdom. Jesus came to bear witness to the truth (John 18:37). God is also love. Israel came to see that God chose them out of sheer love, not because of their merit. The prophets compare his love to a father’s, a mother’s and a bridegroom’s, an everlasting love (Jeremiah 31:3). The New Testament goes further: God so loved the world that he gave his Son (John 3:16), and God is love (1 John 4:8). His inner life is an eternal exchange of love among Father, Son and Spirit.
days.question: Do you find it easier to trust God’s truth or God’s love, and why?

days.title: Living as Believers in One God
days.summary: Believing in one God changes how we live. It means recognizing his greatness, since he is beyond our full understanding (Job 36:26). It means living in gratitude, asking with the psalmist how to repay the Lord for all his goodness (Psalm 116:12). It means seeing the true dignity of every person, all made in his image (Genesis 1:26). It means using created things well and letting go of whatever pulls us from God (Matthew 5:29–30). And it means trusting him in every situation, as Saint Teresa of Avila taught: let nothing disturb you, for God alone is enough. A brief summary closes the paragraph.
days.question: Is God inviting you to grow in gratitude, trust or detachment?

days.title: The Mystery of the Trinity
days.summary: Christians are baptized in the name, not names, of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit (Matthew 28:19), because there is one God. The Trinity is the central mystery of Christian faith and life, the mystery of God’s own inner life, and it sheds light on every other truth. The Fathers distinguished theology, God’s inner life, from the economy, his works in creation and salvation; his works show who he is, and who he is explains his works. The Trinity is a mystery in the strict sense, known only because God revealed it. Even before Christ, Israel called God Father, protector of orphans (Psalm 68:6).
days.question: How does knowing you were baptized into the life of the Trinity change how you pray?

days.title: Father, Son and Spirit Revealed
days.summary: Calling God Father speaks of origin and authority, and also of loving care, which Scripture sometimes pictures as a mother’s tenderness (Psalm 131:2). God is neither man nor woman; he is pure spirit and surpasses every human parent. Jesus revealed something new: God is eternally Father in relation to his only Son. The apostles confess Jesus as the Word (John 1:1) and the image of the invisible God (Colossians 1:15), and the Council of Nicaea taught that the Son is one in being with the Father. Jesus also revealed the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete or helper (John 14:26), a distinct divine person.
days.question: Which person of the Trinity do you find yourself praying to least?

days.title: One God in Three Persons
days.summary: The Latin Creed says the Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, a phrase called the filioque; the East prefers to say the Spirit proceeds from the Father through the Son (John 15:26). Understood rightly, the two express the same faith in complementary ways. From the start the Church’s faith in the Trinity was lived in Baptism and prayer (Ephesians 4:4–6). To explain it, councils gave special meanings to words like substance, person and relation. The dogma holds three truths: there is one God, not three; the Father, Son and Spirit are really distinct; and they are distinct by how each relates to the others.
days.question: What prayer or image helps you hold together God’s oneness and the three Persons?

days.title: The Trinity at Work
days.summary: The divine Persons are distinguished only by their relations to one another; in everything else they are one. God, perfectly happy in himself, freely chose to share his glory, destining us to become his adopted children (Ephesians 1:4–5; Romans 8:15). The three Persons act together as one, yet each in his own way: all comes from the Father, through the Son, in the Spirit. The goal of the whole plan is that we enter the unity of the Trinity, who makes a home in those who love Christ (John 14:23).
days.question: How might you welcome the Trinity dwelling in you as you go through today?

days.title: God the Father Almighty
days.summary: A summary closes the teaching on the Trinity: Baptism calls us to share God’s life, and the three Persons are inseparable in what they do. Then the Creed names one attribute of God: almighty. His power is universal, since he made everything (Genesis 1:1) and does whatever he wills (Psalm 115:3); nothing is impossible for him (Luke 1:37). It is loving, because he is our Father who knows what we need (Matthew 6:32). And it is mysterious, since only faith sees it at work in weakness (2 Corinthians 12:9). He shows his might above all by forgiving sins.
days.question: Where have you seen God’s power at work in your weakness?

days.title: Power Hidden in Weakness
days.summary: God’s power is never arbitrary; in him power, wisdom, justice and goodness are one. Yet evil and suffering can make God seem absent or powerless, and this tests our faith. God answered by showing his greatest power in the humility of his Son, who freely accepted death and was raised. Christ crucified is God’s power and wisdom (1 Corinthians 1:24–25). Only faith can grasp this. Mary is its model, believing that nothing is impossible with God (Luke 1:37), and Paul could say he was able to do all things in Christ who strengthened him (Philippians 4:13). A summary adds that God shows his might above all in mercy and forgiveness.
days.question: When God has seemed silent or powerless to you, what helped you keep believing?

days.title: In the Beginning God Created
days.summary: The Bible opens with God creating the heavens and the earth (Genesis 1:1). Creation is the foundation of all God’s saving plans and the first step in a story that reaches its high point in Christ; all creation still groans as it waits to share in the freedom of God’s children (Romans 8:18–23). Where we come from and where we are going shapes how we live. Scientific discoveries about the universe should fill us with wonder at its Creator (Wisdom 7:17–22), yet science alone cannot say whether the world is ruled by chance or by a wise and good God. People have proposed other answers, such as pantheism and materialism.
days.question: What in the natural world most moves you to wonder at its Creator?

days.title: Creation, Covenant and Trinity
days.summary: Reason can know that a Creator exists, but by faith we understand that the world was made by God’s word (Hebrews 11:3). Paul told the Athenians that God made the world and gives life to all (Acts 17:24–28). For Israel, creation and covenant go together: the God who fixed the order of day and night is the one who keeps faith with his people (Jeremiah 33:25–26). The first chapters of Genesis hold a special place. Creation is the work of the whole Trinity: the Father creates through the Word, by whom all things were made (John 1:3), and through the Spirit who moved over the waters.
days.question: How does trusting God as Creator shape the way you trust his promises?

days.title: Why and How God Creates
days.summary: God created the world for his glory, not to gain anything but to show and share his goodness. Saint Irenaeus said that the glory of God is a human being fully alive. God creates freely, out of wisdom and love (Revelation 4:11), and from nothing, with no material to start from. The mother of seven martyrs trusted this (2 Maccabees 7:28), and it gives hope: the God who made all from nothing can give sinners a clean heart (Psalm 51:12) and give life to the dead (Romans 4:17). God is far above his creation, yet present within it, for in him we live and move (Acts 17:28).
days.question: Where do you need to trust that God can make something new from nothing?

days.title: God’s Providence
days.summary: God does not make the world and leave it. He holds every creature in being moment by moment (Wisdom 11:25). Creation is still on a journey toward its final perfection, and God guides it there with care; this guidance is called providence. Jesus asks us to trust like children, seeking first God’s kingdom instead of worrying about food or clothing (Matthew 6:31–33). God also gives creatures the dignity of acting as real causes. He invites people to cooperate with him and to fill and care for the earth (Genesis 1:28), yet he works within them, since apart from Christ we can do nothing (John 15:5).
days.question: What worry could you hand over to God’s providence today?

days.title: Providence and the Problem of Evil
days.summary: If God is good and all-powerful, why is there evil? Only the whole of Christian faith answers. God made a world still on its way to perfection, so physical evil exists alongside good. He made angels and people free, and they can choose wrong. God never causes moral evil, but he permits it out of respect for freedom and can draw good from it. Joseph told his brothers that God used their evil for good (Genesis 45:8; 50:20). The worst evil ever done, the killing of God’s Son, brought the greatest good, our redemption. For those who love God, all things work together for good (Romans 8:28).
days.question: Looking back, where has God drawn good out of something painful in your life?

days.title: Creation and Providence in Brief
days.summary: This summary gathers the teaching on the Creator. God alone made the universe, freely and directly, with no help; no creature has the infinite power needed to create. He made the world to show and share his glory, so that creatures might have a part in his truth, goodness and beauty. He keeps it in existence by his Word. Through his providence he guides all things toward their goal with wisdom and love, and Christ invites us to trust him as children. God lets us cooperate through our actions, prayers and sufferings. Why he permits evil remains a mystery, lit up by Christ, who died and rose to conquer it.
days.question: How could you offer today’s work, prayer or suffering as cooperation with God?

days.title: Heaven, Earth and the Angels
days.summary: The Creed calls God maker of heaven and earth, of all things seen and unseen. Heaven can mean the sky, but also God’s own dwelling and the glory of the saints, as when Jesus speaks of the Father in heaven (Matthew 5:16). Among unseen creatures are the angels, whose existence is a truth of faith. Angel names their task, messenger, not their nature, which is pure spirit. They have intelligence and will, are personal and immortal, and always behold the Father’s face (Matthew 18:10). Christ is the center of the angelic world: they were made through and for him (Colossians 1:16) and serve those who will inherit salvation (Hebrews 1:14).
days.question: How aware are you of the unseen world when you pray?

days.title: Angels in Salvation History
days.summary: Angels appear throughout salvation history: guarding paradise (Genesis 3:24), leading Israel (Exodus 23:20), feeding Elijah (1 Kings 19:5) and announcing births. Christ’s life is surrounded by them, from the shepherds’ night at his birth (Luke 2:13–14) and his time in the desert (Mark 1:13) to his agony (Luke 22:43), the empty tomb and the Ascension. They freed the apostles from prison (Acts 5:19). The Church joins their praise in the liturgy, and each believer has a guardian angel watching over them from infancy to death (Matthew 18:10). The Catechism then turns to the visible world, which God drew out of nothing and Genesis presents as a work of six days.
days.question: When could you remember to thank your guardian angel this week?

days.title: The Goodness and Order of Creation
days.summary: Every creature has its own goodness and reflects God’s wisdom, so we should respect it. God wants creatures to depend on one another: sun and moon, the cedar and the small flower, none is self-sufficient. There is also an order among creatures, with the human person at the summit; Jesus says we are worth more than many sparrows (Luke 12:7), yet God’s mercy reaches all he made (Psalm 145:9). All creatures share a bond, as Saint Francis sang in his Canticle of the Creatures. Creation ends in the Sabbath rest (Genesis 2:2), and its laws stand firm (Jeremiah 31:35–36).
days.question: How could you show respect for God’s creation in a concrete way this week?

days.title: Creation Made for Worship
days.summary: Creation was shaped with the Sabbath in view, which means it was made for the worship of God; adoration is written into the order of things. Saint Benedict asked that nothing come before the work of God, the Church’s prayer. Keeping the Sabbath stands at the heart of Israel’s law. For Christians a new day has dawned, the day of Christ’s Resurrection, sometimes called the eighth day. The seventh day completed the first creation; the eighth begins the new creation in Christ, which is greater still. A summary recalls the angels who serve God and us, the variety and goodness of creatures, and respect for the laws built into creation.
days.question: What small change could make your Sundays more centered on worship?

days.title: Made in God’s Image
days.summary: God created human beings in his image, male and female (Genesis 1:27). We hold a unique place: we bear God’s image, we join the spiritual and the material, and we are made for friendship with God. Of all visible creatures, only we can know and love our Creator, and God willed us for our own sake. Being a person means being someone, not something, able to know ourselves, give ourselves freely and enter communion with others. God made the world for us, and made us to serve and love him. Only in Christ does the mystery of humanity become clear. All people form one family with one origin (Acts 17:26).
days.question: Who in your life do you find hardest to see as made in God’s image?

days.title: Body and Soul, One Person
days.summary: God formed man from the dust and breathed into him the breath of life (Genesis 2:7). We are body and soul, yet truly one. In Scripture, soul can mean a person’s whole life, but it also names our innermost spiritual part, which no one can kill (Matthew 10:28). The body shares the dignity of God’s image and is meant to be a temple of the Spirit. Soul and body are so united that the soul is the form of the body, making it a living human body. God creates each soul directly, and it is immortal. The heart names our deepest center (Matthew 6:21).
days.question: How do you care for your body as part of your life with God?

days.title: Man and Woman Together
days.summary: Man and woman are created with equal dignity, each fully human. God is pure spirit, neither male nor female, yet both sexes reflect something of him; Scripture speaks of his love as a mother’s (Isaiah 49:15) and a father’s (Hosea 11:1–4). God said it is not good for the man to be alone (Genesis 2:18), and made them for one another, a communion of persons. In marriage they become one flesh (Genesis 2:24) and share in passing on life. They are to care for the earth as stewards, not exploit it. In the beginning they lived in friendship with God and in harmony.
days.question: How do your closest relationships reflect God’s design for communion?

days.title: Life in Paradise
days.summary: Before sin, the first man was master of himself, free from the disordered desires that now pull us toward pleasure, possessions and pride (1 John 2:16). God placed him in the garden to cultivate and care for it (Genesis 2:15), so work was not a burden but a sharing in God’s own work. All this harmony, called original justice, was lost by the sin of our first parents. A summary follows: we are made in God’s image and destined to be like his Son; body and soul form one person; man and woman are made for communion; and friendship with God was their first happiness.
days.question: How might you see today’s work as sharing in God’s care for creation?

days.title: The Reality of Sin
days.summary: God is infinitely good, yet evil is everywhere. Only in the light of Revelation can we see sin for what it is: the misuse of the freedom God gives us so we can love him. Sin is understood fully only next to Christ, who frees us from it; where sin increased, grace overflowed (Romans 5:20). Paul sets Adam beside Christ (Romans 5:12–21), and the Church holds that the teaching on original sin cannot be set aside without harming the mystery of Christ. Genesis 3 uses figurative language but tells of a real event at the dawn of human history. Behind the first sin lurks Satan, a fallen angel (Revelation 12:9).
days.question: Do you think of sin mainly as breaking rules or as refusing love?

days.title: Fallen Angels and the First Sin
days.summary: The fall of the angels was a free, radical and permanent rejection of God, echoed in the tempter’s lie that we could be like God (Genesis 3:5). The devil has been a liar from the beginning (John 8:44). His choice cannot be undone, not because God’s mercy falls short, but by its nature. He even tempted Jesus (Matthew 4:1–11), but his power is limited and cannot stop God’s kingdom. Our first parents were free, yet dependent on their Creator; the forbidden tree marks limits they were to accept with trust. Tempted, they let that trust die and disobeyed. In that sin, man chose himself over God.
days.question: Where are you tempted to want things your own way instead of trusting God?

days.title: The Wounds of Original Sin
days.summary: After the first sin, Adam and Eve lost original holiness and began to fear God (Genesis 3:10). Harmony broke within themselves, between man and woman, and with creation, and death entered the world (Romans 5:12). Sin then spread, as in Cain’s murder of Abel (Genesis 4). All humanity shares in Adam’s sin, for through one man’s disobedience many became sinners (Romans 5:19). Original sin is a mystery: it is contracted, not committed, a state and not a personal act. Human nature is not totally corrupt, but wounded, weakened and inclined to sin, which is called concupiscence. Baptism erases original sin, though the struggle against its effects remains.
days.question: Where do you notice the inner struggle between what you want and what is good?

days.title: The Battle and the Promise
days.summary: The Church sharpened this teaching against two errors: Pelagius, who thought we could live well without grace, and early Protestant reformers, who held that human nature was utterly corrupted. Since the fall the devil has a certain hold on humanity (Hebrews 2:14), and ignoring our wounded nature leads to grave mistakes. Christ is the Lamb who takes away the sin of the world (John 1:29). God did not abandon fallen humanity. Genesis 3:15 announces victory over the serpent, and tradition sees Christ as the new Adam and Mary as the new Eve. The Easter Exsultet even calls it a happy fault that won us such a Redeemer.
days.question: How does hope in Christ’s victory change the way you face your own sin?

days.title: The Fall in Brief
days.summary: This summary gathers the teaching on the fall. The devil and the other demons are angels who freely refused to serve God, and they try to draw us into their revolt. Adam lost original holiness and justice for himself and for all of us, and passed on a wounded nature: this is original sin. Its effects include ignorance, suffering, death and an inclination to sin. It is passed on with human nature itself, not by copying bad example. Yet Christ’s victory gives us more than sin took away. The world, made and kept by love, has been set free by Christ crucified and risen.
days.question: Which truth in this summary gives you the most hope?

days.title: The Good News of Jesus Christ
days.summary: When the fullness of time came, God sent his Son, born of a woman (Galatians 4:4–5). God has visited his people and kept his promises. We confess that Jesus of Nazareth, a Jew born in Bethlehem in the days of Herod, a carpenter crucified under Pontius Pilate, is the eternal Son of God made man (John 1:14). Peter confessed him as the Christ, the Son of the living God, and on that faith Christ built his Church (Matthew 16:16–18). Catechesis exists to lead people into communion with Jesus. Whoever knows him wants to share him, like Paul, who counted all else as loss beside Christ (Philippians 3:8).
days.question: How would you tell a friend, in one sentence, who Jesus is to you?

days.title: The Holy Name of Jesus
days.summary: The name Jesus means God saves. Gabriel gave it at the Annunciation, for he would save his people from their sins (Matthew 1:21). In Jesus God’s own saving name is present among us; there is no other name by which we are saved (Acts 4:12). In Israel the high priest once a year sprinkled blood on the mercy seat, the place of God’s presence, to atone for sin (Leviticus 16); now God reconciles the world to himself in Christ (2 Corinthians 5:19). Since the Resurrection, his name is above every name (Philippians 2:9–10). It lies at the heart of Christian prayer, as in the Jesus Prayer.
days.question: How might you pray the name of Jesus more slowly and reverently today?

days.title: Christ, the Anointed Son
days.summary: Christ is the Greek form of the Hebrew Messiah, meaning anointed. In Israel kings, priests and sometimes prophets were anointed for their mission, and the Messiah was to be anointed by the Spirit as king, priest and prophet (Luke 4:18). Jesus accepted the title with caution, since many expected a political ruler; he revealed himself as the Son of Man who would suffer and give his life as a ransom (Matthew 20:28). His kingship shows most clearly on the cross. Son of God could mean an adopted son, but when Peter confessed it, Jesus said the Father had revealed it (Matthew 16:16–17). Jesus spoke of his unique sonship.
days.question: Is the Messiah you hope for the one who reigns from the cross?

days.title: Son of God and Lord
days.summary: At Jesus’ baptism and Transfiguration the Father calls him his beloved Son (Matthew 3:17). At the cross a centurion confessed him as Son of God (Mark 15:39), and after the Resurrection his divine sonship shines out in power (Romans 1:4). In the Greek Old Testament, the holy name God revealed to Moses was rendered Lord. The New Testament gives this title to Jesus, confessing him as God; Thomas cried out, my Lord and my God (John 20:28). Since Jesus is Lord, no earthly power may claim our total obedience (Acts 5:29). Christian prayer is full of this title, from the Lord be with you to come, Lord Jesus (Revelation 22:20).
days.question: Which area of your life have you not yet let Jesus be Lord of?

days.title: Why the Word Became Flesh
days.summary: A summary recalls the four titles: Jesus, Christ, Son of God and Lord. Then it asks why the Word became flesh. He came to save us by reconciling us with God, who sent his Son as an offering for our sins (1 John 4:10). He came so that we might know God’s love, for God so loved the world that he gave his only Son (John 3:16). And he came to be our model of holiness: the Father says to listen to him (Mark 9:7), and Jesus invites us to learn from him (Matthew 11:29).
days.question: Which reason for the Incarnation speaks most to you today?

days.title: True God and True Man
days.summary: The Word also became flesh so that we might share in the divine nature (2 Peter 1:4); the Fathers dared to say God became man so we might share his life. In the Incarnation the Son of God took on a human nature to save us; Paul’s hymn tells of him emptying himself and taking the form of a servant (Philippians 2:6–8). Jesus is not part God and part man, but fully both. Councils defended this: Nicaea against Arius, Ephesus against Nestorius, also naming Mary Mother of God, and Chalcedon, which taught two natures in one person, like us in all things but sin (Hebrews 4:15).
days.question: What difference does it make to you that God became fully human?

days.title: Christ’s Human Mind and Will
days.summary: Everything in Christ’s humanity belongs to his divine person, so we can truly say that the Son of God suffered and died in the flesh. Jesus is one person, the eternal Son, with a real human body and a real human soul. Jesus had real human knowledge, which grew: he increased in wisdom (Luke 2:52) and asked questions to learn (Mark 6:38). Yet his human mind also knew the Father intimately and could read hearts (Mark 2:8). He has a human will and a divine will, which never conflict; in Gethsemane his human will embraced the Father’s will (Mark 14:36).
days.question: How does Jesus’ obedience in Gethsemane help you in your own hard choices?

days.title: Christ’s Body and Sacred Heart
days.summary: Because the Word took a real human body, that body had limits, and his face can be pictured. So the Second Council of Nicaea (787) affirmed that holy images of Christ are legitimate; in honoring an icon we honor the person it shows. Jesus knew and loved each of us throughout his life and Passion, and gave himself for each one (Galatians 2:20). He loved with a human heart. His Sacred Heart, pierced on the cross (John 19:34), is the chief sign of that love for the Father and for every person. A summary follows: one divine person in two natures, the one mediator.
days.question: How could an image of Christ or his Sacred Heart help your prayer this week?

days.title: Conceived by the Holy Spirit
days.summary: The Annunciation opens the fullness of time (Galatians 4:4). When Mary asked how she could conceive, since she knew no man, the angel answered that the Holy Spirit would come upon her (Luke 1:34–35). The Spirit’s mission is always joined to the Son’s: he made Mary’s womb fruitful so that she conceived the eternal Son in a humanity drawn from her own. What the Church believes about Mary rests on what she believes about Christ. God freely chose Mary, a young Jewish woman of Nazareth (Luke 1:26–27), and prepared for her through holy women like Eve, Sarah and Hannah. Gabriel greeted her as full of grace (Luke 1:28).
days.question: How can Mary’s openness to the Spirit shape your own response to God?

days.title: Immaculate Mother of God
days.summary: Over the centuries the Church saw more clearly that Mary, full of grace, was redeemed from the first moment of her conception. This is the Immaculate Conception, defined in 1854: by a unique grace, and through the merits of Christ, Mary was kept free from all stain of original sin. Her holiness comes wholly from her Son (Ephesians 1:3–4); she never sinned. At the Annunciation she gave God her free yes (Luke 1:38); as Saint Irenaeus put it, her obedience untied the knot of Eve’s disobedience. Since her son is the eternal Son, she is truly Mother of God. She conceived him by the Spirit (Matthew 1:18–25).
days.question: What would it look like to say yes to God as freely as Mary did?

days.title: Mary Ever-Virgin
days.summary: Some wonder why Mark and the letters are silent on the virginal conception. But this belief met mockery from Jews and pagans alike, so it did not grow out of the ideas of the age; its meaning opens only to faith. The Church confesses that Mary remained a virgin all her life. The brothers of Jesus in the Gospels (Mark 3:31) are understood as close relatives, a usage found in the Old Testament (Genesis 13:8). Jesus is her only son, yet she is spiritual mother of all believers (John 19:26–27). Her virginity shows that God took the initiative: Jesus has God alone as Father, and he is the new Adam.
days.question: How do you relate to Mary as a mother in your own life of faith?

days.title: Virgin and Mother
days.summary: By his virginal conception Jesus, the new Adam, begins a new kind of birth: we become God’s children not by human descent but by the Spirit (John 1:13). Mary’s virginity also signals her undivided faith and complete gift of herself to God. Saint Augustine said Mary was more blessed for believing in Christ than for conceiving him. As both virgin and mother, Mary is a picture of the Church, which receives God’s word in faith and gives birth to new children in Baptism. A summary follows: Mary is full of grace, sinless, Mother of God, ever virgin, and the new Eve.
days.question: How does Mary’s undivided heart challenge the way you give yourself to God?

days.title: Christ’s Whole Life Is Mystery
days.summary: The Creed speaks only of Jesus’ birth and his Passover, but these shed light on his whole life. The Gospels were written so that we might believe Jesus is the Christ and have life in his name (John 20:31). Everything about him, from swaddling clothes to burial cloths, was a sign of who he is. His whole life reveals the Father: whoever sees him sees the Father (John 14:9). His whole life redeems, from the poverty that makes us rich (2 Corinthians 8:9) to his rising for our justification (Romans 4:25). His whole life restores what was lost in Adam, and he lived it all for us.
days.question: Which ordinary moment of Jesus’ life do you rarely think about?

days.title: The Forerunner and the Manger
days.summary: Jesus is our model (Philippians 2:5), and he lets us live his mysteries in union with him. God prepared for his coming over centuries through the rites, symbols and prophets of Israel. John the Baptist, the last and greatest prophet, points to the Lamb of God (John 1:29) and dies a martyr (Mark 6:17–29). Jesus was born poor, and shepherds were the first to see him (Luke 2:8–20). To enter the kingdom we must become like children (Matthew 18:3). On the eighth day he was circumcised, joining Abraham’s people (Luke 2:21).
days.question: What would becoming childlike before God look like for you this week?

days.title: Epiphany and the Hidden Years
days.summary: At the Epiphany, Magi from the East follow a star to worship the newborn king (Matthew 2:1–12). They stand for the nations, who find the Savior by receiving Israel’s promise. At the Presentation, Simeon and Anna recognize Jesus as a light to the nations, and Simeon warns Mary of a sword (Luke 2:22–38). The flight into Egypt and the killing of the innocents show darkness resisting light (Matthew 2:13–18). Then come the long hidden years at Nazareth, ordinary work and family life, where Jesus obeyed Mary and Joseph and grew in wisdom (Luke 2:51–52). The finding in the temple hints at his mission. Then John baptizes him in the Jordan.
days.question: How can your ordinary routine become a place of holiness, as Nazareth was?

days.title: Baptism, Temptation and Kingdom
days.summary: At his baptism Jesus, though sinless, stands among sinners as the Lamb of God (John 1:29), already embracing the death he will call his baptism (Luke 12:50). The heavens open, the Spirit rests on him, and the Father delights in him. In Baptism we go down into the water with him and rise to new life (Romans 6:4). Then the Spirit drives him into the desert, where he resists Satan (Mark 1:12–13). Where Adam and Israel failed, he stays faithful, tested in every way yet without sin (Hebrews 4:15). Then he proclaims that the kingdom of God is at hand (Mark 1:15), gathering people; the Church is its seed.
days.question: Which temptation do you most need Jesus’ strength to resist?

days.title: Signs of the Kingdom
days.summary: The kingdom belongs to the poor and lowly. Jesus brings good news to the poor (Luke 4:18) and makes love for them a condition for entering his kingdom (Matthew 25:31–46). He calls sinners to conversion and shows them the Father’s mercy (Mark 2:17). His parables invite everyone but demand a radical choice, like selling everything for a hidden treasure (Matthew 13:44). His miracles are signs that the kingdom is present and that he is the Messiah, not tricks to satisfy curiosity. He frees people from hunger and illness, above all from sin, and drives out demons. He chose the Twelve, with Peter first among them (Matthew 16:18).
days.question: Which parable most clearly shows you what Jesus is asking of you?

days.title: The Keys and the Transfiguration
days.summary: Jesus gave Peter the keys of the kingdom and the power to bind and loose (Matthew 16:19), meaning authority to forgive sins, teach and govern the Church; after the Resurrection he told him to feed his sheep (John 21:15–17). On the mountain Jesus was transfigured before Peter, James and John; Moses and Elijah spoke of his coming departure, and the Father told them to listen to him (Luke 9:28–36). This glimpse of glory shows that the way to it passes through the cross. Jesus then set his face toward Jerusalem, wept over the city, and entered it humbly on a donkey (Matthew 21:1–11).
days.question: What glimpse of God’s glory has strengthened you for a hard road?

days.title: The Mysteries of Christ in Brief
days.summary: In summary, Christ’s disciples are to be shaped by him until he is formed in them (Galatians 4:19). No one comes to God without kneeling, like the shepherds and Magi, before the child in the manger. By his obedience and humble work at Nazareth, Jesus shows us holiness in family life and daily work. At his baptism he takes up his mission as the servant. In the desert he defeats Satan by holding fast to the Father’s plan. He begins the kingdom on earth, whose seed is the Church and whose keys are entrusted to Peter. The Transfiguration readies the apostles for the cross.
days.question: Which mystery of Christ’s life will you carry into prayer this week?

days.title: Jesus and the Law
days.summary: The Creed now turns to the heart of the Gospel: Christ’s suffering, death and rising, called the paschal mystery. On the road to Emmaus, Jesus showed that the Messiah had to suffer before entering his glory (Luke 24:26). From early on, some religious leaders opposed him, accusing him of blasphemy and even of working with demons (Mark 3:22). Yet he was not at war with every Pharisee; some warned him of danger and one scribe agreed with him on the greatest commandment. Jesus did not come to abolish the Law of Moses but to fulfill it (Matthew 5:17), and he alone kept it perfectly.
days.question: Where do you see Jesus fulfilling, not discarding, what God gave before him?

days.title: Jesus, the Law and the Temple
days.summary: Jesus taught with an authority no rabbi claimed, saying in effect, you have heard this, but I tell you more (Matthew 5). He read the Law from the inside, as its divine author. He declared all foods clean and taught that the Sabbath exists for people, so doing good on it is right. He also loved the Temple. He was presented there as a baby, found there at twelve, and drove out the merchants out of zeal for his Father’s house (John 2:16–17). He foretold its fall and spoke of his own body as the true temple, to be raised in three days (John 2:19–21).
days.question: How do you show reverence for the places where you meet God?

days.title: Jesus, Forgiveness and Faith
days.summary: What scandalized many leaders most was Jesus’ claim to do what only God does. He ate with tax collectors and sinners, and he forgave sins, which only God can do (Mark 2:7). He spoke of himself as greater than the Temple and said, before Abraham was, I am (John 8:58). To accept him meant a real change of heart, and many could not make it. Some judged him a blasphemer and condemned him (Matthew 26:65), often out of ignorance, as Jesus himself said from the cross when he prayed for their forgiveness (Luke 23:34). The section closes with a short In Brief summary.
days.question: Is there a sin you still find hard to believe God has truly forgiven?

days.title: Who Is Responsible for Jesus’ Death
days.summary: The trial of Jesus was not a simple story of one side against another. Some Jewish leaders, like Nicodemus and Joseph of Arimathea, quietly believed in him. Caiaphas argued it was better for one man to die than the nation (John 11:50), and Jesus was handed to Pilate on political charges. The Church firmly teaches that the Jewish people as a whole, then or now, cannot be blamed for his death. All sinners share the blame, and Christians who know him and still sin bear more. His death was no accident: it was part of God’s saving plan, foretold in Scripture (Acts 2:23).
days.question: How does it change your prayer to see your own sins at the foot of the cross?

days.title: Christ Died for Our Sins
days.summary: Scripture says Christ died for our sins in keeping with the Scriptures (1 Corinthians 15:3), especially Isaiah’s suffering servant. He never sinned, yet he took on our condition so fully that he could pray Psalm 22 on the cross: My God, why have you forsaken me? The initiative is God’s love. While we were still sinners, Christ died for us (Romans 5:8), and he died for every person without exception. His whole life was an offering to the Father: I have come to do your will (Hebrews 10:7). John the Baptist named him the Lamb of God (John 1:29), recalling the Passover lamb.
days.question: What does it mean to you that Christ died for you while you were still a sinner?

days.title: The Last Supper and Gethsemane
days.summary: Jesus gave his life freely; no one took it from him (John 10:18). At the Last Supper he showed this in advance by giving his body and blood to the apostles, telling them to do this in memory of him. In that act he made them priests of the New Covenant. In Gethsemane he felt the full horror of death and prayed for the cup to pass, yet he chose the Father’s will (Matthew 26:39). His death is the true Passover sacrifice and seals a new covenant in his blood. Where Adam disobeyed, Christ’s obedience makes many righteous (Romans 5:19), and he makes amends for our sins.
days.question: Where do you need to pray, not my will but yours, this week?

days.title: Sharing in Christ’s Cross
days.summary: What gives the cross its saving power is love. Jesus loved his own to the end (John 13:1), and that love embraced every human being. Because he is a divine person, his self-gift reaches all people and opens the way to justification, being made right with God. Christ is the one mediator (1 Timothy 2:5), and his sacrifice is unique. Yet he invites his followers to take up their cross and follow him (Matthew 16:24), sharing in his saving work. Mary shared in it more closely than anyone. The In Brief paragraphs then gather the teaching on his death into short statements.
days.question: What cross in your life could you unite to Christ’s today?

days.title: Buried in the Tomb
days.summary: Jesus truly died. He tasted death for everyone (Hebrews 2:9), and his body lay in the tomb. This is the mystery of Holy Saturday, God’s great Sabbath rest after finishing the work of salvation. Even in death, his soul and body, though separated, stayed united to his divine person. That is why his body did not decay, as Psalm 16 foretold and Peter preached (Acts 2:27). The third day echoes Hosea and the sign of Jonah (Matthew 12:40). Baptism lets us share this: we are buried with Christ so that we may rise with him to new life (Romans 6:4).
days.question: How can you keep a quiet Holy Saturday kind of waiting in your own life?

days.title: He Descended to the Dead
days.summary: The Creed says Christ descended into hell. Here hell means the realm of the dead, called Sheol or Hades, where all who had died waited without seeing God. He did not go to free the damned. He went to open heaven to the just who had died before him, like those resting in Abraham’s bosom (Luke 16:22). Peter writes that Christ preached even to the spirits in prison (1 Peter 3:19). This is the last stretch of his mission: the Gospel reaches every age. By dying he broke the power of the one who held death (Hebrews 2:14).
days.question: Whom among your beloved dead do you entrust to Christ’s mercy?

days.title: The Witnesses of the Resurrection
days.summary: The Resurrection is the crowning truth of our faith. It really happened in history, with witnesses Paul could name (1 Corinthians 15:3–8). The empty tomb came first, though by itself it proves nothing; the angels asked why the women looked for the living among the dead (Luke 24:5). Mary Magdalene and the holy women met the risen Jesus first, then Peter, then the Twelve and more than five hundred. The apostles were not easily convinced. They thought the women’s report was nonsense, and Thomas demanded to touch the wounds (John 20:25). Their doubts make their witness more believable.
days.question: What helps you most when doubts about the Resurrection come?

days.title: The Risen Body of Christ
days.summary: The risen Jesus was not a ghost. He let the disciples touch him and he ate with them. Yet his body was not simply brought back to ordinary life, as Lazarus was. It was glorified, free of the limits of space and time, so he could appear as he wished. Paul calls this a spiritual body (1 Corinthians 15:44). No one saw the moment of rising itself; it reaches beyond history. The whole Trinity is at work: the Father raises the Son by his power, the Spirit gives life, and the Son lays down his life and takes it up again (John 10:18).
days.question: How does the hope of a glorified body change how you treat your own body?

days.title: What the Resurrection Means
days.summary: The Resurrection confirms everything Jesus did and taught. Without it, Paul says, our faith is in vain (1 Corinthians 15:14). It fulfills the promises of Scripture and proves he is the Son of God (Psalm 2:7). By his death he frees us from sin; by rising he opens new life to us. This new life is justification, being restored to God’s grace, and adoption as God’s children. That is why the risen Jesus calls his disciples his brothers (John 20:17). His rising is also the source of our own future resurrection; he is the firstfruits (1 Corinthians 15:20). The In Brief follows.
days.question: How would you live differently if you truly believed you will rise with Christ?

days.title: The Ascension of the Lord
days.summary: Forty days after Easter, a cloud took Jesus from the apostles’ sight (Acts 1:9). During those days his glory was still veiled as he ate and spoke with them. The Ascension marks a final step: our human nature, in him, has entered God’s glory for good. No one goes up to heaven except the one who came down (John 3:13), and he goes ahead to prepare a place for us. As our high priest he lives always to intercede for us (Hebrews 7:25). Seated at the Father’s right hand, he begins the reign Daniel saw given to the Son of Man (Daniel 7:14).
days.question: What does it mean for you that Jesus is praying for you right now?

days.title: He Will Come Again in Glory
days.summary: Christ already reigns, and the Church on earth is the seed and beginning of his kingdom. But the kingdom is not yet complete. Since the Ascension we live in the last hour (1 John 2:18), a time of witness and also of trial. So the Church prays, come, Lord Jesus (Revelation 22:20), and keeps watch, like the wise virgins with their lamps (Matthew 25:1–13). No one knows the day (Mark 13:32). Before he returns, the Church will pass through a final trial and a great deception that offers false salvation. She will enter glory only by following her Lord through death to resurrection.
days.question: How do you keep watch for Christ in the ordinary days of your life?

days.title: Judgment and the Holy Spirit
days.summary: Christ will judge the living and the dead. What is hidden will be brought to light (Luke 12:2), and we will be judged by how we treated the least of his brothers (Matthew 25:40). The Father gave all judgment to the Son, yet the Son came to save, not condemn (John 3:17). Whoever refuses grace judges himself. After the In Brief, a new chapter opens on the Holy Spirit. No one can say Jesus is Lord except by the Spirit (1 Corinthians 12:3). The Spirit stirs faith in us, and he is God, worshiped and glorified with the Father and the Son.
days.question: When did you last sense the Holy Spirit stirring faith in you?

days.title: Who the Holy Spirit Is
days.summary: Only the Spirit of God knows the depths of God (1 Corinthians 2:11). He does not speak of himself, but we know him by his work in the Church: in Scripture and Tradition, in the Magisterium (the Church’s teaching office), in the sacraments, in prayer, in spiritual gifts and in the saints. The Son and the Spirit are always sent together. Jesus is the Christ, the Anointed, because the Spirit rests on him. The Spirit’s own name comes from Matthew 28:19. Jesus also calls him the Paraclete, an advocate and comforter, and the Spirit of truth (John 16:13).
days.question: Where have you noticed the Holy Spirit at work in your parish or family?

days.title: Symbols of the Holy Spirit
days.summary: Scripture uses many images for the Spirit. Water recalls Baptism and the living water Jesus promised the Samaritan woman (John 4:14). Anointing with oil points to Christ, the Anointed One, and to Confirmation. Fire, as with Elijah and the tongues at Pentecost (Acts 2:3), shows his power to transform. The cloud and light that overshadowed Sinai and Mary reveal God present yet hidden. A seal marks us as belonging to God. The laying on of hands passes on the Spirit. Jesus cast out demons by the finger of God (Luke 11:20). The dove recalls Noah and Jesus’ baptism.
days.question: Which symbol of the Spirit speaks most to you, and why?

days.title: The Spirit in the Promises
days.summary: Long before Christ, the Word and the Spirit were already at work, though hidden. The Spirit hovered over the waters at creation (Genesis 1:2) and gives life to every creature. Humanity was made in God’s image, an image marred by sin and restored in Christ. God promised Abraham that all nations would be blessed through his offspring (Genesis 12:3), and Paul sees that offspring as Christ (Galatians 3:16). God showed himself in theophanies, visible signs of his presence like the cloud and the fire. The Law acted as a tutor (Galatians 3:24), unable to save but awakening a longing for the Savior.
days.question: How has God prepared you, step by step, to receive him?

days.title: Waiting for the Messiah and Spirit
days.summary: Israel was called to be a kingdom of priests (Exodus 19:6), but kings and people often turned from God, and exile followed. Even then God stayed faithful and purified his people. The prophets spoke of something new (Isaiah 43:19): a Messiah on whom the Spirit would rest (Isaiah 11:2), a servant gentle with the bruised reed (Isaiah 42:3), and one anointed to bring good news to the poor, words Jesus read in Nazareth (Luke 4:18). They also foretold a new heart and the Spirit poured out on all people (Joel 3:1). The humble poor of Israel kept this hope alive.
days.question: What do you long for God to make new in you?

days.title: John the Baptist and Mary
days.summary: In the fullness of time, the Spirit prepared the way for Christ. John the Baptist was filled with the Spirit even before birth (Luke 1:15). He came in the spirit of Elijah to ready a people for the Lord, more than a prophet, the voice crying in the wilderness (John 1:23). He saw the Spirit descend on Jesus and pointed him out. In Mary the joint work of Son and Spirit reaches its masterpiece. The Spirit filled her with grace so she could welcome God’s Son. She is the daughter of Zion, and her song, the Magnificat, rejoices in God (Luke 1:46–55).
days.question: How might you, like John, point others toward Jesus?

days.title: The Spirit in Mary and Jesus
days.summary: Through Mary the Spirit shows the world the Son of God made flesh: to the shepherds, the Magi (Matthew 2:11), Simeon and Anna. At the cross she becomes mother of the beloved disciple and of all believers (John 19:26–27), and she prays with the apostles before Pentecost (Acts 1:14). Jesus is the Christ, anointed by the Spirit from the moment he became man. He spoke of the Spirit gradually: to Nicodemus about rebirth, to the Samaritan woman about living water. As his hour came he promised another Advocate (John 14:16). Risen, he breathed on the disciples: receive the Holy Spirit (John 20:22).
days.question: How do you let Mary bring you closer to her Son?

days.title: Pentecost and the Gifts of Love
days.summary: At Pentecost the risen Christ poured out the Spirit (Acts 2:33), and the Holy Trinity was fully revealed. God is love (1 John 4:8), and his love is poured into our hearts by the Spirit (Romans 5:5). That love is the first gift, and it contains all the others, beginning with the forgiveness of sins. The Spirit is a pledge or first installment of the glory to come. By his power we can bear the fruit of the Spirit: love, joy, peace, patience, kindness and more (Galatians 5:22). The Church’s mission is to carry on the shared mission of Christ and the Spirit.
days.question: Which fruit of the Spirit do you most want to grow in you?

days.title: The Spirit Builds the Church
days.summary: Christ is anointed with the Spirit, and as head of the Church he pours that Spirit out on his members, above all through the sacraments. These mighty works of God bear fruit in a new way of living, the theme of the Catechism’s third part. The Spirit also teaches us to pray. When we do not know how to pray as we ought, the Spirit himself intercedes for us (Romans 8:26), the theme of the fourth part. The In Brief paragraphs that follow sum up the Spirit’s work, from creation and the prophets to Mary, Christ, Pentecost and the life of the Church.
days.question: When have you felt unable to pray, and how did God meet you there?

days.title: Images of the Church
days.summary: Christ is the light of the nations, and the Church shines with his light like the moon with the sun’s. Belief in the Church flows from belief in the Holy Spirit. The word church comes from the Greek ekklesia, an assembly called together by God (Acts 19:39). It can mean a local community, a liturgical gathering or the whole Church throughout the world (1 Corinthians 1:2). Scripture paints many pictures of the Church: a sheepfold whose door and shepherd is Christ (John 10:11), God’s cultivated field, an olive tree into which Gentiles are grafted (Romans 11:17), and branches on the true vine (John 15:5).
days.question: Which image of the Church helps you love her more?

days.title: The Church Planned From the Start
days.summary: The Church is also called God’s building, with Christ as the cornerstone the builders rejected (Matthew 21:42). Believers are living stones in a spiritual house (1 Peter 2:5). She is the Jerusalem above, our mother (Galatians 4:26), and the spotless bride of Christ. The Church was in God’s plan from the beginning. The Father created the world to share his divine life, and when sin broke our communion, he began gathering a people again. He called Abraham and chose Israel to be his own (Exodus 19:5). The prophets foresaw all nations streaming to God’s house (Isaiah 2:2).
days.question: How does it feel to be called a living stone in God’s house?

days.title: Founded by Christ, Born at Pentecost
days.summary: Jesus began the Church by announcing the kingdom. He gathered a little flock (Luke 12:32) and called his followers his family. He chose the Twelve with Peter at their head, recalling the twelve tribes of Israel (Matthew 19:28), and shared his mission with them. The Church was born from his self-gift on the cross, symbolized by the blood and water flowing from his side (John 19:34). She was revealed to the world at Pentecost and sent to make disciples of all nations (Matthew 28:19). On earth she is a pilgrim; she will be perfected only in glory (Hebrews 13:14).
days.question: How do you take part in the mission Jesus gave his Church?

days.title: The Church as Sacrament
days.summary: The Church is a mystery: both human and divine, visible and spiritual. In her, God’s plan to unite all things in Christ (Ephesians 1:10) is already underway. Paul calls the bond of Christ and the Church a great mystery (Ephesians 5:32). The Greek word for mystery was translated into Latin as sacrament, a visible sign that carries an invisible reality. So the Church is like a sacrament: a sign and instrument of union with God and of unity among all people. Her goal is holiness and love, which never ends (1 Corinthians 13:8). The In Brief follows.
days.question: Where have you seen the Church act as a sign of God’s love to the world?

days.title: The People of God
days.summary: God chose to save people not one by one in isolation, but by forming them into a people under a new covenant (1 Corinthians 11:25). One enters this people by faith and Baptism, being born from above (John 3:5). Its head is Christ, its law the new commandment of love (John 13:34), its mission to be salt and light (Matthew 5:13–14), and its destiny the kingdom of God. Every member shares in Christ’s roles as priest, prophet and king. For a Christian, to reign means to serve (Matthew 20:28). Jesus also binds his disciples to himself: abide in me (John 15:4).
days.question: How do you live your share in Christ’s role as priest, prophet and king?

days.title: The Body of Christ
days.summary: When Jesus returned to the Father, he did not leave his disciples orphans (John 14:18). By the Spirit he made them his own body. Through Baptism and the Eucharist believers are joined to Christ and to one another (1 Corinthians 12:13). This unity does not erase differences: there are many members and gifts, but if one member suffers, all suffer (1 Corinthians 12:26). In Christ there is neither Jew nor Greek, slave nor free (Galatians 3:28). Christ is the head of the body (Colossians 1:18). He shapes us into his likeness and supplies all we need to grow.
days.question: Who in your parish is suffering, and how could you share their burden?

days.title: Bride and Temple of the Spirit
days.summary: Head and members together form what Saint Augustine called the whole Christ. Scripture also pictures the Church as Christ’s bride. Jesus called himself the bridegroom (Mark 2:19), and Paul says Christ loved the Church and gave himself up for her (Ephesians 5:25). The Church is also the temple of the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 3:16). The Spirit is to the Church what the soul is to the body, the source of her life. He gives charisms, special graces, whether striking or simple, for building up the Church. Pastors must discern them, since each is given for the common good (1 Corinthians 12:7).
days.question: What gift has God given you for building up others?

days.title: In Brief: People, Body, Temple
days.summary: The baptized are a chosen race and a royal priesthood (1 Peter 2:9), God’s own people. They share in Christ’s priestly, prophetic and kingly work. The Church is Christ’s body: through the Spirit and the sacraments, especially the Eucharist, the risen Lord joins believers to himself. Christ is its head, and the Church lives from him and for him. She is also his bride, whom he loved and gave himself for, and the temple of the Holy Spirit, who gives her life. The Church is a people gathered into the unity of the Trinity.
days.question: Which of these three images, people, body or temple, do you most need to remember?

days.title: The Church Is One
days.summary: The Creed names four marks of the Church: one, holy, catholic and apostolic. The Church is one because of her source, the one God in three persons, her founder, Christ, and her soul, the Holy Spirit. Within that unity there is rich variety of peoples, gifts and traditions. Paul urges believers to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace (Ephesians 4:3), and above all to put on love (Colossians 3:14). Unity is also visible in one faith, shared sacraments and bishops in succession from the apostles. Sin wounds unity, yet Christians separated today are still brothers and sisters.
days.question: What could you do to heal a division among believers you know?

days.title: Unity and Holiness
days.summary: Many elements of holiness and truth exist outside the visible Catholic Church: Scripture, grace, faith, hope, love and gifts of the Spirit. These come from Christ and draw toward unity. The fullness of the Church Christ founded subsists, that is, continues to exist fully, in the Catholic Church. Christ prayed that all may be one (John 17:21), so working for Christian unity belongs to everyone, through prayer, conversion and dialogue. The Church is also holy, because Christ loved her and gave himself up to make her holy (Ephesians 5:25–26). Love is the soul of that holiness, as Saint Thérèse of Lisieux knew.
days.question: How could you pray this week for the unity of all Christians?

days.title: Holy and Catholic
days.summary: The Church is holy yet made up of sinners. If we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves (1 John 1:8). Like a field of wheat and weeds (Matthew 13:24–30), she always needs purifying and renewal. By canonizing saints, she holds up models and intercessors, and in Mary she has already reached perfection. Catholic means universal, or whole. The Church has the fullness of Christ and of the means of salvation, and she is sent to the whole human race (Matthew 28:19). Each diocese, a local Church led by its bishop, is fully catholic through communion with the Church of Rome.
days.question: How do you respond when you see sin in the Church?

days.title: Who Belongs to the Church
days.summary: The universal Church is not a federation of local churches but one body, rich in liturgies and traditions. All people are called to belong to her. Those fully joined to her accept her whole faith, sacraments and governance, though only those who persevere in love are saved. The Church is also truly linked with baptized Christians not in full communion, most closely with the Orthodox. Among other faiths, the Jewish people hold a unique place; God’s gifts and call to them are irrevocable (Romans 11:29). Muslims worship the one merciful God. The Church honors what is true and good in other religions as a preparation for the Gospel.
days.question: How can you show respect to people of other faiths while sharing your own?

days.title: Salvation and Mission
days.summary: Human religious searching also contains error (Romans 1:21), so the world needs the Church, which the Fathers compared to Noah’s ark (1 Peter 3:20). The saying outside the Church there is no salvation means that all salvation comes from Christ through his Church. Those who know this and refuse to enter cannot be saved. But those who, through no fault of their own, do not know Christ yet seek God sincerely and follow conscience can be saved. This never cancels the duty to evangelize. Christ sent his Church to all nations (Matthew 28:19), because God wants everyone to be saved (1 Timothy 2:4).
days.question: Who in your life might be waiting to hear about Christ from you?

days.title: The Church Is Apostolic
days.summary: Mission demands humility and renewal. The Church brings the Gospel into each culture, works for Christian unity, and listens respectfully to others. She is apostolic in three ways. She is built on the foundation of the apostles (Ephesians 2:20). She keeps and hands on their teaching (Acts 2:42). And she is still guided by them through their successors, the bishops, with the pope. Jesus sent the apostles as the Father sent him (John 20:21), and whoever receives them receives him (Matthew 10:40). Their role as first witnesses could not be passed on, but their pastoral office was, so the bishops now guard the flock (Acts 20:28).
days.question: How does knowing your faith comes from the apostles strengthen it?

days.title: Every Christian an Apostle
days.summary: Bishops succeed the apostles as shepherds by God’s own design. But the whole Church is apostolic, since every member is sent in some way to spread the kingdom. An apostolate means any activity aimed at that goal. Its source is Christ, and it bears fruit only through living union with him, for apart from him we can do nothing (John 15:5). Love is the soul of every apostolate. In the end, the Church’s deepest identity as one, holy, catholic and apostolic comes from the kingdom already present in her, the holy city Revelation shows coming down from heaven (Revelation 21:10). The In Brief follows.
days.question: What small act of witness could you offer this week?

days.title: Why the Church Has Ministers
days.summary: All the baptized, called Christ’s faithful, share truly equal dignity and help build up the Church. Within that equality there are different roles: the ordained, the laity and those in consecrated life. Why ordained ministers? No one can give himself the authority to preach and to act in Christ’s name. How will people believe without someone sent to preach (Romans 10:14)? So Christ gives this mission through the sacrament of Holy Orders. Ordained ministers are servants, slaves of Christ (Romans 1:1). Their ministry has a shared, collegial side, like the Twelve, and a personal side, since each is called by name: follow me (John 21:22).
days.question: How can you support the priests and deacons who serve you?

days.title: The Pope and the Bishops
days.summary: Christ formed the Twelve as a body, a college, with Peter at its head. He made Peter alone the rock and gave him the keys (Matthew 16:18–19), and he asked him three times to feed his sheep (John 21:15–17). The pope, as Bishop of Rome and Peter’s successor, is the lasting visible source of the Church’s unity, with full and universal authority. The bishops together, the college of bishops, also hold supreme authority, but only in union with the pope, most solemnly in an ecumenical council. Each bishop is the source of unity in his own diocese and cares especially for the poor (Galatians 2:10).
days.question: How do you pray for the pope and your bishop?

days.title: Teaching, Sanctifying, Governing
days.summary: Bishops, with their priests, have three tasks. First, to teach: to preach the Gospel to all (Mark 16:15). To keep the Church in the truth, Christ gave her shepherds the gift of infallibility, freedom from error when the pope, or the bishops united with him, define a teaching on faith or morals. Even their ordinary teaching calls for respectful assent. Second, to sanctify: the bishop oversees the sacraments, above all the Eucharist, and leads by example, not by lording it over others (1 Peter 5:3). Third, to govern, as servants like Christ, who came among us as one who serves (Luke 22:27).
days.question: Which teaching of the Church do you find hardest to accept, and why?

days.title: The Calling of the Laity
days.summary: A bishop’s authority is his own, given by Christ, not borrowed from the pope, though always used in communion with him. His model is the Good Shepherd. The laity are all the faithful who are not ordained or in religious life. Their special calling is to seek God’s kingdom in ordinary life: work, family, politics, culture. They are on the front lines, bringing the Gospel where clergy rarely go. Lay people share Christ’s priesthood by offering their work, prayer, family life, rest and even hardships as spiritual sacrifices (1 Peter 2:5). Parents share it in a special way by raising their children in faith.
days.question: What part of your daily work could you offer to God as a sacrifice today?

days.title: Lay Prophets and Kings
days.summary: Lay people may serve in the liturgy as readers or ministers, and in need may even baptize or give Communion. They share Christ’s prophetic role by the witness of their lives and by their words, evangelizing in ordinary settings. Some teach the faith or work in media and scholarship. They have the right, and at times the duty, to share their views with pastors respectfully. They share his kingly role first by mastering themselves, ruling their own desires rather than being ruled by sin. Christ, obedient unto death, was exalted (Philippians 2:8–9). Lay people also work to heal social structures that lead others into sin.
days.question: Where does God want you to speak up for the Gospel in your daily life?

days.title: Consecrated Life
days.summary: Lay people can help in Church governance too, in councils and synods. They must keep their duties as Church members and as citizens distinct yet joined in a Christian conscience. Each is a witness, according to the measure of Christ’s gift (Ephesians 4:7). Then the Catechism turns to consecrated life, a state of life marked by the public profession of the evangelical counsels. These are the Gospel paths of chastity in celibacy for the kingdom, poverty and obedience. Consecrated people give themselves wholly to God, loved above all. This life, like one great tree, has grown many branches over the centuries.
days.question: How might you practice a little more simplicity, purity or obedience this week?

days.title: Hermits, Virgins and Religious
days.summary: Bishops discern new forms of consecrated life as they arise. Hermits live apart in silence, prayer and penance, showing the hidden heart of the Church: intimacy with Christ alone. From the apostles’ time, some women have consecrated themselves as virgins or widows, and today the bishop still consecrates virgins to Christ. Jesus spoke of those who renounce marriage for the kingdom (Matthew 19:12). Religious life, which began in the East, is marked by public vows, life in common and a liturgical spirit. It witnesses to Christ’s love for the Church. Religious communities serve the local Church and its mission in union with the bishops.
days.question: What could you learn from the silence and prayer of a hermit?

days.title: Consecrated in the World
days.summary: Members of secular institutes live their consecration in the middle of the world, working like leaven to make it holy from within. Societies of apostolic life share a common life and mission without religious vows. Every consecrated person, already given to God in Baptism, is more closely dedicated to him and to the Church’s mission. Their lives are a sign of the world to come. The In Brief then begins: among Christ’s faithful there are ordained ministers and lay people, and from both come those in consecrated life. Christ sent the apostles and their successors, and he made Peter the visible foundation of the Church.
days.question: How have religious sisters, brothers or priests shaped your faith?

days.title: In Brief: The Church’s Members
days.summary: The pope, as Peter’s successor, holds full and supreme authority in the Church, and the bishops, united with him, succeed the apostles. Bishops teach the faith, celebrate the sacraments and guide their flocks, helped by priests and deacons. When they teach together with the pope, or when the pope defines a teaching on faith or morals, Christ keeps them from error. Lay people seek God’s kingdom in the world, ordering earthly affairs by God’s plan, and they share in Christ’s priestly, prophetic and kingly work. Consecrated life, with vows of poverty, chastity and obedience, is a gift to the whole Church.
days.question: Where in the world has God placed you to bring his kingdom?

days.title: Communion in Holy Things
days.summary: After professing faith in the Church, the Creed adds the communion of saints. Since all believers form one body, the good of each is shared with all. The phrase has two senses: a sharing in holy things and a bond among holy people. Believers share one faith handed on from the apostles (Acts 2:42), the sacraments, especially the Eucharist, and charisms given for the common good (1 Corinthians 12:7). The first Christians held everything in common (Acts 4:32), and we are stewards, not owners, of what we have. None of us lives for himself alone (Romans 14:7).
days.question: What do you have that you could share more freely?

days.title: Heaven and Earth United
days.summary: The Church exists in three states: some are pilgrims on earth, some are being purified after death, and some already see God in glory. All belong to one family, and death does not break the bond. The saints in heaven keep praying for us through Christ, the one mediator (1 Timothy 2:5). Saint Dominic promised to help his brothers more after death, and Thérèse of Lisieux hoped to spend heaven doing good on earth. Friendship with the saints draws us closer to Christ. From the earliest days, Christians have prayed for the dead, as Judas Maccabeus did (2 Maccabees 12:45).
days.question: Which saint do you ask to pray for you, and why?

days.title: Mary, Mother of the Church
days.summary: Mary’s place in the Church flows from her union with Christ. She was joined to him from his conception to the cross, where he gave her to the beloved disciple as mother (John 19:26–27), and she prayed with the apostles awaiting the Spirit. Preserved from original sin, she was taken body and soul into heaven at the end of her life. This is the Assumption, a share in her Son’s Resurrection and a pledge of ours. She is a model of faith and our mother in the order of grace, yet her role never rivals Christ’s; it depends on it. Honoring her differs completely from worshiping God.
days.question: How could you make room for Mary in your prayer this week?

days.title: One Baptism for Forgiveness
days.summary: Mary shows what the whole Church is meant to become, a sign of sure hope for God’s pilgrim people. After the In Brief on Mary, the Creed turns to the forgiveness of sins, linked closely to the Spirit and the Church. The risen Jesus breathed the Spirit on the apostles and gave them power to forgive sins (John 20:22–23). Baptism is the first and chief sacrament of forgiveness, washing away every sin (Romans 6:4). Yet our weakness and inclination to sin remain. So Christ gave the Church a way to forgive sins committed after Baptism, the sacrament of Penance, which the Fathers called a laborious kind of Baptism.
days.question: When did you last receive God’s mercy in Confession?

days.title: The Power of the Keys
days.summary: The risen Christ sent the apostles to preach repentance and forgiveness of sins in his name to all nations (Luke 24:47). Paul calls this the ministry of reconciliation (2 Corinthians 5:18). The power of the keys means the Church’s authority, given by Christ, to forgive sins. No sin is so serious that the Church cannot forgive it, as long as the sinner truly repents. Jesus told Peter to forgive not seven times but seventy times seven (Matthew 18:22). Through priests, Christ himself forgives, a gift the Fathers said surpasses anything given to the angels. The In Brief follows.
days.question: What keeps you from bringing your sins to God’s mercy?

days.title: The Resurrection of the Body
days.summary: The Creed reaches its climax in the resurrection of the dead and eternal life. Because Christ truly rose, those who belong to him will rise too (Romans 8:11). Flesh here means our mortal, fragile human nature. We believe that not only our souls but our very bodies will live again. This was revealed gradually. The mother and seven brothers in Maccabees died trusting God would raise them (2 Maccabees 7:9), and Daniel foresaw the dead awakening (Daniel 12:2). Jesus taught it against the Sadducees and linked it to himself: I am the resurrection and the life (John 11:25).
days.question: How does belief in the resurrection shape how you face loss?

days.title: How the Dead Will Rise
days.summary: From the start, people found resurrection hard to believe; in Athens some mocked Paul (Acts 17:32). At death soul and body separate. God will raise our bodies and reunite them with our souls. All the dead will rise, those who did good to life and those who did evil to judgment (John 5:29). We will rise in our own bodies, but transformed and glorified like Christ’s (Philippians 3:21). How this will happen is beyond our imagining. It will happen on the last day, when Christ returns. Even now, through Baptism, we are risen with Christ, so our bodies deserve respect (1 Corinthians 6:13).
days.question: How do you honor your body as a temple that will one day rise?

days.title: Dying in Christ
days.summary: To rise with Christ, we must die with him. Death is the end of earthly life, and it gives urgency to our days: remember your Creator in your youth (Ecclesiastes 12:1). Death entered the world through sin; God did not make it (Wisdom 1:13). But Christ, by his obedient death, changed its meaning. For Paul, to live is Christ and to die is gain (Philippians 1:21). For believers, life is changed, not ended. We die only once (Hebrews 9:27), so there is no reincarnation. The Church urges us to prepare for death and asks Mary to pray for us at that hour.
days.question: How are you preparing, quietly and hopefully, for your own death?

days.title: The Particular Judgment
days.summary: The In Brief recalls that the body matters to salvation, that all will rise, and that Christ has conquered death. Then the final article opens: life everlasting. For a Christian, death is a going home to Christ, and the Church sends the dying off with prayers of commendation. Death closes the time for accepting or refusing God’s grace. Each person is judged at the moment of death, as the rich man and Lazarus show (Luke 16:22). Each soul then enters heaven, either after purification or at once, or is lost forever. Saint John of the Cross said we will be judged on our love.
days.question: If your life ended today, how would you want to be found?

days.title: The Joy of Heaven
days.summary: Those who die in God’s grace and friendship, fully purified, live forever with Christ. They see God as he is (1 John 3:2), face to face (1 Corinthians 13:12). Heaven is perfect communion of life and love with the Trinity, Mary, the angels and the saints. It fulfills the deepest longings of the human heart. To be in heaven is to be with Christ (Philippians 1:23), and there each person finds his true identity, his own name (Revelation 2:17). It is beyond words: no eye has seen what God has prepared (1 Corinthians 2:9). The blessed see God directly, called the beatific vision.
days.question: What do you most look forward to in heaven?

days.title: Purgatory and Hell
days.summary: Some die in God’s friendship but are not yet fully purified. They are sure of heaven, but first they are cleansed. The Church calls this purgatory. Scripture speaks of being saved as through fire (1 Corinthians 3:15), and Judas Maccabeus offered sacrifice for the dead (2 Maccabees 12:46), so the Church prays for them, above all at Mass. Hell is real. We cannot be united to God unless we freely choose to love him and our neighbor (Matthew 25:31–46). To die in mortal sin, unrepentant, means choosing separation from God forever.
