God sends no one there; he wants all to repent (2 Peter 3:9).
days.question: Whom among the dead could you pray for today?

days.title: The Last Judgment
days.summary: All the dead, just and unjust, will rise (Acts 24:15) and stand before Christ. Then the truth of each person’s relationship with God will be laid bare, along with the good done or left undone (Matthew 25:31–46). Only the Father knows when this will be. Through Christ, God will speak the final word on all of history. This truth calls us to conversion now, the acceptable time (2 Corinthians 6:2), and to wait in blessed hope. At the end, the kingdom will come in fullness and God will make a new heaven and a new earth (2 Peter 3:13).
days.question: What good have you been putting off that you could do now?

days.title: A New Heaven and Earth
days.summary: In the new creation, the heavenly Jerusalem, God will dwell with his people and wipe every tear from their eyes (Revelation 21:4). The human family will be united, and the Church will be the bride adorned for her husband (Revelation 21:2). Creation itself, now groaning, will be set free (Romans 8:21). We do not know when or how this will happen. But hope for the new earth does not make this one unimportant. It should make us care more for the world, since the good fruits of human work and love, cleansed and transfigured, will be found again in God’s kingdom.
days.question: How does hope for the new creation shape the way you care for this world?

days.title: In Brief: The Last Things
days.summary: At death, each person receives an eternal destiny in the soul, through a particular judgment by Christ. Those who die in God’s grace and are fully purified enter heaven. With the angels and saints they make up the Church in heaven, seeing God and praying for us. Those who die in God’s friendship but still need cleansing are purified after death in purgatory, and the Church’s prayers, above all the Mass, help them. Those who die in mortal sin, refusing God’s love to the end, are separated from him forever. Hell’s chief pain is this eternal loss of God, for whom we were made.
days.question: Which of the last things do you think about least, and why?

days.title: Our Final Amen
days.summary: The Church prays that no one be lost, and she awaits Christ’s final judgment and the renewal of all creation, when God will be all in all. The Creed ends, as the Bible does (Revelation 22:21), with Amen. In Hebrew this word shares a root with believe and suggests something firm and trustworthy. Isaiah calls the Lord the God of truth, literally the God of Amen (Isaiah 65:16). Jesus often began his teaching with Amen. Saying Amen at the end of the Creed confirms the I believe at its start. Christ himself is the Amen (Revelation 3:14), God’s yes to every promise (2 Corinthians 1:20).
days.question: What does your Amen at Mass really mean to you?

days.title: What the Liturgy Is
days.summary: Part Two of the Catechism turns from what we believe to how we celebrate it. God’s hidden plan (Ephesians 1:9) was accomplished above all in Christ’s paschal mystery, and the Church makes it present in the liturgy. The word liturgy once meant a public work done for the people. In the Church it means the people’s share in God’s own work. In the New Testament it covers worship, preaching and works of charity (Romans 15:16). The liturgy is not the Church’s only activity, but it is the high point toward which all her work leads and the source from which her strength flows.
days.question: How might Sunday Mass become more the center of your week?

days.title: The Father, Source of Blessing
days.summary: After Pentecost, Christ lives and acts in his Church through the sacraments, which the Church calls the sacramental economy, God’s ordered way of giving us grace. The liturgy is the work of the Holy Trinity. It begins with the Father, who has blessed us in Christ with every spiritual blessing (Ephesians 1:3). A divine blessing is both a word and a gift. From creation to the end of time, all God’s work is blessing: to Noah, to Abraham, to Israel in the Exodus, the land, the Temple and the return from exile. In the liturgy we bless the Father in return, thanking him for his gifts.
days.question: What blessing could you thank the Father for today?

days.title: Christ at Work in the Liturgy
days.summary: Christ, seated at the Father’s right hand, pours out blessings through the sacraments, signs we can see and touch that truly give the grace they signify. In the liturgy he makes his paschal mystery present. His death and rising happened once for all (Romans 6:10), yet unlike other events they do not pass into the past; they draw all things to life. He gave the apostles the Spirit and the power to sanctify (John 20:22). He is present in the Mass, in the priest, above all in the Eucharist, in the Word, and when we pray together (Matthew 18:20).
days.question: Where do you most easily recognize Christ’s presence at Mass?

days.title: The Spirit Prepares Us
days.summary: The Holy Spirit is the Church’s teacher of faith and the craftsman of the sacraments. He prepares the Church to meet her Lord. He does this partly through the Old Testament. The Church reads it at Mass and prays the psalms, because the events of the old covenant prefigure the new. This way of reading is called typology. Noah’s ark points to Baptism (1 Peter 3:21), the crossing of the sea and the manna point to Baptism and the Eucharist (1 Corinthians 10:1–6). On the road to Emmaus, Jesus opened the Scriptures to the two disciples (Luke 24:27).
days.question: How could you prepare your heart before you arrive at Mass?

days.title: Remembering and Calling Down
days.summary: The Spirit and the assembly prepare hearts together. The Spirit is the Church’s living memory (John 14:26). He opens the Word of God to us and stirs a response of faith. In each liturgy the Church remembers God’s saving deeds; this remembering is called anamnesis. It is more than recalling the past. The Spirit makes those events present. Christ’s sacrifice is not repeated, but its celebration is, and each time it is truly here for us. The epiclesis is the prayer calling down the Spirit, so the gifts become Christ’s body and blood and we become a living offering (Romans 12:1).
days.question: How can you listen more attentively to the readings at Mass?

days.title: The Seven Sacraments
days.summary: Remembering and calling down the Spirit stand at the heart of every sacrament, above all the Eucharist. The Spirit’s aim in every liturgy is to bring us into communion with Christ, like sap in the vine (John 15:5), so we bear fruit (Galatians 5:22). The fellowship of the Holy Spirit (2 Corinthians 13:13) unites us to God and to one another. After an In Brief, a new article begins. The Church’s whole liturgy centers on the Eucharist and the sacraments. There are seven: Baptism, Confirmation, Eucharist, Penance, Anointing of the Sick, Holy Orders and Matrimony.
days.question: Which of the seven sacraments has most shaped your life?

days.title: Sacraments of Christ and Church
days.summary: All seven sacraments were instituted by Christ. His words and deeds during his life were already saving, and in the sacraments he still gives what he gave then. Like the power that went out from him to heal (Luke 5:17), the sacraments flow from his living body. Over time, guided by the Spirit into all truth (John 16:13), the Church recognized seven. The sacraments are of the Church: done by her, and they build her up. Ordained ministers ensure that Christ himself acts in them. Baptism, Confirmation and Holy Orders also mark the soul with a permanent seal, so they are never repeated.
days.question: How does knowing Christ acts in the sacraments change how you receive them?

days.title: Sacraments of Faith and Salvation
days.summary: Christ sent the apostles to preach and to baptize (Matthew 28:19), so the Word comes first and prepares for the sacraments. Sacraments make us holy, build up the Church and give worship to God. They presuppose faith and also nourish it. The Church’s prayer and belief go together, so no minister may change a rite as he likes. Celebrated worthily, sacraments truly give the grace they signify. They work by the very fact of being done, through Christ’s power, not the minister’s holiness. Still, what they bear in us depends on our openness. Through them we share in God’s own nature (2 Peter 1:4).
days.question: How can you open your heart more fully before receiving a sacrament?

days.title: Sacraments of Eternal Life
days.summary: The Church celebrates the sacraments until the Lord comes (1 Corinthians 11:26). Each one looks back to Christ’s Passion, shows the grace given now and points to future glory. In every sacrament the Spirit and the bride cry, Come (Revelation 22:17). The In Brief gathers this together: sacraments are effective signs of grace, instituted by Christ and entrusted to the Church, through which God’s own life is given to us. They bear fruit both in each person and in the whole Church. A new chapter then asks four questions about the liturgy: who celebrates, how, when and where.
days.question: How does each Mass give you a taste of heaven?

days.title: Who Celebrates the Liturgy
days.summary: The liturgy is the action of the whole Christ, head and members. Revelation shows the heavenly liturgy: a throne, the Lamb who was slain (Revelation 5:6), angels, elders, martyrs and a great crowd from every nation (Revelation 7:9). Isaiah heard the seraphim cry holy, holy, holy (Isaiah 6:3). When we celebrate the sacraments, we join that worship. On earth, the whole assembly of the baptized celebrates, as a holy priesthood (1 Peter 2:5). Members have different roles (Romans 12:4). Ordained ministers act in the person of Christ the head, while readers, servers and singers have their own parts.
days.question: How do you take an active part in the Mass, whatever your role?

days.title: Signs and Symbols in Worship
days.summary: The liturgy speaks through signs and symbols. Because we are body and soul, we grasp spiritual things through the senses. God speaks through creation itself (Wisdom 13:1; Romans 1:20): light and darkness, wind and fire, water and earth. Israel received signs of the covenant, such as circumcision, anointing, the laying on of hands, sacrifices and above all the Passover. Jesus used signs too. He healed a blind man with mud (John 9:6) and spoke of his death as a new exodus (Luke 9:31). Since Pentecost, the Spirit makes us holy through sacramental signs, words and actions together.
days.question: Which sign or gesture in the liturgy helps you pray?

days.title: Word, Song and Sacred Images
days.summary: Liturgy speaks through both words and actions. The readings from Scripture are a true part of every celebration, and what is said explains what is done. Singing and music also belong to worship, not as decoration but as prayer, when they are beautiful, shared by the people and true to the rite. Paul urges the early Christians to sing psalms, hymns and spiritual songs together (Colossians 3:16). Holy images are allowed because God the Son took on a visible human face. Icons of Christ, Mary and the saints draw us toward the one whose likeness we are meant to share (Romans 8:29).
days.question: Which hymn, psalm or sacred image has drawn you closer to God?

days.title: Sunday and the Liturgical Year
days.summary: Christ is the Lord of time, and the liturgy fills time with his presence. Each celebration happens in God’s own today, the today of Psalm 95, when we are invited to hear his voice. Sunday holds first place. It is the day of the Resurrection, the first day of the week and also the eighth day of the new creation, when the risen Jesus broke bread with his friends (Luke 24:30). Around Sunday the Church builds the liturgical year, a cycle of seasons and feasts that unfolds the whole story of salvation. Easter is the feast of feasts at its center.
days.question: How does your Sunday look different from the other six days of your week?

days.title: Saints and the Divine Office
days.summary: The liturgical year walks through the whole mystery of Christ, from his coming to his return. Woven through it are feasts of Mary, honored first because she is joined inseparably to her Son’s saving work, and memorials of martyrs and other saints, who show the paschal mystery lived out. The Liturgy of the Hours, also called the Divine Office, extends the praise of the Mass across the day. Built largely on the psalms, it answers Paul’s call to pray without ceasing (1 Thessalonians 5:17). Clergy and religious pray it daily, and lay people are warmly encouraged to join in.
days.question: Which saint’s feast day could become a small yearly tradition for you or your family?

days.title: Where the Church Worships
days.summary: Since Christ came, true worship is not bound to one mountain or temple. Jesus told the Samaritan woman that the Father seeks worship in spirit and truth (John 4:24). The baptized themselves are living stones built into a spiritual house (1 Peter 2:5). Still, a community needs a place to gather, and church buildings are houses of prayer where the Eucharist is celebrated and reserved. Their parts each carry meaning: the altar, the tabernacle, the chair of the bishop or priest, the ambo for the Word, the font for Baptism and a place for confession. The building points ahead to the Father’s house.
days.question: What part of your parish church helps you pray most, and why?

days.title: Summing Up the Celebration
days.summary: This day gathers the main points of how the liturgy is celebrated. The whole Christ, head and members, is the one who celebrates. All the baptized take part, each in their own role, with ordained ministers serving the assembly. Worship uses signs and symbols drawn from creation, human life and the history of salvation, now filled with the grace of Christ. Word and action belong together. Song and music serve prayer, and sacred images help us contemplate the mystery. Sunday, kept as the day of the Lord, is the foundation and heart of the whole liturgical year.
days.question: Do you think of yourself as a participant in the Mass or as an audience?

days.title: One Mystery, Many Traditions
days.summary: The liturgical year makes present the whole mystery of Christ, the memorials of saints show his victory in his members, and the Liturgy of the Hours sanctifies each day. Christ himself is the true temple, and church buildings serve his people at prayer. Then a new theme opens. The one paschal mystery is celebrated in many ways across the world. From the start the Church carried the Gospel to different peoples, and each received it in its own language and culture. This variety is not a threat to unity. It shows how inexhaustible the mystery of Christ is.
days.question: What have you learned from seeing the faith celebrated in a culture different from your own?

days.title: Rites of East and West
days.summary: The Catholic Church holds several liturgical traditions, or rites. Besides the Latin tradition, mainly the Roman rite, there are Byzantine, Alexandrian or Coptic, Syriac, Armenian, Maronite and Chaldean rites. The Church regards all of them as having equal right and dignity. The liturgy can be expressed through many cultures, yet it contains a part that cannot change because it comes from God, and parts the Church may adapt. What holds every rite together is fidelity to apostolic Tradition, the faith handed on from the apostles. Paul asks Timothy to guard that rich trust (2 Timothy 1:14).
days.question: Have you ever attended an Eastern Catholic liturgy? What would you hope to notice?

days.title: Baptism, the Door to Life
days.summary: The Church has seven sacraments, and together they touch every stage of human life, from birth to death. They form a whole, with the Eucharist at the center. Three are sacraments of Christian initiation: Baptism, Confirmation and the Eucharist. Baptism comes first. It is the gateway to life in the Spirit and the door to the other sacraments. Its name comes from a Greek word meaning to plunge or immerse: we go down into the water with Christ and rise with him. It is also called the washing of rebirth (Titus 3:5) and enlightenment, since the baptized receive Christ, the true light.
days.question: What do you know about the day of your own baptism? Who could tell you more?

days.title: Water Through Salvation History
days.summary: At the Easter Vigil, the prayer blessing the baptismal water recalls how God prepared for this sacrament long before Christ. At creation the Spirit hovered over the waters (Genesis 1:2), making them a source of life. In the great flood, Noah’s ark carried a few people safely through the water, and Peter sees in it a picture of Baptism (1 Peter 3:20). Israel passed through the Red Sea from slavery to freedom, and later crossed the Jordan into the Promised Land. Each of these moments foreshadows how Baptism brings death to sin and new life in God.
days.question: Which of these Old Testament water stories speaks most to your own life?

days.title: Christ’s Baptism and Ours
days.summary: The Old Testament signs are fulfilled in Jesus. He began his public life by being baptized by John in the Jordan, though he had no sin, and the Spirit came upon him as the Father spoke (Matthew 3:13-17). He called his coming death a baptism (Luke 12:50). Blood and water flowing from his pierced side point to Baptism and the Eucharist (John 19:34). After rising, he sent the apostles to baptize all nations (Matthew 28:19). From Pentecost on, the Church did just that. Paul teaches that in Baptism we are buried with Christ and rise to walk in new life (Romans 6:3-4).
days.question: What would it mean today to walk in the newness of life Paul describes?

days.title: Becoming a Christian Step by Step
days.summary: From the earliest days, becoming a Christian has been a journey with several stages. It includes hearing the Gospel, conversion, a profession of faith, Baptism, the gift of the Spirit and reception of the Eucharist. In the early Church adults went through a long catechumenate, a period of formation and testing, before Baptism. The Second Vatican Council restored this path for adults, often called RCIA or OCIA today. When infants are baptized, the formation simply comes afterward, as they grow. The rite of Baptism itself begins with signs that speak clearly, such as the sign of the cross and the proclamation of God’s Word.
days.question: Who helped form your faith as you grew, and have you ever thanked them?

days.title: The Rite of Baptism
days.summary: The baptismal rite unfolds in clear signs. Prayers of exorcism ask freedom from evil, and the person is anointed with the oil of catechumens. The candidate, or the parents and godparents, reject Satan and profess the faith. The water is blessed. Then comes the essential rite: immersion in water three times, or water poured on the head, while the minister baptizes in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. An anointing with chrism follows, along with a white garment, since the baptized have put on Christ (Galatians 3:27), and a candle lit from the Easter candle.
days.question: Do you still have your baptismal candle or garment? What could they remind you of?

days.title: Who Can Be Baptized
days.summary: Any person not yet baptized can receive Baptism. For adults, the catechumenate prepares them, and catechumens are already joined to the Church by their desire. Infants are baptized too. Born with a fallen human nature marked by original sin, they also need the new birth God gives, and the Church does not want to hold back the free gift of grace from them. Paul speaks of God rescuing us from the power of darkness (Colossians 1:13). Infant Baptism is an ancient practice, and Acts tells of whole households being baptized (Acts 16:15). Baptism is the sacrament of faith, a faith meant to grow.
days.question: How is your faith different now from what it was a few years ago?

days.title: Ministers and Necessity of Baptism
days.summary: Faith must keep growing after Baptism, and parents and godparents help it grow. The ordinary ministers of Baptism are bishops, priests and, in the Latin Church, deacons. In an emergency anyone, even someone not baptized, can baptize by pouring water and using the Trinitarian words, if they intend what the Church intends. Jesus taught that Baptism is necessary for salvation (John 3:5). God has bound salvation to Baptism, yet he himself is not bound by his sacraments. Those who die for the faith, or desire Baptism, or seek God sincerely without knowing the Gospel can be saved. Unbaptized children are entrusted to God’s mercy.
days.question: Would you know how to baptize someone in an emergency? Why might that matter?

days.title: What Baptism Does
days.summary: Baptism has two great effects: it cleanses from sin and gives new birth in the Holy Spirit. Original sin and all personal sins are forgiven, along with all punishment for them. A tendency toward sin, called concupiscence, remains, as an area of struggle. The baptized become a new creation (2 Corinthians 5:17), adopted children of God (Galatians 4:5-7) and sharers in the divine nature (2 Peter 1:4). They receive sanctifying grace, which is God’s own life within the soul, along with the virtues of faith, hope and love. Baptism also makes us members of the Church, one body in Christ (1 Corinthians 12:13).
days.question: How might you live today differently if you remembered you are God’s adopted child?

days.title: Belonging to Christ for Good
days.summary: Through Baptism a person no longer belongs to himself but to Christ, who died and rose for us (1 Corinthians 6:19). This brings a call to serve others, like Jesus washing his disciples’ feet (John 13:14), and to respect those who lead the Church. It also brings rights, such as receiving the sacraments and the support of the Church. Baptism unites all Christians, even those not yet in full communion with the Catholic Church. It leaves a permanent spiritual seal, called a character, that marks the person as Christ’s own (Ephesians 4:30). For that reason Baptism can never be repeated.
days.question: In what concrete way could you serve someone this week as Jesus served?

days.title: Baptism in Brief
days.summary: This “In Brief” section on Baptism gathers its main points. Baptism is birth into new life in Christ, and the Lord taught that it is necessary for salvation. Its essential rite is immersion in water, or pouring water on the head, with the invocation of the Trinity. It frees from sin, makes us children of God and members of the Church, and seals us with a mark that can never be erased. Infants are baptized because of the gift of grace, not because they have earned it. Those who die for the faith or long for Baptism are saved by God’s mercy, and unbaptized children are entrusted to him.
days.question: Which effect of Baptism do you find hardest to believe about yourself?

days.title: Confirmation, Completing Baptism
days.summary: Confirmation completes the grace of Baptism. Its roots are in the prophets, who foretold that the Spirit of the Lord would rest on the Messiah (Isaiah 11:2) and be poured out on all people (Joel 3:1). Jesus read the words “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me” in the synagogue at Nazareth and applied them to himself (Luke 4:18). At Pentecost the Spirit came upon the apostles (Acts 2), and they laid hands on new believers to share this gift (Acts 8:15-17). In the West the bishop usually confirms at a later age. In the East a priest confirms right after Baptism, using chrism blessed by the bishop.
days.question: Where in your life do you most need the strength of the Holy Spirit right now?

days.title: Oil and Seal
days.summary: Two signs explain Confirmation. The first is oil. In the Bible and the ancient world, oil was a sign of abundance and joy, it cleansed and healed wounds (Luke 10:34), and it made the body supple and radiant. Anointing with chrism, a perfumed oil blessed by the bishop at the Chrism Mass during Holy Week, expresses all of this. The second sign is a seal, which marks something as belonging to someone and protects it. God has set his seal on Christ (John 6:27), and Christians too are sealed with the Spirit (Ephesians 1:13). The rite opens with the renewal of baptismal promises.
days.question: What would it look like to live as someone sealed and claimed by God?

days.title: The Gift of the Spirit
days.summary: In the rite of Confirmation, the bishop extends his hands over those being confirmed and prays for the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit. The essential rite is the anointing with chrism on the forehead, with the laying on of a hand and words asking that the person be sealed with the Gift of the Holy Spirit. The sign of peace follows. Confirmation deepens our sense of being God’s children, who can cry out “Abba, Father” (Romans 8:15). It binds us more firmly to Christ and the Church and gives strength to witness to the faith (Luke 24:48-49). Like Baptism, it marks us permanently and is received once.
days.question: Who has been a courageous witness to the faith in your life?

days.title: Preparing for Confirmation
days.summary: Every baptized person who has not yet been confirmed should receive this sacrament. In the Latin Church it is usually given around the age of reason, and anyone in danger of death, even a child, should be confirmed. Spiritual maturity does not depend on age (Wisdom 4:8). Preparation aims at a closer bond with Christ and the Holy Spirit and a stronger sense of belonging to the Church. Candidates should go to confession first and pray, as the apostles prayed with Mary while awaiting the Spirit (Acts 1:14). A sponsor, ideally a godparent, helps. The bishop is the original minister, though priests may confirm too.
days.question: If you are confirmed, how has that gift shaped you since? If not, what draws you?

days.title: Confirmation Summed Up, Eucharist Begins
days.summary: This “In Brief” section on Confirmation recalls the apostles laying hands on the new believers in Samaria. It completes Baptism, marks the soul permanently and is conferred by anointing with chrism and the words that seal the gift of the Spirit. Then the Catechism turns to the Eucharist, which completes Christian initiation. Those raised by Baptism and strengthened by Confirmation join the whole community in the Lord’s own sacrifice. At the Last Supper Jesus instituted the Eucharist to make his sacrifice on the cross present through the ages. It is a sacrament of love, a sign of unity and a paschal banquet.
days.question: What first comes to mind when you hear the word Eucharist?

days.title: Source and Summit, Many Names
days.summary: The Eucharist is the source and summit of the whole Christian life. All the other sacraments and works of the Church flow from it and lead back to it, because it contains Christ himself. Its many names each reveal something. It is called the Eucharist, from a word meaning thanksgiving; the Lord’s Supper; and the Breaking of the Bread, the sign by which the Emmaus disciples recognized the risen Jesus (Luke 24:30-35). It is also called the Holy Sacrifice, the memorial of the Lord’s Passion, Holy Communion, since we share in Christ’s body and blood (1 Corinthians 10:16-17), and the Mass, from the sending forth at its end.
days.question: Which name for the Eucharist best captures what it means to you?

days.title: Signs and Institution of the Eucharist
days.summary: At the heart of the Eucharist are bread and wine, gifts of creation and human work. The Old Testament prepares for them: the priest Melchizedek brought out bread and wine (Genesis 14:18), Israel ate unleavened bread at Passover and manna in the desert (Deuteronomy 8:3). Jesus multiplied loaves to feed the crowds and changed water into wine at Cana (John 2:11). When he first spoke of eating his flesh, many walked away (John 6:60, 66). Then, at the Last Supper, loving his own to the end (John 13:1), he took bread and wine and gave them as his body and blood.
days.question: When Jesus’ words are hard to accept, what keeps you from walking away?

days.title: Do This in Memory of Me
days.summary: By celebrating the Last Supper during Passover, Jesus gave that feast its final meaning: his passing over to the Father through his death and resurrection. His command to do this in memory of him asks the Church to keep celebrating his sacrifice until he comes again (1 Corinthians 11:26). From the start the believers devoted themselves to the breaking of bread (Acts 2:42), especially on the first day of the week (Acts 20:7). Around the year 155, Saint Justin Martyr described a Sunday Mass whose shape we still follow. Every Mass has two parts, the Liturgy of the Word and the Liturgy of the Eucharist, forming one act of worship.
days.question: How can you prepare during the week to receive more from Sunday Mass?

days.title: The Shape of the Mass
days.summary: The Mass begins as Christians gather, with Christ himself presiding through the bishop or priest who acts in his person. The Liturgy of the Word follows: readings from Scripture, the homily and prayers for all people (1 Timothy 2:1-2). Bread and wine are then brought to the altar, often with gifts for the poor, as Paul organized collections for the needy (1 Corinthians 16:1). In the Eucharistic Prayer the Church gives thanks, asks the Father to send the Spirit, recalls the Last Supper, and prays for the living and the dead. After the Our Father and the breaking of the bread, the faithful receive Communion.
days.question: Which part of the Mass do you tend to drift through? How could you engage it?

days.title: Thanksgiving and Memorial
days.summary: The Eucharist is first a sacrifice of thanksgiving and praise to the Father. Through it the Church thanks God for creation, redemption and sanctification, offering praise through Christ, with him and in him. It is also a memorial. In the Bible, a memorial is more than remembering a past event. When Israel kept Passover, the deliverance from Egypt became present to each generation (Exodus 13:3). In the same way, when the Church celebrates the Eucharist and recalls Christ’s Passover, that saving event becomes truly present. Jesus’ command to do this in remembrance of him (1 Corinthians 11:24) carries that full biblical meaning.
days.question: What are three things you could thank God for at your next Mass?

days.title: One Sacrifice Made Present
days.summary: Because it is a memorial of Christ’s Passover, the Eucharist is also a sacrifice. Jesus’ own words show it: his body given for you, his blood poured out for many (Luke 22:19-20). The Mass does not add a new sacrifice. It makes present the one sacrifice of the cross. The victim is the same, Christ, and the one offering is the same, Christ through the priest; only the manner differs, bloody on Calvary and unbloody on the altar. The whole Church joins in, uniting its prayers, work and suffering to his. The Mass is offered for the living and also for the faithful departed.
days.question: What struggle or joy could you consciously offer with Christ at your next Mass?

days.title: The Real Presence
days.summary: Christ is present to his Church in many ways: in the Word, in prayer, where two or three gather in his name (Matthew 18:20), in the poor and in the minister. Yet he is present in a unique way in the Eucharist. Under the appearances of bread and wine, he is truly, really and substantially present, body and blood, soul and divinity. The Church calls this change transubstantiation. Christ is wholly present in each part of the host and remains as long as the appearances last. For this reason the Church adores the Blessed Sacrament, reserves it in the tabernacle and honors it outside Mass.
days.question: When did you last spend quiet time before the Blessed Sacrament?

days.title: Receiving Communion Worthily
days.summary: The Mass is both a sacrifice and a sacred banquet in which we receive the Lord. Jesus said that unless we eat his flesh and drink his blood we have no life in us (John 6:53). Paul warns believers to examine themselves before receiving (1 Corinthians 11:27-29). Anyone aware of mortal sin should go to confession before receiving Communion. Before receiving, we echo the humble words of the centurion: Lord, I am not worthy (Matthew 8:8). The Church asks a short fast beforehand and reverent dress and posture. Catholics must attend Mass on Sundays and holy days, and receive Communion at least once a year, ideally during the Easter season.
days.question: How do you usually prepare in the moments before receiving Communion?

days.title: The Fruits of Communion
days.summary: Christ is wholly present under either the bread or the wine, so receiving one alone is complete, though receiving both is a fuller sign. Holy Communion deepens our union with Christ: whoever eats his flesh remains in him (John 6:56). As bodily food sustains the body, Communion nourishes the life of grace. It separates us from sin, wiping away venial sins and strengthening us against mortal sin. It also builds the Church, making many into one body (1 Corinthians 10:17). Finally, receiving Christ commits us to the poor, since he identifies himself with the least of his brothers and sisters (Matthew 25:40).
days.question: How has receiving the Eucharist ever changed how you treat others?

days.title: Unity and the Glory to Come
days.summary: The Eucharist is the sacrament of unity, so divisions among Christians are deeply painful at the altar. The Eastern Orthodox Churches have true sacraments, and some sharing in the Eucharist is possible with them in certain cases. Communities born of the Reformation have not kept the sacrament of Holy Orders, so the Church cannot share Communion with them in the ordinary way, though exceptions exist in grave need. The Eucharist also looks ahead. Jesus spoke of drinking the cup new in his Father’s kingdom (Matthew 26:29), and the early Christians prayed, Come, Lord (1 Corinthians 16:22). It is a pledge of future glory.
days.question: How could you pray for Christian unity this week?

days.title: The Eucharist in Brief, Part One
days.summary: This “In Brief” section on the Eucharist opens with Jesus’ promise that he is the living bread from heaven. The Eucharist is the heart and summit of the Church’s life, because in it Christ unites the Church to his own sacrifice of praise to the Father. Its essential signs are wheat bread and grape wine, over which the blessing of the Holy Spirit is invoked and the priest speaks Jesus’ words from the Last Supper. Only validly ordained priests can preside and consecrate. It is a memorial of Christ’s Passover, a thanksgiving to the Father, and a sacrifice offered for the whole Church.
days.question: Why do you think Jesus chose ordinary bread and wine to give himself?

days.title: The Eucharist in Brief, Part Two
days.summary: By the consecration, bread and wine become the body and blood of Christ, and he is wholly present under each. As a sacrifice, the Eucharist is offered for the sins of the living and the dead and to obtain blessings from God. Anyone who wishes to receive Communion must be in a state of grace, so someone conscious of mortal sin should first go to confession. The Church encourages the faithful to receive often, even daily. Because Christ is present, the Blessed Sacrament deserves our adoration. Communion with him is a foretaste of heaven.
days.question: What would make it easier for you to receive the Eucharist more often?

days.title: Why Confession After Baptism
days.summary: We carry the new life of grace in earthen vessels (2 Corinthians 4:7), still subject to suffering, sickness, sin and death. So Christ, the physician of souls and bodies, gave the Church two sacraments of healing: Penance and the Anointing of the Sick. He showed this power when he forgave and healed the paralyzed man (Mark 2:1-12). Penance has many names: conversion, confession, forgiveness and reconciliation (2 Corinthians 5:20). It is needed because Baptism does not remove our weakness or tendency to sin. If we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves (1 John 1:8).
days.question: What keeps you from going to confession more often?

days.title: Conversion of the Heart
days.summary: Jesus’ first preaching was a call to repent and believe (Mark 1:15). The first and basic conversion happens at Baptism, but conversion continues throughout life, since the Church, holy as she is, always needs purification. Peter’s tears after denying Jesus (Luke 22:61) and his later threefold profession of love (John 21:15-17) show this second conversion. Interior penance means a change of heart, not just outward acts. Joel urges people to tear their hearts, not their clothes (Joel 2:13). It begins in grace, when God gives a new heart (Ezekiel 36:26), and grows as we look on Christ, whom we pierced.
days.question: What is one area of your heart that still needs conversion?

days.title: Penance in Daily Life
days.summary: Interior conversion shows itself in many ways. Scripture and tradition stress three: fasting, prayer and almsgiving (Tobit 12:8; Matthew 6:1-18). Penance is also lived through reconciling with others, caring for the poor, defending justice (Amos 5:24), admitting faults, accepting correction and taking up the cross each day (Luke 9:23). Love covers a multitude of sins (1 Peter 4:8). The Eucharist feeds this daily conversion, as do reading Scripture and praying. Lent and every Friday are special times of penance. The parable of the prodigal son (Luke 15:11-24) shows the whole path, from leaving home to the Father’s embrace.
days.question: Which small, regular penance could you take on this week?

days.title: Christ Gives Power to Forgive
days.summary: Only God forgives sins. Jesus, the Son of God, claimed that power and used it, telling sinners their sins were forgiven (Mark 2:5; Luke 7:48). After his resurrection he breathed on the apostles, gave them the Holy Spirit and sent them to forgive sins in his name (John 20:21-23). Because sin wounds our communion with the Church as well as with God, forgiveness also brings reconciliation with the Church. Christ gave Peter and the apostles the power to bind and to loose (Matthew 16:19; 18:18). Early writers called this sacrament a second plank of rescue after the shipwreck of losing grace.
days.question: Is there anyone you need to be reconciled with as well as with God?

days.title: How Penance Took Shape
days.summary: The way this sacrament is celebrated has changed over the centuries, while its core stays the same. In the early Church, people who had committed very serious sins, like murder or adultery, did public penance, sometimes for years, before being reconciled. Later, Irish monks spread a private practice that became the confession we know. In every age the sacrament has two parts: the penitent’s acts of contrition, confession and satisfaction, and God’s forgiveness given through the priest’s absolution. Contrition is sorrow for sin with a resolve not to sin again. Sorrow that comes from love of God is called perfect; sorrow from other motives still helps.
days.question: Does your sorrow for sin come more from fear or from love?

days.title: Confession and Making Amends
days.summary: Preparation for confession begins with an examination of conscience, looking at our lives in light of God’s Word, such as the Ten Commandments and the Sermon on the Mount. Every mortal sin that we remember after a careful examination must be confessed, including hidden sins of the heart (Matthew 5:28). Catholics must confess serious sins at least once a year, and confessing everyday faults is also strongly encouraged. After absolution, sin’s damage remains, so the penitent does a penance, or satisfaction, to repair what can be repaired, like returning stolen goods. This joins us to Christ, in whom we can do all things (Philippians 4:13).
days.question: What questions would you ask yourself in an honest examination of conscience tonight?

days.title: The Confessor’s Role
days.summary: Christ entrusted the ministry of reconciliation to his apostles (2 Corinthians 5:18), and so bishops and the priests who work with them forgive sins through the sacrament of Holy Orders. Some very serious sins carry a penalty called excommunication, which only the pope, the bishop or priests they authorize can lift, though any priest can absolve anyone in danger of death. Priests should be readily available for confession. The confessor acts as the Good Shepherd seeking the lost sheep, the Good Samaritan binding wounds and the father awaiting the prodigal son. He is bound by the seal of confession and may never reveal what he hears.
days.question: How might it change your confession to see the priest as Christ the Good Shepherd?

days.title: Effects of Penance, Indulgences
days.summary: The sacrament of Penance restores us to God’s grace and friendship. It often brings deep peace of conscience. It also reconciles us with the Church, since every sin harms the whole body (1 Corinthians 12:26). In it we pass from death to life (John 5:24). Then the Catechism explains indulgences. Sin has a double consequence. Grave sin cuts us off from God and, unforgiven, brings eternal punishment. Every sin leaves an unhealthy attachment that needs purifying, which is temporal punishment. Forgiveness removes the first. An indulgence, granted through the Church, removes some or all of the second, for ourselves or for the dead.
days.question: Which unhealthy attachment in your life most needs God’s healing?

days.title: The Church’s Treasury and Rite
days.summary: Indulgences rest on the communion of saints. The holy lives and prayers of Christ, Mary and all the saints form what is called the Church’s treasury, and the Church draws from it for her members, living and dead. The celebration of confession follows a pattern: greeting and blessing, reading God’s Word, confession of sins, receiving a penance, absolution and dismissal. Sometimes confession takes place within a communal service. In grave necessity, such as imminent danger of death, general absolution may be given, with the duty to confess individually later. Individual confession remains the ordinary way, since Christ speaks to each person (Mark 2:5).
days.question: When could you next go to confession? Could you put it on your calendar?

days.title: Penance in Brief
days.summary: This summary recalls that on Easter evening the risen Jesus gave his apostles the Holy Spirit and the power to forgive sins (John 20:22-23). Those who sin after Baptism are forgiven through this sacrament. Sin offends God and also damages our communion with the Church, and nothing is more harmful to us. Turning back to God is called conversion, and it grows from sorrow for sin and a firm resolve not to sin again. The penitent’s part has three elements: repentance, confession of sins to the priest, and the intention to make reparation. God’s mercy meets every honest return.
days.question: What would it feel like to leave confession truly free and at peace?

days.title: Anointing of the Sick Begins
days.summary: This “In Brief” section on Penance continues: all serious sins must be confessed, everyday faults are wisely confessed too, and only priests authorized by the Church can absolve. The effects are reconciliation with God and the Church, peace of conscience and strength for the Christian struggle. Then the Anointing of the Sick begins. Through it the whole Church entrusts the sick to the suffering and glorified Lord. James describes elders praying over the sick and anointing them with oil (James 5:14-15). The sick are also encouraged to unite their sufferings to Christ’s Passion (Colossians 1:24).
days.question: Who among the sick in your life could you remember in prayer today?

days.title: Christ the Physician
days.summary: Illness and suffering are among the hardest trials of life. They can lead to anguish or despair, but they can also bring maturity and a search for God. In the Old Testament, the sick cry out to God, who says, I am the Lord, your healer (Exodus 15:26), and Isaiah foresees a servant who bears our pains (Isaiah 53:4). Jesus showed great compassion for the sick, healing many and even identifying himself with them (Matthew 25:36). He often used touch and simple signs. He sent the Twelve to anoint the sick with oil and heal them (Mark 6:13).
days.question: How have you seen suffering draw someone closer to God?

days.title: The Sacrament for the Seriously Ill
days.summary: The Holy Spirit gives some people a special gift of healing (1 Corinthians 12:9), yet not every illness is cured. Paul learned that God’s grace is enough even in weakness (2 Corinthians 12:9). Following Christ’s command to heal the sick (Matthew 10:8), the Church celebrates a sacrament for them, described in James 5:14-15. Over time it came to be given mainly to the dying and was called Extreme Unction. Today it is meant for anyone in danger because of serious illness or old age, and it may be repeated if the illness worsens. Only priests and bishops can confer it.
days.question: Is there someone you know who should be offered the Anointing of the Sick?

days.title: Graces of the Anointing
days.summary: The Anointing of the Sick is a liturgical and communal celebration, whether at home, in a hospital or in church, ideally linked with confession and the Eucharist. Its core is simple: priests lay hands on the sick, pray over them in the faith of the Church, and anoint them with blessed oil. Its graces are many. It brings strength, peace and courage, forgives sins, and can restore health if that serves salvation. It unites the sick person to Christ’s Passion, so that suffering gains new meaning and helps the whole Church. It prepares for the final passage, freeing us from fear of death (Hebrews 2:15).
days.question: How could a period of illness become a time of grace for you or someone you love?

days.title: Viaticum, Food for the Journey
days.summary: To those about to leave this life, the Church offers the Eucharist as Viaticum, a Latin word for provisions for a journey. Receiving Christ’s body and blood at this moment is a seed of eternal life and a promise of resurrection: whoever eats his flesh will be raised on the last day (John 6:54). Just as Baptism, Confirmation and the Eucharist begin the Christian life, so Penance, Anointing and Viaticum together complete the earthly pilgrimage. The summary that follows repeats the key points: James 5 describes this sacrament, it is given to the seriously ill, and it strengthens and comforts them.
days.question: How would you want to be spiritually prepared when your own death comes?

days.title: Sacraments of Service and Orders
days.summary: Two sacraments are directed to the salvation of others: Holy Orders and Matrimony. They help their recipients grow in holiness by serving others and building up the Church. Holy Orders is the sacrament by which the mission Christ gave his apostles continues in the Church until the end of time. It has three degrees: bishops, priests and deacons. The word order comes from Roman civil life, where it meant an established body, especially of those who govern. Being ordained means being brought into such an order. Christ himself is called a priest forever, in the line of Melchizedek (Hebrews 5:6; Psalm 110:4).
days.question: How can you support the bishops, priests and deacons who serve you?

days.title: Priesthood Before Christ
days.summary: God made Israel a kingdom of priests (Exodus 19:6), yet he set apart the tribe of Levi for liturgical service (Numbers 1:48-53), and priests were consecrated by a special rite (Exodus 29). They offered sacrifices, taught God’s Word (Malachi 2:7) and stood between the people and God. Moses also shared the spirit of leadership with seventy elders (Numbers 11:24-25). But this priesthood could not bring salvation, so its sacrifices had to be repeated again and again. Its true fulfillment is Christ, the one high priest. The mysterious king and priest Melchizedek, who offered bread and wine (Genesis 14:18), foreshadows him.
days.question: What do you think it means that Christ is the one true priest?

days.title: Two Ways to Share Christ’s Priesthood
days.summary: All the baptized share in Christ’s priesthood. They are a holy priesthood offering spiritual sacrifices (1 Peter 2:5) through faith, hope, love and daily life. This is the common priesthood of the faithful. The ministerial priesthood of bishops and priests is a different way of sharing Christ’s one priesthood, not just a higher degree of the same thing. It exists to serve the common priesthood. In the ordained minister, Christ himself acts as head of his Body. The minister’s own weakness does not stop Christ’s grace in the sacraments. This office is service, as Jesus came to serve (Mark 10:45).
days.question: How do you offer your daily life as a spiritual sacrifice?

days.title: Bishops and the Fullness of Orders
days.summary: Since the earliest times, the Church has known three degrees of ordained ministry: bishop, priest and deacon. Saint Ignatius of Antioch wrote that without them one cannot speak of the Church. Bishops receive the fullness of the sacrament. They are successors of the apostles, through an unbroken line going back to them, and they receive the Spirit by the laying on of hands (2 Timothy 1:6). A bishop shepherds a local church, teaching, sanctifying and governing in Christ’s name, and with the pope he shares concern for the whole Church. Priests are consecrated to share in that mission.
days.question: How could you pray for your bishop by name this week?

days.title: Priests and Deacons
days.summary: Priests are coworkers of the bishops, configured to Christ the priest, preaching the Gospel, shepherding the faithful and celebrating divine worship. They depend on their bishop for their ministry and promise him respect and obedience. Their mission is universal, reaching to the ends of the earth (Acts 1:8), and it reaches its high point in the Eucharist. Priests of a diocese form one body with their bishop, linked by brotherhood. Deacons are ordained for service, not for priesthood. They assist at the Eucharist, proclaim the Gospel, preach, witness marriages, lead funerals and serve in charity. Married men may be permanent deacons.
days.question: How do the priests and deacons of your parish show Christ the servant?

days.title: Ordination and Who May Receive
days.summary: Ordination is usually celebrated within Mass, ideally on Sunday in the cathedral. The essential rite is the bishop’s laying on of hands with a prayer of consecration asking for the Holy Spirit. Christ chose the apostles himself (Mark 3:14-19), and validly ordained bishops, as their successors, confer all three degrees. Only a baptized man can validly receive Orders, since Christ chose men as apostles, and the Church sees herself bound by that choice. No one has a right to ordination; it is a call from God (Hebrews 5:4). In the Latin Church priests are normally celibate. Eastern Churches ordain married men as priests.
days.question: How could you encourage someone who may be called to priesthood or religious life?

days.title: The Grace of Holy Orders
days.summary: Like Baptism and Confirmation, Holy Orders leaves a permanent spiritual character. A man is ordained once and forever. For serious reasons he may be released from the duties of ministry, but he cannot become a layman again in the strict sense. Christ works through the sacrament even when the minister is unworthy, though a priest’s sins can harm the fruit of his ministry. The sacrament also gives special grace: to bishops, strength to guide and defend their people; to priests, grace to proclaim the Gospel and offer sacrifice; to deacons, grace to serve. Saint John Vianney saw priesthood as the love of Jesus’ heart.
days.question: What priest has shown you something of Christ’s heart?

days.title: Holy Orders in Brief
days.summary: This “In Brief” section on Holy Orders begins with Paul urging Timothy to rekindle the gift he received through the laying on of hands (2 Timothy 1:6). Christ’s one priesthood is shared in two ways: the common priesthood of all the baptized and the ministerial priesthood. The sacrament has three degrees. Bishops receive its fullness and lead their churches as successors of the apostles. Priests are united with their bishops in priestly dignity and serve as their coworkers. Deacons are ordained for ministries of service. Ordination gives a permanent mark that configures a man to Christ for the sake of the Church.
days.question: What gift of God in you needs to be rekindled?

days.title: Marriage in God’s Plan
days.summary: This “In Brief” section on Orders closes: bishops confer the sacrament, it is given to baptized men, and in the Latin Church to those who embrace celibacy. Then the Catechism turns to Matrimony. Marriage is a covenant in which a man and a woman form a partnership of their whole life, ordered to their mutual good and to having and raising children. Christ raised it to a sacrament between the baptized. Scripture begins with the creation of man and woman in God’s image (Genesis 1:27) and ends with the wedding feast of the Lamb (Revelation 19:7). God is the author of marriage, and God is love (1 John 4:8).
days.question: What marriage around you most clearly shows God’s faithful love?

days.title: Marriage From Eden to the Prophets
days.summary: In Genesis God makes woman as a partner suited to man, and the two become one flesh (Genesis 2:18-24). Jesus later adds: what God has joined, let no one separate (Matthew 19:6). But sin wounded this communion, bringing blame, domination and lust (Genesis 3:12, 16). Marriage still needs God’s grace to reach its full meaning. In the Old Testament, polygamy was tolerated and Moses permitted divorce because of hardness of heart (Matthew 19:8). The prophets, though, described God’s covenant with Israel as a faithful marriage, and Malachi condemns broken vows (Malachi 2:13-16). The Song of Songs praises love as strong as death.
days.question: Where does sin most strain the relationships closest to you?

days.title: Marriage in the Lord
days.summary: Jesus performed his first sign at a wedding in Cana (John 2:1-11), showing the goodness of marriage. He taught clearly that marriage cannot be dissolved, returning to God’s original plan (Matthew 19:3-9). This may seem too demanding, but Christ gives the strength to live it, through his cross and his easy yoke. Paul compares a husband’s love for his wife to Christ’s love for the Church (Ephesians 5:25). Christ also invited some to give up marriage for the sake of the kingdom (Matthew 19:12). Virginity for the kingdom and Christian marriage both come from the Lord, and each honors the other.
days.question: How does the love between Christ and the Church challenge the way you love?

days.title: Consent Makes a Marriage
days.summary: In the Latin Church, marriage between Catholics usually takes place within Mass, linking it to Christ’s self-gift and the Eucharist. Confession beforehand is fitting. In the Latin tradition the bride and groom are the ministers of the sacrament, giving it to each other before the Church. In Eastern traditions the priest or bishop is the minister and crowns the couple. What makes a marriage is the consent of a baptized man and woman who are free to marry and who freely give themselves to each other for life. By this exchange the two become one flesh (Genesis 2:24).
days.question: What does it mean to you to give yourself freely and for life?

days.title: Free Consent and Mixed Marriages
days.summary: Consent to marriage must be a free act, without fear or pressure. Without true consent there is no marriage. For this reason a Church tribunal may examine a marriage and declare it null, meaning it never existed as a valid bond, and the parties are then free to marry. The priest or deacon receives the couple’s consent in the Church’s name, and Catholics normally marry in a church ceremony, because marriage is a public, ecclesial state. Good preparation matters. When a Catholic marries a baptized non-Catholic, or someone not baptized, their differences require special care and the Church’s permission.
days.question: What helps a couple you know prepare well for marriage?

days.title: A Lasting Bond and Its Grace
days.summary: In a mixed marriage the Catholic partner commits to living the faith and raising the children Catholic, and couples can live a real ecumenism at home. Paul says an unbelieving spouse is made holy through a believing one (1 Corinthians 7:14). Valid marriage creates a bond that is lifelong and exclusive. God himself seals it, so it cannot be dissolved (Mark 10:9). The sacrament gives the couple grace to love each other with Christ’s love, to strengthen their unity and to grow in holiness together. They are to be subject to one another out of reverence for Christ (Ephesians 5:21) and bear one another’s burdens (Galatians 6:2).
days.question: Whose burdens could you help carry this week?

days.title: Unity, Fidelity, Indissolubility
days.summary: Married love involves the whole person, body and soul, and it calls for unity, permanence and faithfulness. Polygamy contradicts the equal dignity of husband and wife. Faithful love mirrors God’s own fidelity to his covenant and Christ’s to his Church. Jesus taught that whoever divorces and remarries commits adultery (Mark 10:11-12). For serious reasons a couple may separate, but the bond remains. Divorced Catholics who remarry civilly are in a situation that conflicts with God’s law and so cannot receive Communion while it lasts. Yet they remain part of the Church and are urged to pray, attend Mass, serve and raise their children in faith.
days.question: How can you show welcome to people in difficult marriage situations?

days.title: Open to Life, Domestic Church
days.summary: Married love is by its nature open to new life. Children are the supreme gift of marriage (Genesis 1:28), and parents are their first teachers in the faith. Couples who cannot have children can still live a fruitful life of love, hospitality and service. In Acts, whole households came to believe (Acts 16:31). The Christian family is therefore called a domestic church, a home where faith is first proclaimed, where prayer is learned and where people practice forgiveness and generous love. Many people live without a family of their own. The Church should be a home for them as well (Matthew 11:28).
days.question: What simple practice could make your home more like a domestic church?

days.title: Matrimony in Brief
days.summary: This “In Brief” section on Matrimony recalls Paul’s teaching that marriage is a great mystery that refers to Christ and the Church (Ephesians 5:32). The marriage covenant was created by God and raised by Christ to a sacrament between baptized spouses. It is formed by the free consent of the couple, normally exchanged before the Church. Its essential marks are unity and indissolubility, and it is open to new life. The Church cannot accept the remarriage of divorced persons while the first spouse lives. The Christian home is a domestic church, where children first hear the Gospel.
days.question: How can you pray for the marriages and families in your parish?

days.title: Sacramentals and Blessings
days.summary: Besides the seven sacraments, the Church has sacramentals: sacred signs she has established, such as blessings, holy water, ashes and medals. They do not give grace the way sacraments do. Rather, through the Church’s prayer, they prepare us to receive grace and help make many moments of life holy. Every baptized person is called to be a blessing (Genesis 12:2) and to bless, even those who curse us (Luke 6:28). Blessings come first among sacramentals. Exorcism, which Jesus himself performed (Mark 1:25), is another. Popular devotions such as the rosary, pilgrimages and the Stations of the Cross extend the liturgy without replacing it.
days.question: Which sacramental or devotion could help you pray more often during the day?

days.title: The Christian’s Last Passover
days.summary: This “In Brief” section on sacramentals notes that the laity may lead certain blessings and that popular piety should flow from and lead back to the liturgy. Then the Catechism turns to Christian funerals. All the sacraments, especially those of initiation, lead toward the final Passover, death, when a Christian passes through Christ’s death into life. For a believer, the day of death completes the new birth begun at Baptism. Paul longed to leave the body and be at home with the Lord (2 Corinthians 5:8). The body is sown in weakness and raised in glory (1 Corinthians 15:42-44).
days.question: How does Baptism change the way you think about your own death?

days.title: The Celebration of Funerals
days.summary: A Christian funeral is a liturgy of the Church. It does not give a sacrament to the deceased, who has already passed beyond them. It shows the communion between the deceased and the living and proclaims eternal life. In the Roman rite there are three stations: the home, the church and the cemetery. The community gathers and offers consolation in light of faith. God’s Word is read, announcing Christ’s resurrection while honoring grief. The Eucharist is the heart of the funeral, offered for the one who has died. The final commendation entrusts the person to God, with hope of meeting again.
days.question: Whom have you lost that you could commend to God in prayer today?

days.title: Christian, Know Your Dignity
days.summary: Part Three of the Catechism turns to life in Christ, the moral life. It begins from our dignity: by grace we share in God’s own nature (2 Peter 1:4) and are children of God (John 1:12). Christians are called to live in a way worthy of the Gospel (Philippians 1:27), following Jesus, who always did what pleased the Father. Through Baptism we are dead to sin and alive for God in Christ (Romans 6:11), and the Spirit produces his fruit in us (Galatians 5:22). Scripture sets two ways before us, of life and of death (Deuteronomy 30:15). Christ himself is the way (John 14:6).
days.question: How would remembering your dignity as God’s child shape one choice today?

days.title: Created in God’s Image
days.summary: Life in the Spirit fulfills our human calling. The dignity of every person rests on being created in God’s image and likeness, and it reaches its goal in eternal happiness with him. Christ, the image of the invisible God (Colossians 1:15), shows us who we truly are. Because the divine image is in every person, we are made for communion with others, reflecting the unity of the Trinity. The human person has a spiritual and immortal soul, and is the only creature on earth God willed for its own sake. With intellect and will we can seek truth and goodness. Freedom is a striking sign of the divine image.
days.question: How does seeing God’s image in a difficult person change how you treat them?

days.title: Wounded and Restored
days.summary: At the very beginning, humanity misused its freedom, giving in to the tempter. Since then human nature has been wounded and inclined to sin, though not completely corrupted. By his Passion, Christ freed us from Satan and sin, and he won for us the new life of the Spirit. Those who believe in him become children of God, and this adoption transforms them, so they can follow his example and act rightly. The summary that follows gathers these points: Christ reveals who we are, each person has a soul with intellect and will, freedom is a gift to be used for good, and grace restores what sin damaged.
days.question: Where do you most need God’s grace to use your freedom well?

days.title: The Beatitudes and True Happiness
days.summary: The Beatitudes stand at the heart of Jesus’ preaching (Matthew 5:3-12). They paint a portrait of Christ himself and describe the attitudes of a disciple: poverty of spirit, mercy, purity of heart, peacemaking. They answer the desire for happiness that God placed in every heart, a desire only he can fill. God promises the kingdom of heaven, the vision of God, for the pure in heart will see him (Matthew 5:8), and sharing in his rest. This happiness is a free gift beyond our natural powers. It teaches that lasting joy is not found in wealth, fame or power, but in God alone.
days.question: Which Beatitude do you find hardest to live? Why?

days.title: Happiness and Freedom
days.summary: This day closes the teaching on the Beatitudes and opens the teaching on freedom. The Beatitudes gather up God’s promises from Abraham onward and point to our true goal: the Kingdom, the vision of God, a share in his own life, and rest in him. That happiness is a gift no one can earn or build. It also helps us weigh earthly goods like money, fame and power, which cannot fill the heart. Then a new theme begins. God made us able to reason and choose, giving us the dignity of acting from within. Sirach 15:14 says God left us in the hand of our own counsel.
days.question: What earthly good do you most often expect to make you happy?

days.title: Freedom and Responsibility
days.summary: Freedom is the power, rooted in reason and will, to act or not to act. It reaches its full shape when it is directed toward God, our true good. The more a person does good, the freer he becomes; choosing evil leads to slavery to sin (Romans 6:17). We answer for the acts we truly will. Ignorance, fear, pressure, habit or strong attachments can lessen that responsibility. Scripture shows God asking for an account: of Eve in Genesis 3, of Cain in Genesis 4, and through Nathan of David in 2 Samuel 12. Everyone has a right to use freedom, above all in moral and religious matters.
days.question: When has doing the right thing left you feeling freer, not more restricted?

days.title: Freedom Wounded and Set Free
days.summary: From the start, humanity misused its freedom. Our first parents turned away from God, and since then freedom has been weakened and inclined toward sin. Poverty, injustice and pressure can also threaten it from outside. Christ came to set us free: Galatians 5:1 says that for freedom Christ has set us free. Grace is God’s free gift of his own life and help. It does not compete with our freedom; it frees it from within, so we can cooperate more fully with the Holy Spirit. Romans 8:21 speaks of the glorious liberty of God’s children. A short review follows.
days.question: Where do you feel least free right now, and could you ask Christ to free you there?

days.title: The Sources of Morality
days.summary: The review of freedom ends by recalling that the right to act freely belongs to human dignity, and that Christ’s grace sets freedom free. Then it asks how we judge whether a free act is good. Three things are weighed: the object, what is actually chosen; the intention, the purpose behind it; and the circumstances, including consequences. A good intention cannot make an evil act good, so the end does not justify the means. A bad motive, like giving alms to be praised, spoils an act that is good in itself. Circumstances can increase or lessen guilt, but cannot make a wrong act right.
days.question: Is there a good thing you do for a mixed motive?

days.title: Good Acts and the Passions
days.summary: A morally good act needs all three sources to be good together: a good object, a good intention and fitting circumstances. Some acts are always wrong to choose because of what they are, whatever the motive or situation, such as blasphemy, perjury, murder and adultery. Doing evil so that good may come of it is never allowed. A short review repeats these points. Then a new article begins on the passions, meaning our feelings and emotions. We move toward the happiness God offers through free, deliberate choices, and our feelings can help prepare us for those choices or make them harder.
days.question: When have your feelings helped you do good, and when have they pulled you away?

days.title: Feelings in the Moral Life
days.summary: Passions are the feelings and emotions that move us toward what seems good or away from what seems harmful. Love, the attraction to what is good, is the most basic; others include desire, joy, hatred, fear, sadness and anger. In themselves, passions are neither good nor evil. They become morally good or bad as reason and will take them up. Jesus taught that evil comes from within the heart (Mark 7:21). The goal is a whole person moved to good with heart and body too, as Psalm 84:2 sings of heart and flesh crying out for the living God.
days.question: Which emotion most often shapes your choices, and how might you offer it to God?

days.title: The Voice of Conscience
days.summary: A short review gathers up the teaching on the passions: they are movements of feeling that incline us to act, they are not sinful in themselves, and they become part of virtue or vice depending on how reason and will direct them. Then a new article opens on conscience. Deep within, a person discovers a law he did not make for himself, which calls him to love what is good and avoid what is evil. Conscience is the innermost room of the person, where each of us stands alone before God and hears him. It is a place of meeting with God, not merely a list of rules.
days.question: When did you last take quiet time to listen to your conscience before God?

days.title: Judging and Forming Conscience
days.summary: Conscience is a judgment of reason by which we recognize whether a concrete act, past, present or planned, is good or evil. Saint Paul says the law is written on human hearts, with conscience bearing witness (Romans 2:14–16). To hear it, we need some quiet and reflection. Everyone has the right to act in conscience and freedom. But conscience must be formed, and that formation is lifelong. It begins in childhood and grows through prayer, examination of conscience, good advice and the Church’s teaching. Psalm 119:105 calls God’s word a lamp for our feet. A conscience left untrained can be swayed by selfishness, bad example or pressure.
days.question: What helps you form your conscience, and what tends to cloud it?

days.title: Following Conscience Rightly
days.summary: Sometimes conscience must decide among hard options. A few rules always apply. Never do evil so that good may result. Treat others as you would want to be treated, the Golden Rule found in Matthew 7:12, Luke 6:31 and Tobit 4:15. Charity respects a neighbor’s conscience, and Paul warns against wounding weaker consciences (1 Corinthians 8:12). A person must obey the certain judgment of conscience. Yet conscience can be wrong. When ignorance is our own fault, because we took little care to seek the truth, we are responsible. When ignorance is not our fault, the act is not held against us, but it is still a wrong that needs correcting.
days.question: Is there a question of right and wrong you have avoided looking into?

days.title: Conscience in Brief
days.summary: This review sums up the teaching on conscience. Conscience is the innermost place where each person meets God. It is a judgment of reason that tells us what we ought to do and afterward lets us know whether we did well. Even after we sin, it bears witness to the truth and calls us back. A well-formed conscience is honest and true, shaped by reason and by God’s word. We must always obey the sure judgment of our conscience, but we can be mistaken, sometimes through ignorance that is our own fault. The word of God is the light that helps form and correct it.
days.question: How could you make a daily examination of conscience part of your evenings?

days.title: The Human Virtues
days.summary: A virtue is a steady habit of doing good, so that good acts come readily and gladly. Paul urges us to think about whatever is true, just and pure (Philippians 4:8). Human virtues are built by repeated good choices. Four are called cardinal, or hinge, virtues, and Wisdom 8:7 names them together. Prudence sees the right course in each case. Justice gives God and neighbor their due. Fortitude stands firm in difficulty, even against fear of death. Temperance keeps the desire for pleasure in balance. Education, effort and perseverance help them grow, and God’s grace purifies and lifts them up, which we need because sin has wounded us.
days.question: Which of the four cardinal virtues do you most need to practice this week?

days.title: Faith and Hope
days.summary: The theological virtues are faith, hope and charity. They are called theological because they come from God, who pours them into the soul, and lead straight to him. Faith is believing God and all he has revealed, which the Church proposes for belief. Living faith works through love (Galatians 5:6), since faith without works is dead (James 2:26). Believers must also profess it openly (Matthew 10:32–33). Hope is the desire for God’s Kingdom and eternal life, trusting in Christ’s promises and the help of the Holy Spirit. Abraham hoped against hope (Romans 4:18), and Hebrews 6:19 calls hope a sure anchor of the soul.
days.question: What anchors your hope when life feels uncertain?

days.title: Hope and Charity
days.summary: Hope guards against discouragement and opens the heart to heaven. In hope the Church prays that all people be saved (1 Timothy 2:4), and each believer asks for the grace to persevere to the end (Matthew 10:22). Charity is the virtue by which we love God above all things for his own sake, and our neighbor as ourselves for love of God. Jesus made it his new commandment, to love as he has loved us (John 13:34), even our enemies. It is the greatest of the virtues and gives life and shape to all the others.
days.question: Who in your life is hardest to love, and what small act of charity could you offer?

days.title: Gifts and Fruits of the Spirit
days.summary: The Holy Spirit gives seven gifts, lasting dispositions that make us ready to follow his promptings: wisdom, understanding, counsel, fortitude, knowledge, piety and fear of the Lord. They come from the description of the Messiah in Isaiah 11:1–2, and they complete and perfect the virtues. Romans 8:14 says that all who are led by the Spirit of God are children of God. The fruits of the Spirit are good works he forms in us as a foretaste of eternal glory. Tradition counts twelve, building on Galatians 5:22–23: love, joy, peace, patience and more. A review then begins, recalling what virtue is and restating prudence, justice and fortitude.
days.question: Which fruit of the Spirit would you most like to see grow in you?

days.title: The Virtues in Brief
days.summary: This review completes the summary of the virtues. Temperance moderates our attraction to pleasure and keeps created goods in balance. The moral virtues grow through education, deliberate acts and perseverance, and grace purifies and raises them. The theological virtues dispose Christians to live in relationship with the Holy Trinity. Faith believes in God and all he has revealed. Hope desires and awaits eternal life from God, trusting in his help. Charity loves God above all things and neighbor as oneself for God’s sake; it binds every virtue together. Last come the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, which make us docile to his promptings.
days.question: Which virtue have you seen grow in yourself over the past year?

days.title: Mercy and the Reality of Sin
days.summary: The Gospel is the revelation of God’s mercy to sinners. Jesus is named because he will save his people from their sins (Matthew 1:21), and where sin increased, grace abounded all the more (Romans 5:20). To receive that mercy, we must admit our faults. Sin is an offense against reason, truth and right conscience, and above all against God (Psalm 51:4). It is a failure of real love, a turning toward self that sets God aside, the opposite of Christ’s humble obedience (Philippians 2:6–9). There are many kinds of sin, as Paul’s lists show (Galatians 5:19–21). Sins can be committed in thought, word, deed or omission.
days.question: Is it easier for you to admit your faults or to trust God’s mercy for them?

days.title: Mortal and Venial Sin
days.summary: Sins differ in gravity. Mortal sin destroys charity in the heart by a serious violation of God’s law; venial sin offends and wounds charity but does not destroy it. Three conditions make a sin mortal: grave matter, as the Ten Commandments spell out (Mark 10:19); full knowledge; and deliberate consent. Ignorance that is not our fault can lessen or remove guilt, but pretended ignorance and a hardened heart increase it (Mark 3:5). Mortal sin left unrepented cuts us off from Christ’s Kingdom and leads to the eternal death of hell. Still, while we can judge that an act is gravely wrong, the judgment of persons belongs to God alone.
days.question: How might you leave the judgment of others to God this week?

days.title: How Sin Spreads
days.summary: Venial sin weakens charity and, when chosen deliberately and left unrepented, prepares the way for mortal sin. Jesus warns that blasphemy against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven (Mark 3:29); this means stubbornly refusing God’s mercy by refusing to repent. Sin also breeds sin. Repeated acts form vices, which cloud conscience. Tradition names seven capital sins, including pride, greed, envy and anger. Scripture speaks of sins that cry to heaven, such as the blood of Abel (Genesis 4:10), the oppression of Israel in Egypt, and wages withheld from workers (James 5:4). We share in others’ sins when we take part in, approve or fail to prevent them.
days.question: Is there a small habit of sin you have stopped noticing?

days.title: Sin in Brief
days.summary: This review gathers the teaching on sin. God has allowed all to fall into disobedience so that he might show mercy to all (Romans 11:32). Saint Augustine described sin as any word, act or desire against God’s eternal law. It goes against reason and wounds human nature and human solidarity. Its root is in the heart. To choose deliberately, with knowledge and consent, something gravely contrary to God’s law is mortal sin. Venial sin is a lesser disorder that does not break our covenant with God and can be healed by his grace. Repeated sins, even venial ones, grow into vices, chief among them the capital sins.
days.question: Where do you most need God’s mercy today?

days.title: Called to Live in Communion
days.summary: Chapter Two turns to our life together. Humanity is called to show the image of God, and there is a likeness between the unity of the three divine Persons and the brotherhood people are meant to build in truth and love. We are social by nature, not by accident; through family, neighbors and wider society we develop our gifts. In the parable, the master tells his servants to trade with what he has entrusted to them (Luke 19:13). The person is the beginning, subject and goal of every social institution. Some communities, like the family and the state, flow directly from human nature.
days.question: Which community in your life most helps you grow, and how do you help it?

days.title: Subsidiarity and Conversion
days.summary: Too much state control can threaten freedom and initiative. So the Church teaches subsidiarity: a larger community should not take over the proper work of a smaller one, such as a family or local group, but should support it when needed. God himself shares his governance, entrusting creatures with roles of their own. Society needs a right order of values, putting spiritual and interior goods above material ones.
