Reforming institutions matters, but lasting change also needs inner conversion. Charity is the greatest social commandment. Jesus’ words apply here: whoever seeks to gain his life will lose it, and whoever loses it will keep it (Luke 17:33).
days.question: What change in society do you long for that must also begin in your own heart?

days.title: The Person and Society in Brief
days.summary: This review sums up the teaching on human community. There is a likeness between the unity of the divine Persons and the brotherhood people are called to build. People need social life to grow, and the person is the root, subject and purpose of every social body. Taking part in voluntary groups and associations should be encouraged. Subsidiarity means larger bodies support, rather than replace, smaller ones. Society should make virtue easier, not harder, and keep a right order of values. Where sin has bent the social climate, the answer is conversion of hearts and God’s grace. Charity calls for and makes possible the work of justice.
days.question: Where could you give some time to a group that serves others?

days.title: Authority in Society
days.summary: Every human community needs authority to guide it and serve the common good. Authority’s moral basis comes from God, as Paul teaches in Romans 13:1–2 and Peter in 1 Peter 2:13–17. Christians are urged to pray for rulers (1 Timothy 2:1–2). The particular form of government is left to the free choice of citizens. Authority is legitimate only when it seeks the common good and uses morally acceptable means. Laws that are unjust or contrary to the moral order do not bind in conscience. Power is best balanced by other powers and limits, so that the rule of law prevails over the arbitrary will of anyone.
days.question: Do you pray for those who govern, including leaders you disagree with?

days.title: The Common Good
days.summary: The common good is the sum of social conditions that let groups and individuals reach their fulfillment more fully and easily. It has three essential parts. First, respect for the person and for basic rights, such as freedom of conscience and religion. Second, the social well-being and development of the group, making available what people need for a truly human life: food, clothing, health, work, education, culture and the right to found a family. Third, peace, the stability and security of a just order. The state is to defend and promote the common good. Today it also reaches worldwide, calling for international cooperation and care for refugees and migrants.
days.question: What is one way you could serve the common good in your neighborhood?

days.title: Responsibility and Participation
days.summary: Participation means each person freely and generously taking part in social life. It starts close to home, in caring for one’s family and doing one’s work well. As far as possible, citizens should also take an active part in public life. Fraud and other tricks to dodge the law or civic duties are wrong and must be firmly rejected. Those who hold authority should strengthen the values that earn trust and help people live with hope. A review then begins: the ultimate source of authority is God (Romans 13:1), and every human community needs authority to hold it together and help it reach its goals.
days.question: Where are you being asked to take more responsibility for those around you?

days.title: Society’s Order in Brief
days.summary: This review continues the summary on social life. Political community and its authority are rooted in human nature and belong to the order God created. Authority acts rightly when it serves the common good and uses moral means. Different forms of government are legitimate as long as they seek the good of their people. Authority must work within the moral order and protect the conditions for freedom. The common good includes respect for persons, social well-being and development, and peace. Everyone shares responsibility for it. The state must defend it, and the good of the whole human family calls for cooperation among nations.
days.question: How do your daily choices affect people you will never meet?

days.title: Respect for the Human Person
days.summary: Social justice means arranging society so that people and groups can receive what is due to them by their nature and calling. It depends on respect for each person’s dignity, which society does not grant but must recognize. Each neighbor is to be seen as another self, especially the poor and vulnerable. Jesus said that what we do for the least of his brethren we do for him (Matthew 25:40). This duty grows stronger the more needy someone is. It reaches even enemies, since Jesus commands us to love them (Matthew 5:43–44). We can reject an error while still loving the person who holds it.
days.question: Whom do you find it hardest to see as another self?

days.title: Equality, Differences, Solidarity
days.summary: All people share equal dignity: made in God’s image, redeemed by Christ and called to the same happiness. So every form of unjust discrimination is contrary to God’s plan. Yet people differ in age, ability, health and resources. In the parable of the talents (Matthew 25:14–30), each servant receives a different amount. Such differences are meant to encourage generosity and sharing; sinful inequalities that crush millions are not. Solidarity, or social friendship, means sharing goods and work and seeking fair solutions between rich and poor, workers and employers, and nations. Jesus says to seek first the Kingdom, and the rest will be added (Matthew 6:33).
days.question: What gift or resource could you share more generously with someone in need?

days.title: Law and Grace Begin
days.summary: A review sums up the teaching on social justice. Society gives people their due by respecting their dignity. Equal dignity rules out unjust inequality, while legitimate differences invite us to share. Solidarity is an expression of Christian love and covers spiritual as well as material goods. Then Chapter Three, on law and grace, opens. We are called to happiness with God but wounded by sin, so we need salvation. God’s help comes in Christ through the law that guides us and the grace that sustains us. Paul writes: work out your salvation with fear and trembling, for God is at work in you (Philippians 2:12–13).
days.question: How have you seen God at work in you, even in your efforts to do good?

days.title: The Natural Moral Law
days.summary: Moral law is God’s fatherly teaching for our good. It points out the ways that lead to happiness and forbids the paths that lead away. Christ is the end of the law (Romans 10:4). The law takes several forms: the eternal law in God, the natural law, the revealed law of the Old and New Testaments, and civil and Church laws. Natural law is written in the human heart. It is the light of reason God gives us so we can tell good from evil. Its main precepts appear in the Ten Commandments, and it binds all people everywhere.
days.question: When have you sensed a moral truth before anyone taught it to you?

days.title: Natural Law and the Old Law
days.summary: Natural law stays the same through history, beneath changing customs; even when people deny it, it rises again in human hearts. It is the foundation for moral rules and for just civil law. But in our fallen state not everyone sees its demands clearly, so grace and revelation help us know them with certainty. The Old Law, given through Moses, is the first stage of revealed law. Its core is the Ten Commandments. Paul calls it holy (Romans 7:12), yet it was imperfect: it showed what to do but did not give the strength of the Spirit to do it. It served as a tutor leading toward Christ (Galatians 3:24).
days.question: Where do you know what is right but need God’s strength to do it?

days.title: The New Law of the Gospel
days.summary: The New Law, or Law of the Gospel, is the perfection of God’s law, natural and revealed. It is above all the grace of the Holy Spirit, given through faith in Christ and working through love. Jeremiah foresaw a covenant written on hearts (Jeremiah 31:31–34). The Sermon on the Mount expresses it best. Jesus did not abolish the Law but fulfilled it (Matthew 5:17–19), drawing out its hidden depth and reaching into the heart, where good and evil begin (Matthew 15:18–19). It shapes our almsgiving, prayer and fasting, done for the Father who sees in secret (Matthew 6:1–18), and teaches us to pray the Our Father.
days.question: Which line of the Sermon on the Mount challenges you most right now?

days.title: Law of Love and the Counsels
days.summary: The New Law is a law of love, since we act from the love the Spirit gives rather than from fear. It is a law of grace, giving the strength to act, and a law of freedom, making us friends of Christ (John 15:15) and children who cry Abba, Father (Romans 8:15). Besides the commandments, it offers the evangelical counsels of poverty, chastity and obedience. The commandments remove what is opposed to charity; the counsels remove what might hinder it, even if not opposed to it. A review then begins: law is a rule of conduct given for the common good, and Christ is its end.
days.question: Do you relate to God more as a servant who fears or as a friend who trusts?

days.title: Moral Law in Brief
days.summary: This review finishes the moral law. Natural law is unchanging and lasts through history; it is the basis of moral rules and civil law. The Old Law is the first stage of revealed law, summed up in the Ten Commandments, and many of its truths can be reached by reason. It prepared the way for the Gospel. The New Law is the grace of the Holy Spirit received through faith in Christ, expressed above all in the Sermon on the Mount. It fulfills and perfects the Old Law. It is a law of love, grace and freedom, and it includes the evangelical counsels beyond the commandments.
days.question: How might you live one of the evangelical counsels in your own state of life?

days.title: Made Right With God
days.summary: Justification means being made right with God. The Holy Spirit’s grace cleanses us from sin and gives us God’s own righteousness through faith in Jesus Christ (Romans 3:22). Through Baptism we die to sin and live for God in Christ (Romans 6:8–11), joined to him like branches to the vine (John 15:1). Its first work is conversion, answering Jesus’ call to repent (Matthew 4:17). Justification brings forgiveness of sins and the renewal of the inner person. Christ merited it for us by his Passion. It is God’s free gift, yet it calls for our free cooperation. Saint Augustine thought it a greater work than creating heaven and earth.
days.question: What does it mean to you that God makes you righteous, not only forgiven?

days.title: The Gift of Grace
days.summary: Grace is God’s favor: the free, undeserved help he gives us to answer his call to become his children and share in his divine life (2 Peter 1:3–4; John 1:12–18). It is supernatural, beyond what human nature could reach. Sanctifying grace is a lasting gift that heals the soul and makes it holy, first received in Baptism. Actual graces are God’s help at particular moments. Even our first turning to God is prompted by grace, yet God wants a free response. In Christ we become a new creation (2 Corinthians 5:17), and Jesus promises water welling up to eternal life (John 4:14).
days.question: When have you felt God’s help arrive at just the right moment?

days.title: Charisms, Graces and Merit
days.summary: God also gives special graces, such as the graces of each sacrament. Charisms are gifts given to serve others and build up the Church, like those Paul lists in Romans 12:6–8. Because grace is supernatural, we cannot feel it directly, but we can see its effects: by their fruits you will know them (Matthew 7:20). Merit means a reward that is due. Strictly, no one has a claim on God or can merit the first grace. But God freely chose to let us share in his work, so our merits are first his gifts. Moved by the Spirit and charity, we can merit graces for ourselves and others.
days.question: What gift has God given you to serve others, and how are you using it?

days.title: Called to Be Holy
days.summary: All the baptized are called to holiness, to the fullness of Christian life and the perfection of charity. Jesus says, be perfect as your heavenly Father is perfect (Matthew 5:48). God works all things for good for those who love him (Romans 8:28–30). Growth in holiness leads toward ever closer union with Christ. The way passes through the cross: there is no holiness without self-denial and spiritual struggle, which lead step by step to peace and joy. We hope for the grace to persevere and for the New Jerusalem (Revelation 21:2). A review then recalls that justification, merited by Christ’s Passion, frees us from sin and renews us within.
days.question: What small act of self-denial could help you grow closer to Christ this week?

days.title: Grace and Holiness in Brief
days.summary: This review sums up grace, merit and holiness. Grace is the help God gives so we can answer our call to be his adopted children. God always moves first, preparing and calling forth our free response. Sanctifying grace is a free gift that makes us pleasing to God, while charisms serve the good of the Church. We have merit before God only because he freely chose to include us in his work, and no one can earn the first grace of forgiveness. All Christians are called to holiness. Following Jesus means denying ourselves and taking up our cross, as he asked (Matthew 16:24).
days.question: What cross are you carrying now, and how might you carry it with Jesus?

days.title: The Church as Mother and Teacher
days.summary: We live our Christian calling within the Church. There we receive God’s word, grace through the sacraments, and the example of the saints, above all Mary. Our moral life is a form of worship, offering ourselves to God (Romans 12:1). Paul calls the Church the pillar and bulwark of the truth (1 Timothy 3:15). The Magisterium, the teaching office of the Pope and the bishops in communion with him, teaches faith and morals with Christ’s authority, usually through catechesis and preaching built around the Ten Commandments. Its teaching extends to the natural law. The gift of infallibility protects the deposit of faith, the truth handed down from the apostles.
days.question: How has the Church been a mother to you in your life of faith?

days.title: Conscience and the Precepts
days.summary: God’s law is entrusted to the Church, and the faithful have a right to be taught it. Personal conscience and reason should not be set against the Magisterium. With the Spirit’s help (1 Corinthians 2:10–15), Christians receive it with trust. The precepts of the Church set a bare minimum of prayer and moral effort. Catholics are to attend Mass on Sundays and holy days and rest from work; go to confession at least once a year; receive Communion at least during the Easter season; keep the days of fasting and abstinence; and help provide for the Church’s needs. These help us grow in love of God and neighbor.
days.question: Which precept of the Church do you find easiest, and which hardest, to keep?

days.title: Living as Witnesses
days.summary: The faithful lives of the baptized are the first condition for proclaiming the Gospel. Holiness draws others toward Christ, and a good life prepares hearts for the word. Christians help build up the Church as it grows toward the full stature of Christ (Ephesians 4:13), and so they hasten the coming of God’s Kingdom. A review then closes this part. Moral life is spiritual worship, nourished by the liturgy and the sacraments. The Church’s pastors teach the faithful what to believe and how to live, and its precepts set out the minimum. The gift of infallibility protects the truths God has revealed.
days.question: Who might come to know Christ through the way you live?

days.title: Teacher, What Must I Do?
days.summary: Section Two opens with the rich young man asking Jesus what good he must do to gain eternal life (Matthew 19:16–21). Jesus answers: keep the commandments, and then invites him to follow. Jesus did not abolish the Law but fulfilled it (Matthew 5:17), asking for a righteousness deeper than outward observance. Asked which commandment is greatest, he named love of God with all one’s heart and love of neighbor as oneself (Matthew 22:36–40), drawing on Deuteronomy 6:5 and Leviticus 19:18. The Ten Commandments, literally the ten words, were given by God himself. They are the heart of the covenant and are best understood in the light of Christ.
days.question: If you asked Jesus what you still lack, what might he say?

days.title: The Decalogue and the Covenant
days.summary: The Ten Commandments were given in a moment of revelation and covenant, as God spoke to his people face to face at the mountain (Deuteronomy 5:2–4). They begin with God’s saving act: I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of Egypt (Exodus 20:2). So the commandments are first a response of love and gratitude to the God who set Israel free. The people answered that they would do all the Lord had spoken (Exodus 24:7). The commandments describe the life of those freed from slavery to sin. The Church’s Tradition has always given them a central place in teaching the faith, though numbering them in different ways.
days.question: How does remembering what God has done for you change how you see his commands?

days.title: The Unity of the Commandments
days.summary: The Ten Commandments fall into two tables: the first three about love of God, the other seven about love of neighbor. They form one whole. To break one is to offend against all, as James teaches (James 2:10–11). They express the natural law, and they were also revealed because sin had darkened human reason. Their obligations are basically grave and unchanging, though some acts in a given matter may be less serious. Yet we cannot keep them by our own strength. Jesus says, apart from me you can do nothing (John 15:5). United to him, we can love one another as he has loved us (John 15:12).
days.question: Which commandment do you most need Christ’s help to keep?

days.title: The Ten Commandments in Brief
days.summary: This review sums up the teaching on the Decalogue. To the question of what good we must do to have eternal life, Jesus points to the commandments and calls us to follow him. By his life and teaching he showed they remain valid. The Ten Commandments were given within God’s covenant with his people, and the Church has always kept them at the center of its teaching. They form a single whole and state the natural law in clear terms. They bind seriously. What God commands, he also makes possible by his grace, so keeping them is not a burden we carry alone.
days.question: Do you see the commandments more as a burden or as a gift?

days.title: Worship God Alone
days.summary: Chapter One covers the first three commandments, about loving God with all our heart, soul and mind (Deuteronomy 6:4–5; Matthew 22:37). The first commandment calls us to adore and serve God alone (Deuteronomy 6:13). God made himself known through his saving deeds, and he asks for faith, hope and love in return. Faith comes first: we must nourish and protect it with care and reject what opposes it. Paul warns that people who knew God but did not honor him fell into darkness and idolatry (Romans 1:18–25). Voluntary doubt, which neglects or refuses to hold as true what God has revealed, is a sin against faith.
days.question: How are you feeding your faith so that it keeps growing?

days.title: Sins Against Faith, Hope, Love
days.summary: Some sins oppose faith directly. Incredulity neglects revealed truth or refuses to assent to it. Heresy is the stubborn denial, after Baptism, of a truth that must be believed; apostasy is total rejection of the faith; schism is refusal to submit to the Pope or to remain in communion with the Church. Hope can be lost through despair, which stops trusting God’s goodness and mercy, or through presumption, which expects salvation without effort or forgiveness without conversion. Love of God is wounded by indifference, ingratitude, lukewarmness, spiritual sloth (acedia) and, worst of all, hatred of God. Scripture asks us to love God with all our heart (Deuteronomy 6:5).
days.question: Do you lean more toward discouragement or toward taking God’s mercy for granted?

days.title: The Virtue of Religion
days.summary: The virtue of religion gives God what is due to him. Adoration comes first: acknowledging God as Creator and Savior, Lord of all. Jesus said to worship the Lord your God and serve him alone (Luke 4:8). Mary’s Magnificat shows a humble heart praising God (Luke 1:46–49). Prayer lifts the mind to God and is needed to keep the commandments; Jesus taught us to pray always (Luke 18:1). Sacrifice is a sign of adoration, but the prophets warned that outward offerings without a changed heart do not please God (Amos 5:21–25; Hosea 6:6). Christ’s offering on the cross is the perfect sacrifice.
days.question: When did you last simply adore God, asking nothing?

days.title: Vows and Religious Freedom
days.summary: A vow is a deliberate, free promise made to God about some better good. Paul himself made a vow (Acts 18:18). The Church especially values the vows of religious life. Each person also has a duty to seek the truth about God and his Church and to embrace it once known. At the same time, every person has a right to religious freedom: no one may be forced to act against conscience in religious matters, nor prevented from acting by it, within just limits. This right rests on human dignity, not on any claim that error has rights.
days.question: What promise have you made to God, and how are you keeping it?

days.title: Superstition, Idolatry, Divination
days.summary: The first commandment forbids honoring any god but the one Lord. Superstition distorts religion, as when we credit power to the mere outward form of prayers or sacred signs, apart from the inner attitude they require; Jesus criticized such thinking (Matthew 23:16–22). Idolatry gives divine worship to a creature, whether false gods, money, power, the state, or anything put in God’s place. The story of Daniel and the idol Bel (Daniel 14) mocks gods made by hands. Divination is also rejected, including horoscopes, astrology, palm reading, fortune tellers and mediums. These try to control time and history and to seek hidden powers, rather than trusting God.
days.question: What in your life competes most with God for first place?

days.title: Magic, Sacrilege and Unbelief
days.summary: Magic and sorcery try to tame hidden powers and gain power over others; they are gravely contrary to the virtue of religion. Irreligion also offends God. Tempting God means putting his goodness to the test, like Israel at Massah (Exodus 17:1–7) or Satan urging Jesus to jump from the Temple (Luke 4:9). Sacrilege treats sacred things, persons or places with irreverence, above all the Eucharist. Simony is trying to buy or sell spiritual things, as Simon the magician tried to do (Acts 8:9–24). Atheism rejects or denies the existence of God. It takes many forms, including practical materialism and the claim that human freedom requires denying God.
days.question: Have you ever tried to bargain with God or test him?

days.title: Atheism and Holy Images
days.summary: Atheism is a sin against the virtue of religion, though circumstances can lessen guilt, and believers share the blame when their poor example hides God’s face. Agnosticism holds that God’s existence cannot be known, or makes no judgment about it; it often amounts to practical atheism. The command against graven images forbids idols, since God showed no visible form at Sinai (Deuteronomy 4:15–16). Yet God told Moses to make cherubim for the ark (Exodus 25:18–22). By becoming man, Christ opened a new way of picturing God. Venerating images is not idolatry; as Saint Basil taught, honor given to an image passes to the one it shows.
days.question: Does your daily example make God easier or harder for others to see?

days.title: The First Commandment in Brief
days.summary: This review sums up the first commandment. We are to love God with our whole heart, soul and strength. This means believing in him, hoping in him and loving him above all. Adoration, prayer, sacrifice and promises made to him are ways of honoring him. People must be free to worship God according to conscience, without coercion. Superstition distorts the worship owed to God, and idolatry puts something else in his place. Tempting God, sacrilege and simony are sins of irreligion. Atheism denies God. Holy images are honored, not worshiped, because the Son of God truly became man.
days.question: How could your home show more clearly that God comes first?

days.title: The Holy Name of God
days.summary: The second commandment calls us to respect the Lord’s name. A name expresses who someone is, and God revealed his name to his people as an act of trust. So it is to be spoken only to bless, praise and glorify him (Psalm 29:2). A sense of the sacred belongs to the virtue of religion. Believers must witness to the Lord’s name without fear (Matthew 10:32). Promises made to others in God’s name engage his honor, and breaking them misuses his name. Blasphemy, speaking hatred, insult or defiance against God, the Church, the saints or holy things, is directly opposed to this commandment (James 2:7).
days.question: How do you speak God’s name in ordinary conversation?

days.title: Oaths and the Christian Name
days.summary: This commandment forbids false oaths. An oath calls God as witness, so lying under oath, or perjury, insults him. Jesus taught, do not swear at all, but let your yes mean yes (Matthew 5:33–37; James 5:12). The Church reads this as forbidding needless oaths, not all oaths; Paul himself called on God as witness (2 Corinthians 1:23). Serious and just reasons can justify an oath. Baptism is given in the name of the Father, Son and Holy Spirit (Matthew 28:19), and there we receive our name. God calls each of us by name (Isaiah 43:1), and promises a new name in heaven (Revelation 2:17).
days.question: Can people count on your simple yes and no?

days.title: The Second Commandment in Brief
days.summary: This review sums up the second commandment. God’s name is holy, as the psalmist sings: how majestic is your name in all the earth (Psalm 8:1). The commandment forbids every improper use of God’s name, and blasphemy is a serious sin. A false oath calls on God to witness a lie. Saint Ignatius of Loyola advised against swearing by God or by any creature except with truth, need and reverence. In Baptism we receive a name in the Church, often that of a saint who becomes our model and helper. Christians begin prayer with the Sign of the Cross. God calls each of us by our own name.
days.question: What does your baptismal name, or your patron saint, mean to you?

days.title: Keep the Sabbath Holy
days.summary: The third commandment says to remember the Sabbath day and keep it holy. Scripture gives two reasons. God rested on the seventh day after creation (Exodus 20:11), and God freed Israel from slavery in Egypt (Deuteronomy 5:15). The Sabbath is a sign of the covenant (Exodus 31:16–17) and a day of rest from work. Nehemiah enforced it against trading (Nehemiah 13:15–22). Jesus was accused of breaking it, yet he respected its holiness and showed its true meaning: the Sabbath was made for man, and the Son of Man is lord of the Sabbath (Mark 2:27–28). It is a day for doing good, such as healing (Mark 3:4).
days.question: What keeps you from truly resting, and what would Sabbath rest look like for you?

days.title: The Lord’s Day
days.summary: Jesus rose from the dead on the first day of the week (Matthew 28:1; Mark 16:1–2; Luke 24:1; John 20:1). So Christians call it the Lord’s Day, Sunday. It is also called the eighth day, the beginning of the new creation. For Christians, Sunday fulfills the Sabbath and takes its place. From the start, believers gathered for the apostles’ teaching and the breaking of bread (Acts 2:42–46), and Hebrews 10:25 urges them not to neglect meeting together. The Sunday Eucharist is at the heart of the Church’s life, and the parish is its usual home. Catholics are obliged to attend Mass on Sundays and holy days of obligation.
days.question: How could you make Sunday feel more like a celebration of the Resurrection?

days.title: Rest, Worship and Sunday
days.summary: The Sunday Eucharist anchors Christian life, so deliberately missing Mass without a serious reason, such as illness or the care of infants, is a grave sin. Sunday is a day of rest too, echoing God’s rest after creation (Genesis 2:2). Christians should avoid work or activities that keep them from worshiping God, from the joy of the day, from works of mercy and from rest of mind and body. It suits family time, prayer and visiting the sick. Christians should respect others’ Sunday rest and seek its recognition in society, as a foretaste of heaven’s festive gathering (Hebrews 12:22–23).
days.question: Whom could you visit or call on a Sunday soon?

days.title: Love Your Neighbor
days.summary: A review sums up the third commandment: keep the Lord’s Day holy by celebrating the Eucharist and resting from work, and help society honor Sunday. Then Chapter Two opens with Jesus’ answer to the question of the greatest commandment: love God with all your heart, and love your neighbor as yourself (Matthew 22:34–40; Mark 12:29–31). The second table of the Ten Commandments spells out what love of neighbor requires. Jesus also gave a new command, to love one another as he has loved us. Paul says the commandments are summed up in one, love your neighbor, because love is the fulfilling of the law (Romans 13:8–10).
days.question: Who is the neighbor God is asking you to love more today?

days.title: The Family in God’s Plan
days.summary: The fourth commandment, honor your father and mother (Exodus 20:12; Deuteronomy 5:16), begins the second table. It concerns first our parents, then relatives, teachers, employers and civil authorities. It carries a promise of long life and peace. A man and a woman united in marriage, together with their children, form a family. This bond comes before any recognition by public authority. The Christian family is a communion of persons that reflects the communion of the Father, Son and Holy Spirit, and it is called a domestic church. Scripture describes mutual love and respect between spouses, parents and children (Colossians 3:18–21; Ephesians 5:21).
days.question: How could your family, or your closest community, become more of a domestic church?

days.title: The Family and Society
days.summary: The family is the first cell of social life. There we learn moral values, honor God and learn to use freedom well. Society must support and strengthen families and respect their rights. These include the right to found a family and raise children according to one’s convictions, to own property, work, find housing and receive medical care, and to form associations. Families are called to care for the young and the old, the sick, the disabled and the poor. James writes that true religion includes caring for orphans and widows in their distress (James 1:27). We are to see others as brothers and sisters.
days.question: Which family near you could use some practical help?

days.title: Duties of Children
days.summary: Children owe their parents respect, which grows from gratitude for the gift of life and for their love and work (Sirach 7:27–28). While living at home, children should obey their parents in all that is for their good (Ephesians 6:1; Colossians 3:20; Proverbs 6:20). Once grown, they still owe respect and, as needed, material and moral support in old age, sickness or loneliness (Sirach 3:12–13). Jesus rebuked those who used religious excuses to neglect their parents (Mark 7:10–12). The commandment also calls for harmony among brothers and sisters, and gratitude to those who passed on the faith (2 Timothy 1:5).
days.question: How can you show gratitude to those who gave you life and faith?

days.title: Duties of Parents
days.summary: Parents are the first teachers of their children. They educate first by creating a home where tenderness, forgiveness, respect, faithfulness and generous service are the rule. Good example teaches most, including parents admitting their own failings. Parents should correct their children wisely without provoking them (Ephesians 6:4; Sirach 30:1–2). From the earliest years they share the faith, helping children grow through prayer and the sacraments. Children in turn help their parents grow in holiness, and everyone in the family must forgive one another (Matthew 18:21–22). Parents may choose schools that fit their convictions, and they should respect their grown children’s free choice of work and state of life.
days.question: What example are you setting for the young people who watch you?

days.title: Family, Kingdom and Authority
days.summary: Family bonds are important but not absolute. Our first calling is to follow Jesus: whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me (Matthew 10:37). Parents should respect a child’s call to religious life or the priesthood. The fourth commandment also asks us to honor all who rightly hold authority. Authority is meant as service (Matthew 20:26). Those in power must respect human rights and govern justly. Citizens should see in their rulers servants of God’s order (Romans 13:1–2; 1 Peter 2:13) and work with them for the common good.
days.question: How do you use whatever authority you have, at home or at work?

days.title: Duties of Citizens
days.summary: Citizens share responsibility for the common good with those in authority. That includes loving and serving one’s country, paying taxes, voting and defending the nation (Romans 13:7). Christians are to pray for those in authority (1 Timothy 2:2). Wealthier nations should welcome foreigners seeking security and a livelihood, as far as they are able, and immigrants should respect their new country’s laws and heritage. A citizen must refuse to obey laws that contradict the moral order or the Gospel, for we must obey God rather than men (Acts 5:29). Jesus taught to give Caesar what is Caesar’s and God what is God’s (Matthew 22:21).
days.question: How do you weigh your duties to your country and to God?

days.title: The Fourth Commandment in Brief
days.summary: This review sums up the fourth commandment: honor your father and your mother. The commandment orders family life and the duties of children, parents and those in authority. The marriage covenant of a man and a woman, open to children, is the foundation of the family. A healthy family life is closely tied to the well-being of society. Children owe their parents respect, gratitude, obedience while at home, and help when it is needed. Parents are the first ones responsible for raising their children in the faith, and they should respect and encourage their children’s vocations, remembering that following Jesus comes first.
days.question: Is there a family relationship that needs your forgiveness or patience today?

days.title: Human Life Is Sacred
days.summary: The review of the fourth commandment ends: authorities must respect human rights, and no one may obey commands that violate the moral order. Then comes the fifth commandment, you shall not kill. Human life is sacred from its beginning, because God creates it for relationship with him. God alone is Lord of life. No one may directly take the life of an innocent person. Cain’s murder of Abel shows anger and envy at work from the start, and Abel’s blood cries out to God (Genesis 4:8–12). God’s covenant with Noah affirms the worth of human life (Genesis 9:5–6).
days.question: Where do you see human life treated as less than sacred, and how can you respond?

days.title: Legitimate Defense
days.summary: Scripture forbids killing the innocent and just (Exodus 23:7). Jesus goes further, forbidding even anger and hatred, and asks us to turn the other cheek and love our enemies (Matthew 5:21–44). Yet defending oneself is legitimate. Loving oneself is a basic duty, and someone who kills an attacker in true self-defense, using no more force than needed, is not guilty of murder. For those responsible for others’ lives, defense can be a grave duty. Public authority may punish crime in proportion to the offense, aiming at justice and the offender’s reform. The Church now teaches that the death penalty is inadmissible.
days.question: Is there anger in your heart that Jesus is asking you to let go?

days.title: Murder and Unborn Life
days.summary: The fifth commandment forbids direct and intentional killing as gravely sinful; Abel’s blood cries out to heaven (Genesis 4:10). It is also wrong to cause death indirectly, for example by refusing help to someone in danger or tolerating famine without trying to remedy it. The prophet Amos condemns those who trample the needy (Amos 8:4–10). Human life must be protected from the moment of conception. God tells Jeremiah that he knew him before forming him in the womb (Jeremiah 1:5; see also Psalm 139:15). Deliberately procuring an abortion is gravely wrong. Civil law should protect the rights of the unborn, and the human embryo must be treated as a person.
days.question: How can you support mothers and families who are struggling to welcome a child?

days.title: Euthanasia and Suicide
days.summary: The sick and disabled deserve special respect. Direct euthanasia, ending such lives by act or omission, is morally unacceptable. Stopping burdensome or disproportionate treatment can be legitimate; it accepts death rather than causing it. Ordinary care is still owed. Painkillers may be used even if they might shorten life, if death is not intended. We are stewards, not owners, of the life God gives. Suicide is gravely contrary to love of self, neighbor and God. Yet grave suffering or fear can lessen responsibility, so we do not despair of the salvation of those who die this way, and the Church prays for them.
days.question: Who in your life is sick or lonely and needs your presence?

days.title: Scandal and Care for Health
days.summary: Scandal is an attitude or behavior that leads another person to do evil. It is a grave fault when it deliberately draws someone into serious sin, especially when done by people with authority or influence. Jesus warned that it would be better to be drowned with a millstone than to cause a little one to sin (Matthew 18:6). Life and health are gifts to care for reasonably, without worshiping the body. Temperance avoids excess in food, alcohol, tobacco or medicine. Using drugs outside medical need is a grave offense. Scientific research must serve the human person.
days.question: Is anything in your habits leading someone else, or yourself, toward harm?

days.title: Science, the Body, and the Dead
days.summary: Science and medicine are good gifts, but they must serve people and never treat them as raw material. Research on human beings needs their free and informed consent. Giving organs, in life or after death, can be a generous act of love, as long as the donor consents and is not killed or gravely harmed for it. Kidnapping, terrorism, and torture are grave wrongs. The dying deserve care, prayer, and the sacraments. The bodies of the dead deserve reverence, as Tobit shows by burying his slain countrymen (Tobit 1:16–18). Cremation is allowed when it does not deny faith in the resurrection.
days.question: How do you show respect for the sick, the dying, or the dead in your family?

days.title: Peace Begins in the Heart
days.summary: The fifth commandment also guards peace. Jesus traces murder back to the angry heart (Matthew 5:21–22) and asks us to love even our enemies (Matthew 5:44). Peace is more than the absence of war: it is the calm of a rightly ordered society, the fruit of justice and love. Christ, the Prince of Peace, reconciled us to God through his cross (Ephesians 2:14–16). Everyone must work to avoid war, yet a nation may defend itself by force under strict conditions: the harm must be grave and certain, other means must have failed, success must be likely, and the response must not cause worse evils.
days.question: Is there anger or resentment in you that keeps you from peace with someone?

days.title: War, Conscience, and Arms
days.summary: Those who serve in the military can be true servants of their nation’s security and of peace. Governments should also make room for conscientious objectors, who serve the community in another way. Once war breaks out, the moral law still holds: civilians, wounded soldiers, and prisoners must be treated humanely, and orders to commit genocide must be refused. Destroying whole cities along with their people is a crime against God and humanity. Piling up weapons does not secure lasting peace, and it drains resources the poor need. Injustice, envy, distrust, and pride are the deeper roots of war. Isaiah foresees swords beaten into plowshares (Isaiah 2:4).
days.question: What small seeds of injustice or distrust could you help uproot where you live?

days.title: Every Human Life Is Sacred
days.summary: This summary gathers the teaching of the fifth commandment. Every human life, from conception until natural death, is sacred, because each person is made in God’s image and belongs to him. Deliberately killing an innocent person is gravely wrong. Defending yourself and others against an unjust attacker is a different act, and for those responsible for others it can even be a duty. From its very first moment, the unborn child has the right to life, so direct abortion is a grave sin. The human embryo must be protected, cared for, and healed like any other human being, never treated as material for experiments.
days.question: How can you honor the dignity of a life that others overlook?

days.title: Euthanasia, Suicide, and Peacemaking
days.summary: Intentionally ending the life of the sick, disabled, or dying is murder, whatever the motive. Suicide contradicts the love we owe to God, to ourselves, and to others, though the Church teaches that we should not despair of the salvation of those who have taken their lives. Scandal, leading another person into sin, is a serious wrong. Because war brings so much evil, everyone is bound to pray and work to prevent it, and the moral law still binds during armed conflict. The arms race endangers humanity and harms the poor. Jesus calls peacemakers blessed, for they will be called children of God (Matthew 5:9).
days.question: Who in your life needs you to be a peacemaker this week?

days.title: Created Male and Female
days.summary: The sixth commandment opens with God’s design. God is love, and he made man and woman in his image, with a calling to love and communion (Genesis 1:27–28). Our sexuality touches every part of us: body, mind, and heart, including our capacity to form bonds with others. Each person should accept his or her identity as a man or a woman. Men and women are equal in dignity and made to complete each other. In marriage the two become one flesh (Genesis 2:24). Jesus restored God’s original plan, teaching that marriage is lifelong (Matthew 19:6) and that lust in the heart is already adultery (Matthew 5:27–28).
days.question: How do you see God’s image in the men and women around you?

days.title: The Virtue of Chastity
days.summary: Chastity is the virtue that brings our sexuality into harmony with the whole person, so that body and spirit work together in love. It rules out a double life (Matthew 5:37). Chastity is learned gradually as we grow in self-control, which makes us truly free: desires that rule us leave us unhappy, while desires we govern leave room for peace. Helps include self-knowledge, self-denial, the commandments, and prayer. Chastity belongs to temperance, the virtue that moderates our appetites. It is never won once for all; it grows by stages, with effort at every age, and God is patient with our weakness.
days.question: Which habit could help you grow in self-control and inner freedom?

days.title: Chastity, Friendship, and Lust
days.summary: Chastity is a task for society as well as for each person. It is a moral virtue, yet also a gift of God and a fruit of the Holy Spirit (Galatians 5:22). Charity is the soul of every virtue, and chastity teaches us to give ourselves to others. It also opens the way to deep friendship. All the baptized have put on Christ (Galatians 3:27) and are called to chastity according to their state of life: married people within marriage, others through continence, and engaged couples by waiting until their wedding. Lust is a disordered desire for sexual pleasure sought for its own sake.
days.question: Which of your friendships most helps you grow toward God?

days.title: Sins Against Chastity
days.summary: The Church names acts that go against chastity: masturbation, fornication (sex between people not married to each other), pornography, prostitution, and rape. Each separates sex from the love and gift of self it is meant to express, and rape is a grave violence that can never be justified. Immaturity, habit, or anxiety can lessen a person’s guilt. The body is a temple of the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 6:19). The Church teaches that sexual acts between people of the same sex are contrary to God’s plan, while people with same-sex attraction must be treated with respect, compassion, and sensitivity. They too are called to chastity and holiness, helped by grace.
days.question: Where do you need God’s mercy and strength to live chastely today?

days.title: The Gift of Married Love
days.summary: Sexuality is ordered to the love of husband and wife. In marriage, their bodily union is a sign and pledge of their spiritual communion. Before their first night together, Tobias and Sarah pray side by side (Tobit 8:4–9). Married intimacy is good, and God meant spouses to find joy in it. Marriage has two purposes: the good of the spouses and the passing on of life. It calls for lifelong fidelity, because Christ taught that what God has joined no one may separate (Matthew 19:6). Children are a gift, and each marital act should stay open to life. Parents share in God’s fatherhood (Ephesians 3:14–15).
days.question: How can you support the faithfulness of the married couples you know?

days.title: Responsible Parenthood
days.summary: Spouses may have good reasons to space births, but their motives must be honest and their methods must respect God’s design. Natural family planning, which relies on periods of abstinence, respects the bodies of husband and wife and keeps together the two meanings of the marital act: union and openness to life. Contraception deliberately breaks that link, and the Church teaches it is wrong in itself. The state must not override parents’ decisions. Large families are a sign of God’s blessing. Infertility brings real grief, like that of Abraham and Rachel (Genesis 15:2; 30:1), and research to heal it is welcome when it serves the person.
days.question: How do you receive children, your own or others’, as gifts rather than burdens?

days.title: The Child as Gift; Adultery
days.summary: Techniques that bring a third person into conception, such as donated sperm or eggs or a surrogate mother, are gravely wrong. Methods that use only the couple’s own cells are also not acceptable, because they separate conception from the act of love. A child is a gift, not something owed. Childless couples can still live fruitful lives, through adoption or service. Adultery is a grave injustice to the spouse (Matthew 5:27–28). Jesus restored the permanence of marriage (Mark 10:9). Separation is sometimes permitted, and a civil divorce may be tolerated to protect legal rights, but the marriage bond remains.
days.question: Whom could you quietly support who carries the pain of infertility or a broken marriage?

days.title: Wounds to Marriage and Family
days.summary: Divorce claims to break a covenant the spouses freely made for life, and a new union adds to the harm. Divorce also unsettles families and society, and children often suffer most. A spouse who tried to stay faithful and was abandoned may be an innocent victim. Polygamy contradicts the equal dignity of husband and wife. Incest, condemned in Leviticus 18 and by Paul (1 Corinthians 5:1), corrupts family relationships, and sexual abuse of children by adults entrusted with their care is a grave scandal. Living together without marriage, or a so-called trial marriage, cannot express the total and lasting gift of self that sexual union is meant to seal.
days.question: How can you help protect children and families in your parish or neighborhood?

days.title: Love and Marriage in Brief
days.summary: This summary gathers the teaching of the sixth commandment. Love is the basic calling of every human being. Man and woman are equal in dignity, and Christ is the model of chastity. Chastity unites our sexuality with the whole person, and every baptized person is called to it. Masturbation, fornication, pornography, and homosexual acts are named as grave sins against it. Spouses owe each other faithfulness, and their love is meant to bear fruit in children. Couples may space births for serious reasons, using morally acceptable means rather than sterilization or contraception. Adultery, divorce, polygamy, and living together outside marriage offend the dignity of marriage.
days.question: What part of the Church’s teaching on love and sexuality do you most want to understand better?

days.title: You Shall Not Steal
days.summary: The seventh commandment asks for justice and charity in how we use the earth’s goods and the fruits of work. God gave the earth to the whole human race (Genesis 1:26–29). Private property is legitimate and protects freedom and family security, yet owners are stewards whose goods should also benefit others. Theft, taking what belongs to another against the owner’s reasonable will, is wrong, though taking what one urgently needs to survive, such as food, is not theft. Other injustices include fraud, unjust wages, rigging prices, shoddy work, tax evasion, and waste. Amos and James condemn those who cheat workers and the poor (Amos 8:4–6; James 5:4).
days.question: Is there anything you owe, in money, time, or honest work, that you need to set right?

days.title: Promises, Restitution, and Creation
days.summary: Promises and fair contracts must be kept. When we have wronged someone we must make amends, like Zacchaeus, who repaid fourfold what he had taken (Luke 19:8). Gambling is not wrong in itself, but it becomes wrong when it takes what a person needs for himself or his family. Enslaving people or treating them as merchandise is a grave sin. This commandment also asks respect for creation. Animals are God’s creatures and bless him in their own way (Daniel 3:79–81). We may use them for food, clothing, work, and reasonable research, but causing them needless suffering is wrong.
days.question: How could you show greater care for the creatures and the world entrusted to you?

days.title: The Church’s Social Teaching
days.summary: Christian faith sheds light on how society should be ordered. The Church speaks to economic and social questions when basic human rights or the salvation of souls are at stake. Her social doctrine took shape especially from the nineteenth century, as the Gospel met the industrial age. It gives Catholics principles to think with and guidance for acting justly. An economy that makes profit the only rule is unacceptable: no one can serve both God and money (Matthew 6:24). The Church has rejected the atheistic and totalitarian ideologies of communism and socialism, and also a capitalism that puts the market above human work and dignity.
days.question: Where does money compete with God for first place in your decisions?

days.title: Work and the Economy
days.summary: Economic life exists to serve people, not the other way around. Work is both a duty and a dignity: through it we share in God’s work of creation, provide for our families, and serve others (2 Thessalonians 3:10). Though toil became hard after the Fall (Genesis 3:17–19), work united to Christ can make us holy. The worker matters more than the product. People have a right to economic initiative, and the state should protect freedom, property, sound money, and reliable public services. Businesses must weigh the good of people, not only profit. Access to work should be open to all, without unjust discrimination.
days.question: How might you offer your daily work, paid or unpaid, to God today?

days.title: Just Wages and Solidarity
days.summary: A just wage is the fair fruit of work, and withholding it is a grave injustice; the Law and James both warn against cheating laborers (Leviticus 19:13; James 5:4). A strike can be legitimate when it is unavoidable and aims at a just goal. Among nations, the gap between rich and poor calls for solidarity. Wealthy nations bear serious responsibility to help those that cannot develop on their own, through direct aid and fairer trade and financial systems. Shaping political and economic life is chiefly the work of lay people, while pastors teach the moral principles.
days.question: How do your purchases and habits affect workers you will never meet?

days.title: Love for the Poor
days.summary: Jesus will judge us by what we did for the hungry, the stranger, and the prisoner (Matthew 25:31–46). The Church has always loved the poor with a special love, and this love cannot live alongside greed (James 5:1–6). Early Church Fathers taught that giving to the poor returns what is already theirs. The works of mercy put this love into practice: feeding, clothing, and visiting, and also teaching, comforting, and forgiving. Almsgiving is also a work of justice. Jesus’ words that the poor are always with us (John 12:8) are no excuse; they call us to open our hands (Deuteronomy 15:11).
days.question: Who is the poor person God has placed closest to you right now?

days.title: The Seventh Commandment in Brief
days.summary: This summary gathers the main points. The seventh commandment calls for justice and charity in how we hold and use earthly goods. Creation is meant for everyone, and the right to private property does not cancel that purpose. Theft, and every unjust taking or use of another’s property, is forbidden. Restitution, giving back what was wrongly taken, is part of true repentance. Buying, selling, or enslaving human beings for profit is a grave offense against their dignity. Our dominion over minerals, plants, and animals is not absolute: it must respect the moral law, including our duties to generations still to come.
days.question: What would it look like for you to hold your possessions more loosely?

days.title: Justice, Labor, and Lazarus
days.summary: Animals are entrusted to our care, and we owe them kindness. The Church judges economic and social matters when human rights or salvation are at stake. People are the source, center, and goal of economic life, and the value of work lies first in the worker. Real development seeks the good of the whole person and of every person. Giving to the poor is a witness of love and a work of justice. The rich man in Jesus’ parable never saw Lazarus lying at his gate (Luke 16:19–31). In the poor, Christ himself asks for our help (Matthew 25:45).
days.question: Is there a Lazarus at your gate whom you have stopped noticing?

days.title: Living in the Truth
days.summary: The eighth commandment forbids twisting the truth in our dealings with others. God is the source of all truth, and his word can be trusted (2 Samuel 7:28). In Jesus, full of grace and truth, God’s truth is fully revealed (John 1:14), and he promises that the truth will set us free (John 8:32). By nature we seek the truth and are bound to honor it. Truthfulness is the virtue of being honest in what we say and do, avoiding duplicity and hypocrisy. It also calls for discretion, since not everything needs to be told. Without trust, people could not live together at all.
days.question: Where are you tempted to shade the truth to protect yourself?

days.title: Witness and False Witness
days.summary: Before Pilate, Jesus said he came to bear witness to the truth (John 18:37). His followers should not be ashamed to witness to him either (2 Timothy 1:8), in word and deed. Martyrdom, giving one’s life for the faith, is the highest witness, and the Church treasures the records of her martyrs. Offenses against truth include false witness in court and perjury, lying under oath, which can condemn the innocent (Proverbs 19:9). We must also guard our neighbor’s good name. Rash judgment assumes the worst without good reason, while charity tries to read another’s words and actions in the best light it honestly can.
days.question: Whose words or actions could you interpret more generously today?

days.title: Lies, Gossip, and Flattery
days.summary: Detraction reveals another person’s real faults to people who had no need to know; calumny spreads falsehoods that damage a reputation. Both wound justice and charity. Flattery that encourages wrongdoing, boasting, and mocking irony also offend against truth. Lying means saying what is false in order to deceive. Jesus calls the devil the father of lies (John 8:44). A lie’s seriousness depends on the truth it distorts, the intention behind it, and the harm done. Lies betray the purpose of speech, which is to share what we know, and they eat away at trust between people. Anyone who has lied or damaged a reputation must try to repair the harm.
days.question: Is there a reputation you have harmed that you could help restore?

days.title: Discretion and the Media
days.summary: Not everyone has a right to every truth. Charity and respect guide when to speak and when to keep silent, and no one must reveal the truth to someone with no right to know it. The seal of confession can never be broken, for any reason. Professional secrets, such as those of doctors, lawyers, or public officials, must be kept unless grave harm would follow. Private lives deserve respect, and Proverbs warns against betraying another’s secret (Proverbs 25:9–10). The section on media follows. Newspapers, broadcasting, and other media shape society, and the information they share should be truthful, complete, fair, and charitable.
days.question: Whose confidence has been entrusted to you, and how do you guard it?

days.title: Truth, Beauty, and Sacred Art
days.summary: Media can make audiences passive and less discerning, so users need moderation and self-discipline. Journalists should serve the truth without harming anyone’s good name. Governments should protect a free flow of information and must never use propaganda that distorts the truth. Truth is also beautiful. Creation reflects the beauty of its Maker (Wisdom 13:3), and human art shares in God’s creative work. Sacred art is true to its purpose when it draws people to worship the God revealed in Christ, the radiance of the Father’s glory (Hebrews 1:3). Bishops should encourage good sacred art and remove what does not serve the faith.
days.question: What image, song, or place of beauty has drawn you closer to God?

days.title: The Eighth Commandment in Brief
days.summary: This summary gathers the teaching on truth. We may not bear false witness against our neighbor. Truthfulness means being honest in word and deed. Christians should witness to the Gospel without shame, and martyrdom is the highest witness. Respect for others’ reputations rules out detraction and calumny. Lying is speaking falsehood with the intent to deceive, and every offense against truth calls for repair. When deciding whether to reveal something, we ask what is good and fitting, guided by the Golden Rule: treat others as you would want to be treated. The seal of confession is absolute, and professional secrets must be kept.
days.question: Who in your life needs to hear an honest and kind word from you?

days.title: Purity of Heart
days.summary: This “In Brief” section ends: society has a right to information based on truth, freedom, and justice, and the arts, especially sacred art, should lift people toward God. The ninth commandment begins. Scripture names three kinds of disordered desire: the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life (1 John 2:16). The ninth commandment addresses carnal desire; the tenth, greed for others’ goods. Concupiscence, the inclination to sin that remains in us after original sin, sets the flesh against the spirit (Galatians 5:16). The battle is fought in the heart (Matthew 15:19), and Jesus promises that the pure in heart will see God (Matthew 5:8).
days.question: What fills your heart that might be clouding your sight of God?

days.title: The Battle for Purity
days.summary: Baptism cleanses us of sin, but the struggle with disordered desire goes on. With God’s grace we fight it through the virtue of chastity, through pure intentions that seek God’s will, through purity of vision that guards the eyes and imagination, and through prayer. Purity needs modesty, which protects what is intimate in a person, shapes how we look at others, and keeps love from being cheapened. Modesty looks different in different cultures, but everywhere it honors human dignity. Christians also work to purify the wider culture, including entertainment and advertising that treat the body as an object. The Gospel can renew every culture (Romans 12:2).
days.question: What do you watch or read that helps, or hinders, your purity of heart?

days.title: Purity Summed Up; Coveting
days.summary: This “In Brief” section on the ninth commandment recalls Jesus’ warning about looking with lust (Matthew 5:28). We fight carnal desire by purifying the heart and practicing temperance, and purity of heart prepares us to see God. It grows through prayer, chastity, and purity of intention and vision, and it calls for modesty in our feelings and our bodies. The tenth commandment then begins. It completes the ninth by forbidding us to covet our neighbor’s goods. Greed lies at the root of theft, robbery, and fraud, and the prophet Micah condemns those who covet fields and seize them (Micah 2:2).
days.question: Which of your desires most needs to be brought before God in prayer?

days.title: Greed and Envy
days.summary: Wanting good things is natural, but desire easily runs past what is reasonable. The tenth commandment forbids greed, the hunger to pile up goods without limit, though we may hope to gain what our neighbor has by fair means. Envy, sadness at another’s good fortune and a wish to have it for ourselves, is a capital sin, one that breeds other sins. It drove Cain against Abel (Genesis 4:3–8), and Ahab’s craving for Naboth’s vineyard ended in murder (1 Kings 21). We overcome envy by goodwill, humility, and rejoicing in others’ gifts. The Law exposes our covetousness (Romans 7:7), but only the Holy Spirit frees the heart (Romans 8:14).
days.question: Whose success do you find hard to celebrate, and why?

days.title: Poverty of Heart
days.summary: Jesus asks his disciples to prefer him to everything and everyone (Luke 14:33). He praised the poor widow who gave all she had to live on (Luke 21:4). Letting go of attachment to riches is necessary to enter the Kingdom. Blessed are the poor in spirit (Matthew 5:3), while Jesus warns the rich who already have their comfort (Luke 6:24). Trusting the Father’s care frees us from anxious worry (Matthew 6:25–34). The longing for true happiness loosens our grip on the things of this world, and that longing is fulfilled only in seeing God, who will be all in all (1 Corinthians 15:28).
days.question: What would you find hardest to let go of if Jesus asked?

days.title: The Tenth Commandment in Brief
days.summary: This summary gathers the teaching on desire. Where our treasure is, there our heart will be. The tenth commandment forbids greed born of a passion for wealth and power, and envy, which is sadness at another’s good and a capital sin. The baptized fight envy with goodwill, humility, and trust in God’s providence, his loving care for all he has made. Those who belong to Christ have crucified the flesh with its passions (Galatians 5:24). Detachment from riches is needed to enter the Kingdom of heaven. The deepest human longing is to see God, and only in him do we find the joy we were made for.
days.question: Where is your treasure right now, and where is your heart?

days.title: What Is Prayer?
days.summary: The final part of the Catechism turns to prayer, the way we live the faith we profess and celebrate. Prayer is the lifting of mind and heart to God, and humility is its foundation, as the tax collector shows (Luke 18:9–14). We do not even know how to pray as we should (Romans 8:26). At the well, Jesus asks the Samaritan woman for a drink (John 4:10): God thirsts for us before we thirst for him. Prayer comes from the heart, our hidden center, where we make our choices and meet God. Christian prayer is a covenant relationship with the Father, through Christ, in the Holy Spirit.
days.question: When did you last pray from the heart rather than only with words?

days.title: God Calls, Abraham Answers
days.summary: Every human being searches for God, but God calls first: “Where are you?” he asks Adam (Genesis 3:9). The Old Testament shows prayer slowly revealed. Abel offers the firstlings of his flock, Enoch walks with God, and Noah is found righteous. Abraham’s prayer is above all obedience: he sets out as God told him (Genesis 12:4). He welcomes mysterious guests at Mamre (Genesis 18), and in the testing of Isaac he trusts that God will provide (Genesis 22:8). Jacob wrestles through the night and will not let go without a blessing (Genesis 32), a picture of prayer as a struggle of faith that perseveres.
days.question: Where is God calling you to step out in trust, as Abraham did?

days.title: Moses, David, and the Temple
days.summary: At the burning bush God calls Moses and reveals his name and his mercy (Exodus 3). Moses speaks with God face to face, as with a friend (Exodus 33:11), and his prayer becomes intercession for his people: arms raised during the battle with Amalek (Exodus 17), and pleading after the golden calf (Exodus 32). The boy Samuel learns to say, “Speak, Lord, for your servant is listening” (1 Samuel 3:9–10). David, the shepherd king, prays with humble trust in God’s promise (2 Samuel 7:18–29). Solomon dedicates the Temple with a great prayer (1 Kings 8), and the Temple becomes a school of prayer for Israel.
days.question: For whom could you stand before God and intercede today, as Moses did?

days.title: Elijah, the Prophets, the Psalms
days.summary: Elijah, father of the prophets, prays and the widow’s son is restored to life (1 Kings 17); on Mount Carmel fire falls and the people turn back to God (1 Kings 18:39). James says the prayer of a righteous person is powerful (James 5:16). On Horeb, Elijah meets God not in wind or fire but in a gentle breeze (1 Kings 19). The prophets drew light and strength from prayer, often wrestling honestly with God (Isaiah 6:5; Jeremiah 1:6). The Psalms are Israel’s great prayer book: personal yet shared, full of praise, lament, thanksgiving, and longing for God. Jesus prayed them, and the Church still does.
days.question: Which psalm puts into words what your heart wants to say to God?

days.title: Old Testament Prayer in Brief
days.summary: This summary gathers the Old Testament’s witness to prayer. Prayer is lifting the mind and heart to God, and God tirelessly calls each person to meet him. Abraham shows the prayer of faith and obedience. Moses shows the prayer of intercession, standing between God and his people. Israel’s prayer grew around the Ark and later the Temple, guided by priests, kings, and prophets. The prophets called the people to conversion of heart and sought God’s face. The Psalms are the masterpiece of prayer in the Old Testament. Fulfilled in Christ, they remain at the heart of the Church’s prayer.
days.question: Which Old Testament figure’s way of praying is closest to your own?

days.title: Jesus Learns and Teaches Prayer
days.summary: In Jesus, prayer is fully revealed. He learned to pray from his mother and from the prayers of his people, yet at twelve he speaks of being in his Father’s house (Luke 2:49). Luke shows him praying at key moments: at his baptism (Luke 3:21), before choosing the apostles (Luke 6:12), and often alone (Luke 5:16; Mark 1:35). Seeing him pray, the disciples ask him to teach them (Luke 11:1). Two prayers from his ministry begin with thanks: praise for revealing the Kingdom to little ones (Matthew 11:25), and thanks before raising Lazarus (John 11:41–42).
days.question: What could change if you began your prayer with thanksgiving?

days.title: Jesus Prays and Teaches Us
days.summary: In his Passion, Jesus’ prayer reaches its fullness. Facing death, he surrenders to the Father: “not my will, but yours” (Luke 22:42). From the cross he forgives his executioners, promises paradise to the thief, cries out the words of Psalm 22, and commends his spirit to the Father (Luke 23:46). The Father answers by raising him from the dead. Jesus also teaches us how to pray: first through conversion, being reconciled with others before we bring our gifts (Matthew 5:23–24), then with bold faith: ask, seek, knock (Matthew 7:7). True prayer means doing the Father’s will (Matthew 7:21).
days.question: Is there someone you need to forgive before you can pray freely?

days.title: Parables of Prayer and Mary
days.summary: Since the Kingdom is near, Jesus calls us to watchful prayer (Luke 21:36). Three parables in Luke teach us: the friend who knocks at midnight (Luke 11:5–13), the widow who wears down an unjust judge (Luke 18:1–8), and the Pharisee and the tax collector (Luke 18:9–14). We must persist, and pray humbly. Jesus invites us to ask in his name (John 14:13) and promises the Holy Spirit. During his ministry he answered those who prayed in faith, like the leper and the good thief. Mary’s prayer is a model: her yes at the Annunciation, her trust at Cana (John 2), and her Magnificat (Luke 1:46–55).
days.question: What prayer have you stopped praying that Jesus may want you to keep asking?

days.title: Prayer in the Early Church
days.summary: This “In Brief” section first recalls Jesus’ prayer as our model and Mary’s as one of faith and self-offering. Then it turns to the Church. At Pentecost the Spirit came on disciples gathered in prayer (Acts 1:14; 2:1), and the first believers devoted themselves to the apostles’ teaching, fellowship, the breaking of bread, and the prayers (Acts 2:42). The Spirit teaches the Church every form of prayer. The first is blessing: God blesses us, and we bless him in return (Ephesians 1:3–14). Adoration, the creature bowing before its Creator, is the first attitude of prayer: “Come, let us adore” (Psalm 95:6).
days.question: When did you last simply adore God, asking for nothing?

days.title: Petition and Intercession
days.summary: In petition we ask God for what we need. Creation itself groans, and the Spirit groans within us (Romans 8:22–26). Christian petition begins with asking forgiveness, like the tax collector (Luke 18:13), and seeks first the Kingdom: “Thy kingdom come” (Matthew 6:10). Then every need, great or small, can be brought to God (Philippians 4:6). Intercession means praying for others. Jesus is our one mediator and lives always to intercede for us (1 Timothy 2:5; Hebrews 7:25). Sharing in his prayer, we look to the interests of others (Philippians 2:4) and even pray for those who persecute us (Romans 12:14).
days.question: Who has no one praying for them, and could you be that person?

days.title: Thanksgiving and Praise
days.summary: Thanksgiving marks the Church’s prayer, above all in the Eucharist, a word that means thanksgiving. Every joy, trial, and event can become a reason to thank God (1 Thessalonians 5:18). Praise goes further: it honors God simply because he is God, for his own sake, apart from what he does for us. The first Christians sang psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs (Colossians 3:16), including hymns to Christ like Philippians 2:6–11. Revelation shows the heavenly liturgy in endless praise (Revelation 4:8–11). The Eucharist gathers up every form of prayer and is the pure offering foretold by Malachi (Malachi 1:11).
days.question: What three things could you thank God for before this day ends?

days.title: Learning a Tradition of Prayer
days.summary: This “In Brief” section lists the forms of prayer the Holy Spirit teaches: blessing, petition, intercession, thanksgiving, and praise. Because God blesses us, we can bless him. We ask for forgiveness, for the Kingdom, and for every real need. Intercession knows no limits and includes our enemies. Every event can be a reason for thanks, and praise asks nothing in return. Chapter two then explains that prayer is more than a spontaneous impulse: it has to be learned. The Holy Spirit teaches the Church to pray through Tradition, the living handing on of the faith, so that the way we pray grows with the way we believe.
days.question: Who first taught you to pray, and what did you learn from them?

days.title: The Wellsprings of Prayer
days.summary: The Holy Spirit is the living water welling up within us (John 4:14), and he leads us to the sources of prayer. The first is Scripture: we pray as we read, so that God’s word becomes a conversation. The second is the liturgy, the Church’s public worship, which prayer prepares for and carries into daily life. The theological virtues of faith, hope, and love, gifts that unite us directly to God, are also doorways to prayer. Finally, we learn to pray in the events of today: “Today, if you hear his voice” (Psalm 95:7). Like leaven in dough (Luke 13:20–21), prayer works quietly through each day.
days.question: Where in today’s ordinary events might God be speaking to you?

days.title: Praying in the Name of Jesus
days.summary: This “In Brief” section names the sources of prayer: God’s word, the liturgy, and faith, hope, and love. Then it describes the way of prayer. Christian prayer is mostly addressed to the Father, but it can also be addressed to Jesus, and there is no way to the Father except through Christ. The name Jesus means “God saves” (Matthew 1:21), and everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved (Romans 10:13). The simple invocation of his name, as in the Jesus Prayer, “Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me, a sinner,” echoes blind Bartimaeus (Mark 10:47) and the tax collector.
days.question: Could you whisper the name of Jesus through the day as a simple prayer?

days.title: Come, Holy Spirit
days.summary: Calling on the holy name of Jesus is the simplest way to pray always. It needs no pile of empty words (Matthew 6:7), only a patient, faithful heart (Luke 8:15). The Church’s devotion also turns to the Heart of Jesus and follows him on the Way of the Cross. No one can say “Jesus is Lord” except by the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 12:3), and the Father gives the Spirit to those who ask (Luke 11:13). So the Church invites us to call on the Spirit every day, as the inner teacher of prayer. We also pray in communion with Mary, who was with the disciples in prayer (Acts 1:14).
days.question: How might you invite the Holy Spirit into your prayer each morning?

days.title: Praying with Mary
days.summary: The Church’s prayer to Mary has two movements: praising God for what he did in her, as she does in the Magnificat (Luke 1:46–55), and entrusting our needs to her. The Hail Mary joins Gabriel’s greeting and Elizabeth’s blessing (Luke 1:28, 42) to a plea for her help now and at the hour of our death. In the medieval West, the Rosary grew as a popular prayer for those who could not pray the Liturgy of the Hours, the Church’s daily cycle of psalms. Mary, entrusted to the beloved disciple at the cross (John 19:27), prays with us and for us. The summary repeats these points.
days.question: What could the Hail Mary teach you if you prayed it slowly today?

days.title: Guides for Prayer
days.summary: We do not learn to pray alone. The saints, a great cloud of witnesses (Hebrews 12:1), share in our story and pray for us. Different schools of spirituality help people pray in many ways, as Elijah’s spirit passed on to Elisha (2 Kings 2:9). The Christian family is the first school of prayer. Clergy, religious communities, catechists, prayer groups, and spiritual directors all help us grow. Places help too: a church, a prayer corner at home, a monastery, a shrine for pilgrims. Jesus also tells us to go into our room and pray to the Father in secret (Matthew 6:6).
days.question: Who could guide or encourage you in prayer in this season of life?

days.title: The Rhythm of Prayer
days.summary: This “In Brief” section recalls the guides for prayer: the saints, the schools of spirituality, the family, ministers and catechists, and fitting places to pray. Chapter three then turns to the life of prayer. We are meant to pray always, and praying always grows out of praying regularly at set times. The Church offers rhythms: morning and evening prayer, grace at meals, the Liturgy of the Hours, Sunday Eucharist, and the seasons of the liturgical year. Tradition knows three main expressions of prayer: vocal prayer, meditation, and contemplative prayer. All three need a gathered, attentive heart.
days.question: What fixed time of prayer could anchor your day?

days.title: Vocal Prayer and Meditation
days.summary: Vocal prayer uses words, spoken or sung. Jesus taught the Our Father and prayed aloud himself, in Gethsemane and in praise of his Father (Mark 14:36; Matthew 11:25–26). Because we are body and soul, we pray with our whole selves. Vocal prayer is the easiest way in, and when we mean what we say, it can open into contemplation. Meditation is a prayerful search for understanding, using Scripture, icons, the liturgy, the writings of the saints, and creation. It engages thought, imagination, feeling, and desire, so the word takes root and does not wither like seed on rocky ground (Mark 4:4–7).
days.question: Which Gospel scene could you slowly imagine and ponder this week?

days.title: Contemplative Prayer
days.summary: Saint Teresa of Avila spoke of contemplative prayer as friendship: spending time alone with the God who loves us. It seeks the one whom the heart loves (Song of Songs 1:7). We choose a time and keep it faithfully, even when prayer feels dry. We gather ourselves, let the Spirit draw us in, and come as forgiven sinners, like the woman who loved much (Luke 7:36–50). Contemplation is a gift we can only receive humbly. It is simply looking at Jesus in faith and letting him look at us, while we listen quietly to his word and let the Father strengthen our inner selves (Ephesians 3:16–17).
days.question: Could you sit quietly with Jesus for ten minutes, simply letting him look at you?

days.title: Silence and Watching
days.summary: Contemplative prayer is silent love, a stillness in which the Father speaks his Word and the Spirit is at work. It unites us to the prayer of Christ and becomes a communion of love that bears fruit for many. It can lead through the night of faith, where we keep watch with Jesus, who asked his disciples to stay awake one hour with him (Matthew 26:40). The summary follows: the Church calls us to regular prayer, daily and weekly, and names its three forms. Vocal prayer joins body and soul, meditation searches, and contemplation rests in faith and love.
