days.question: What noise could you set aside to make room for silence with God?

days.title: The Battle of Prayer
days.summary: Prayer is a gift of grace, but it also takes effort; it is a battle against ourselves and against the tempter. Some think prayer is merely psychology, emptying the mind, or rote ritual, while modern culture prizes only what can be measured or produced. Discouragement in dry seasons tempts us to quit, like the rich young man who went away sad (Mark 10:22). Distraction is common: rather than chase every stray thought, we turn back to the Lord and learn what our heart clings to (Matthew 6:21). Dryness calls for pure faith, like the grain of wheat that dies (John 12:24). Acedia, a spiritual sloth, saps our zeal.
days.question: What distraction or discouragement most often pulls you away from prayer?

days.title: Trust When Prayer Seems Unanswered
days.summary: Our trust is tested when it seems God does not hear us. The Father knows what we need before we ask (Matthew 6:8), and though we do not know how to pray as we should, the Spirit helps us (Romans 8:26–27). James warns that we sometimes ask badly, for selfish ends (James 4:3). Christian prayer can be bold because it rests on Jesus’ own prayer: he was heard (Hebrews 5:7), and he still prays for us. Hope does not disappoint, because God’s love has been poured into our hearts (Romans 5:5).
days.question: What unanswered prayer could you hand over to the Father with renewed trust?

days.title: Pray Without Ceasing
days.summary: Paul urges us to pray constantly (1 Thessalonians 5:17) and to give thanks always (Ephesians 5:20). This is possible, since the risen Christ is with us always (Matthew 28:20), at work, in the kitchen, or on the road. Prayer is a vital need: without it we drift toward sin, and prayer and Christian life cannot be separated. Then the Catechism turns to Jesus’ prayer at the Last Supper (John 17), often called his priestly prayer. In it he offers himself to the Father, prays for his disciples and for all who will believe, and asks that they be one and kept from evil. It gathers up all of God’s work.
days.question: How could you turn an ordinary task today into a moment of prayer?

days.title: The Battle of Prayer in Brief
days.summary: This summary gathers the teaching on the struggle of prayer. Prayer takes effort against ourselves and the tempter. We must face mistaken ideas of prayer, worldly attitudes, and the experience of failure. The main difficulties are distraction and dryness, met with faith, conversion, and watchfulness. Two common temptations are lack of faith and acedia, a sluggish discouragement. Our trust is tested when prayer seems unheard, yet the Father gives what is truly good. We are to pray at all times, since prayer is always possible and truly necessary. Jesus’ priestly prayer sums up God’s whole plan and inspires the Our Father.
days.question: Which difficulty in prayer do you most need God’s help to face?

days.title: Summary of the Whole Gospel
days.summary: When a disciple asked, “Lord, teach us to pray,” Jesus gave the Our Father (Luke 11:1–4). Luke records five petitions and Matthew seven (Matthew 6:9–13), and the Church’s liturgy uses Matthew’s version. Early on, Christians added a closing doxology, a short hymn of praise to God. Tertullian called this prayer a summary of the whole Gospel, and Augustine taught that every prayer in Scripture is contained in it. It stands at the center of the Scriptures, which are fulfilled in Christ (Luke 24:44). Saint Thomas Aquinas saw it as the most perfect prayer, teaching us both what to ask for and in what order.
days.question: Which line of the Our Father do you find hardest to mean?

days.title: The Prayer of the Church
days.summary: This is the Lord’s Prayer because Jesus, the only Son, gives us the words the Father gave him. It is not a formula to rattle off mechanically, like the frantic cries of Baal’s prophets (1 Kings 18:26–29). The Spirit of the Son teaches us to pray it from the heart, crying “Abba, Father” (Galatians 4:6). From the start the Church prayed it, early Christians three times a day. It belongs to the liturgy: it is handed on to new Christians at Baptism (1 Peter 1:23), and it is prayed at every Mass before Communion, as we wait for the Lord to come (1 Corinthians 11:26).
days.question: How could you pray the Our Father more attentively at your next Mass?

days.title: We Dare to Say
days.summary: This “In Brief” section recalls that the Our Father, given by the Lord himself, sums up the Gospel and is the Church’s essential prayer. Then the Catechism begins to explain its words. At Mass the priest introduces it by saying that we dare to pray as Jesus taught us. Like Moses removing his sandals at the burning bush (Exodus 3:5), we approach God with reverence. Yet Christ has made us God’s children, so we may come with boldness, simple trust, and joyful confidence (Ephesians 3:12; Hebrews 3:6). The New Testament word for this is parrhesia: frank and humble confidence, the certainty of being loved.
days.question: Do you approach God more with fear, or with the confidence of a loved child?

days.title: Abba, Father
days.summary: Before calling God “Father,” we may need to set aside images of fatherhood shaped by our own wounds or culture. God is not limited by human categories; he is Father as no one else is. We can call him Father only because the Son has revealed him (Matthew 11:25–27), and in praying this way we enter communion with the Father and the Son (1 John 1:3). The Our Father reveals God to us and also shows us who we are: his adopted children. This gift asks for ongoing conversion and a humble, trusting heart. Jesus says we must become like little children (Matthew 18:3).
days.question: What wounds or images might shape how you picture God as Father?

days.title: Our Father
days.summary: Saying “our” does not mean we own God. It speaks of a new covenant relationship: God is ours and we are his people (Revelation 21:7). We pray as the one people of God, not as isolated individuals; the first believers were of one heart and soul (Acts 4:32). Praying “our” leaves individualism behind. Since Christians are still divided, this word also calls us to pray for unity. Our love must exclude no one, because Christ died to gather God’s scattered children into one (John 11:52). Before we say “our Father,” we should seek to be reconciled with our brothers and sisters (Matthew 5:23–24).
days.question: Whom do you find hardest to include when you pray “our” Father?

days.title: Who Art in Heaven
days.summary: “In heaven” does not name a faraway place. It speaks of God’s majesty and of his presence in the hearts of the just, where he makes his dwelling. Heaven is the Father’s house, our true homeland, which sin made us leave and to which we return like the prodigal son (Luke 15:18). In Christ we are already seated in the heavenly places (Ephesians 2:6), though we still long for our full home (2 Corinthians 5:2). Our citizenship is in heaven (Philippians 3:20). The summary that follows recalls that we pray with simple trust and humble joy, because the Son has revealed the Father.
days.question: How does knowing heaven is your true home change how you see today?

days.title: The Seven Petitions
days.summary: This “In Brief” section closes: praying to our Father should make us want to become like him, and “in heaven” points to his majesty, not a place. Then the seven petitions begin. Deep calls to deep (Psalm 42:7). The first three draw us toward God for his own sake: his name, his kingdom, his will. They strengthen faith, fill us with hope, and set us on fire with love. The last four bring our needs to him: daily bread, forgiveness, help in temptation, and deliverance from evil. We pray them looking toward the day when God will be all in all (1 Corinthians 15:28).
days.question: Do your prayers usually begin with God’s glory or with your own needs?

days.title: Hallowed Be Thy Name
days.summary: To hallow God’s name means to recognize it as holy and treat it with reverence; we do not make God holy, for only he makes holy. God revealed his name step by step: to Moses, to Israel as his holy people (Exodus 19:5–6), and finally in Jesus, whose name is above every name (Philippians 2:9–11). We were made holy in Baptism, and God asks us to be holy as he is holy (Leviticus 19:2). His name is honored or dishonored by how we live; when his people sin, his name is mocked among the nations (Ezekiel 36:20–22; Romans 2:24). This petition holds all the others.
days.question: Does your daily life lead others to honor God’s name?

days.title: Thy Kingdom Come
days.summary: The Kingdom of God drew near in Jesus, came in his death and Resurrection, and comes to us in the Eucharist, yet we still await its fullness. This petition prays first for Christ’s return in glory (Titus 2:13), echoing the early Christian cry “Marana tha,” “Come, Lord.” The Kingdom is righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit (Romans 14:17), and it grows as we live by the Spirit rather than the flesh (Galatians 5:16–25). Waiting for heaven does not excuse us from serving the world; it gives that service its deepest meaning. Jesus calls us salt and light (Matthew 5:13–16).
days.question: Where can you be salt and light for the Kingdom this week?

days.title: Thy Will and Our Bread
days.summary: The Father wants all people to be saved and to come to know the truth (1 Timothy 2:3–4), and his command is that we love one another (John 13:34). Jesus fulfilled the Father’s will perfectly: “not my will, but yours” (Luke 22:42). Though he was the Son, he learned obedience through suffering (Hebrews 5:8). Through prayer we come to know God’s will and receive strength to do it (Romans 12:2), as Mary did (Luke 1:38). The next petition begins with “give us,” turning to our needs with the trust of children. The Father makes his sun rise on good and bad alike (Matthew 5:45).
days.question: Where is God’s will hardest for you to accept right now?

days.title: Our Daily Bread
days.summary: The Father who gives life also gives what sustains it, so we ask with trust and without anxious worry (Matthew 6:25–34). But many people go hungry, and this petition makes us responsible for them, as the rich man who ignored Lazarus (Luke 16:19–31) and the Last Judgment (Matthew 25:31–46) show. We pray, and we also work (2 Thessalonians 3:10). We hunger for more than bread: for God’s word (Deuteronomy 8:3) and for the Bread of Life, Jesus in the Eucharist (John 6). “Daily” asks for what we need today, as with the manna (Exodus 16), and also points to this heavenly bread.
days.question: Whose hunger, for bread or for God, could you help satisfy this week?

days.title: Forgive Us as We Forgive
days.summary: In Christ we have redemption and the forgiveness of sins (Ephesians 1:7), and we come back to the Father like the prodigal son (Luke 15:11–32). But God’s mercy cannot reach a heart closed to others: if we refuse to forgive, we shut ourselves off, as the unforgiving servant learns (Matthew 18:23–35). We cannot forgive by willpower alone; the Holy Spirit helps us, turning hurt into compassion and into prayer for the one who hurt us. We may still feel the wound, and we may not forget, yet we can forgive. Forgiveness reaches even to enemies (Matthew 5:44) and has no limit: seventy times seven (Matthew 18:22).
days.question: Whom are you still struggling to forgive, and can you pray for them today?

days.title: Temptation and the Evil One
days.summary: We ask God not to let us enter into temptation or give in to it; God himself tempts no one (James 1:13). The Spirit helps us tell trials that make us grow from temptations that lead to sin, which often look good at first (Genesis 3:6). God will not let us be tested beyond our strength (1 Corinthians 10:13). Like Jesus in the desert and in Gethsemane, we watch and pray (Matthew 26:41). “Deliver us from evil” names not an abstraction but a person, Satan, the father of lies (John 8:44). Christ has already defeated him, and we pray to be freed from every evil as we await his coming.
days.question: What temptation do you most need to bring to God in honest prayer?

days.title: The Final Doxology and Amen
days.summary: The Church’s liturgy closes the Our Father with praise: “For the kingdom, the power, and the glory are yours.” This takes up the first three petitions and gives back to God the kingdom, power, and glory the devil falsely claimed when he tempted Jesus (Luke 4:5–6). In the end Christ will hand over the Kingdom to the Father, and God will be all in all (1 Corinthians 15:24–28). We close with “Amen,” which means “so be it,” echoing Mary’s yes (Luke 1:38). The final summary reviews the seven petitions, ending the Catechism with this prayer of praise and trust.
days.question: As you finish this journey, what will you carry into your daily prayer?

courses.title: Mark in 16 Days
courses.summary: The shortest Gospel, one chapter a day
courses.intro: Mark is the shortest and fastest of the four Gospels, full of action and the word "immediately." Tradition says Mark wrote down the preaching of Saint Peter in Rome. One chapter a day takes you from the Jordan River to the empty tomb in about two weeks: a good first step into the Bible.

days.title: The Gospel Begins
days.intro: Mark moves fast. John baptizes in the Jordan, the Spirit descends on Jesus, and he is tested in the desert. Then he calls four fishermen, drives out an unclean spirit, heals Peter’s mother-in-law and touches a leper.
days.question: What would it take for you to leave your nets today?

days.title: Friends Who Lower the Roof
days.intro: Four friends lower a paralyzed man through a roof, and Jesus forgives his sins before healing him. He calls Levi the tax collector, eats with sinners, and answers critics about fasting and the Sabbath.
days.question: Who has carried you to Jesus when you could not go yourself?

days.title: Jesus Chooses the Twelve
days.intro: Jesus heals a withered hand on the Sabbath, and his enemies start to plot. He chooses twelve apostles, answers the charge that he works by Beelzebub, and names as family all who do God’s will.
days.question: Whom has Jesus called you to stand beside, as he called the Twelve?

days.title: The Sower and the Storm
days.intro: Jesus teaches in parables: the sower and four kinds of soil, a lamp on a stand, seed that grows while the farmer sleeps, and the tiny mustard seed. That evening he calms a storm, and the disciples ask who he is.
days.question: What kind of soil is your heart offering God’s word right now?

days.title: Power Over Death
days.intro: Across the lake Jesus frees a man possessed by a legion of demons. Back home, a woman who has bled for twelve years touches his cloak and is healed, and he raises Jairus’s daughter with the words Talitha cumi.
days.question: Where do you need to reach out and touch the hem of his cloak?

days.title: Bread in the Wilderness
days.intro: His hometown rejects the carpenter’s son. Jesus sends the Twelve out two by two, and Mark tells how Herod had John the Baptist beheaded. Then Jesus feeds five thousand with five loaves and walks on the water.
days.question: What small thing could you place in his hands today?

days.title: What Comes From the Heart
days.intro: Jesus challenges traditions about washing, teaching that evil comes from within, not from food. A Gentile mother asks for crumbs from the table and her daughter is healed. He opens a deaf man’s ears: Ephphatha.
days.question: What is Jesus asking to open in you: your ears, your lips, or your heart?

days.title: Who Do You Say I Am?
days.intro: Jesus feeds four thousand and heals a blind man in two stages. At Caesarea Philippi Peter names him the Christ, but Jesus foretells his suffering and death and calls every disciple to take up the cross.
days.question: How would you answer if Jesus asked you, “Who do you say I am?”

days.title: The Transfiguration
days.intro: On a high mountain Jesus is transfigured before Peter, James and John, with Moses and Elijah. Below, a father cries, “I do believe; help my unbelief,” and his son is freed. Jesus teaches that the greatest must serve.
days.question: Where do you need to pray, “Lord, help my unbelief”?

days.title: The Last Will Be First
days.intro: Jesus teaches that marriage is for life and welcomes the little children. A rich man walks away sad, James and John ask for places of honor, and Jesus says he came to serve. Blind Bartimaeus receives his sight.
days.question: What are you still holding on to that keeps you from following freely?

days.title: Jesus Enters Jerusalem
days.intro: Jesus rides into Jerusalem on a colt as crowds shout Hosanna. He curses a fruitless fig tree, drives the merchants from the Temple, teaches about faith and forgiveness in prayer, and silences a challenge to his authority.
days.question: What needs clearing out so your heart can be a house of prayer?

days.title: The Greatest Commandment
days.intro: In the Temple, Jesus tells the parable of the wicked tenants, answers questions about taxes to Caesar and the resurrection, and names the greatest commandments: love God and neighbor. A poor widow gives everything she has.
days.question: What would it look like for you to give from your poverty, like the widow?

days.title: Stay Awake
days.intro: Leaving the Temple, Jesus foretells its destruction. He warns of false messiahs, wars and persecution, and speaks of the Son of Man coming on the clouds. No one knows the day or the hour, so his followers must keep watch.
days.question: What helps you stay spiritually awake in ordinary days?

days.title: The Supper and the Garden
days.intro: A woman anoints Jesus at Bethany, and Judas agrees to betray him. At the Passover meal Jesus gives his Body and Blood. He prays in Gethsemane, is arrested, and is condemned by the council while Peter denies him three times.
days.question: When have you, like Peter, failed Jesus, and how did he meet you afterward?

days.title: The Crucifixion
days.intro: Pilate hands Jesus over and frees Barabbas. Soldiers mock him with thorns, and Simon of Cyrene carries his cross. Jesus cries out to God and dies, the Temple veil is torn, and a centurion confesses him as Son of God.
days.question: Standing at the foot of the cross today, what do you want to say to him?

days.title: He Is Risen
days.intro: At dawn the women find the stone rolled back and a young man in white: Jesus is risen. He appears to Mary Magdalene and the disciples, sends them to preach to all creation, and is taken up into heaven.
days.question: Whom could you tell this week about the hope of the Resurrection?

courses.title: Psalms in 30 Days
courses.summary: The prayer book of the Bible in a month
courses.intro: The 150 Psalms are the prayers Jesus himself prayed, and the Church still prays them every day. They hold praise, thanks, sorrow, anger and hope. Pray about five a day and you will pass through all of them in a month. The Douay-Rheims numbers most Psalms one lower than modern Bibles, so both numbers are shown.

days.title: Two Ways and God’s Anointed
days.intro: Psalm 1 sets out the two paths: the just who delight in God’s law and the wicked who blow away like chaff. Psalm 2 crowns God’s anointed king. In Psalms 3 to 7 David cries for help, rests in trust, and repents.
days.question: Which of the two paths in Psalm 1 does your week most resemble?

days.title: What Is Man?
days.intro: Psalm 8 marvels that the Maker of the stars cares for human beings. Then come prayers of the poor and the hunted: “How long, O Lord?” in Psalm 12 (13), and the fool who says there is no God in Psalm 13 (14).
days.question: When did you last stop and wonder at how God cares for you?

days.title: The Lord Is My Portion
days.intro: Psalm 14 (15) asks who may dwell with God. Psalm 15 (16) rejoices in the Lord as one’s portion; Peter later reads its hope beyond the grave as fulfilled in Jesus. Psalm 17 (18) is David’s great song of rescue.
days.question: What would change if the Lord truly were your whole portion?

days.title: Why Have You Forsaken Me?
days.intro: The heavens declare God’s glory in Psalm 18 (19). Psalm 21 (22) begins with the cry Jesus prayed on the cross and ends in praise. Then comes the shepherd psalm, 22 (23), and the King of glory entering his gates.
days.question: Where in your life does God feel far away, and can you still speak to him?

days.title: The Lord Is My Light
days.intro: Psalm 24 (25) asks God to teach his ways. Psalm 26 (27) declares, “The Lord is my light and my salvation.” Psalm 28 (29) hears God’s voice in the thunder, and Psalm 29 (30) gives thanks for mourning turned to joy.
days.question: What fear could you hand over today to the Lord who is your light?

days.title: Into Your Hands
days.intro: Psalm 30 (31) gives the words Jesus spoke as he died: “Into your hands I commend my spirit.” Psalm 31 (32) rejoices in sins forgiven. Psalm 33 (34) invites us to taste and see that the Lord is good.
days.question: What part of your life do you most need to place into God’s hands?

days.title: Do Not Fret Over the Wicked
days.intro: Psalm 34 (35) asks God to defend the innocent. Psalm 35 (36) contrasts human malice with God’s mercy, the fountain of life. Psalm 36 (37) counsels patience: the wicked fade, and the meek will inherit the land.
days.question: Whose success or wrongdoing stirs up envy or anger in you right now?

days.title: As the Deer Longs
days.intro: Psalm 37 (38) is a raw prayer of repentance, and Psalm 38 (39) ponders how short life is. In Psalm 39 (40) the psalmist comes to do God’s will. Psalm 41 (42) longs for God like a deer panting for water.
days.question: What are you thirsting for most deeply right now?

days.title: God Is Our Refuge
days.intro: Psalm 42 (43) longs to go to God’s altar. Psalm 43 (44) laments defeat, and Psalm 44 (45) sings at a royal wedding. Psalm 45 (46) says “Be still and see that I am God,” and Psalms 46 and 47 (47 and 48) hail the great King.
days.question: Where could you make room today simply to be still before God?

days.title: Have Mercy on Me, O God
days.intro: Psalm 48 (49) warns that wealth cannot buy anyone out of death. In Psalm 49 (50) God asks for thanksgiving more than sacrifice. Psalm 50 (51) is David’s prayer after his sin with Bathsheba: “Create a clean heart in me.”
days.question: What would you ask God to wash clean in you today?

days.title: Cast Your Care on the Lord
days.intro: These are prayers from danger, several tied to David’s flight from Saul. In Psalm 54 (55) a trusted friend has turned traitor, yet the psalmist hands his burden to God. Psalm 56 (57) wakes the dawn with song.
days.question: What burden have you been carrying alone that you could give to God?

days.title: My Soul Thirsts for You
days.intro: Psalm 61 (62) finds rest in God alone. Psalm 62 (63) seeks God at daybreak like dry land longing for rain. Psalm 64 (65) thanks him for the harvest, and Psalm 65 (66) invites all to come and see what God has done.
days.question: When in your day are you most aware of your thirst for God?

days.title: Let God Arise
days.intro: Psalm 66 (67) prays that all nations will know God. Psalm 67 (68) is a triumphal march. In Psalm 68 (69) the waters rise to the neck and the sufferer is given vinegar to drink. Psalm 69 (70) cries, “O God, come to my assistance.”
days.question: Where do you need God to hurry to help you right now?

days.title: From My Youth
days.intro: Psalm 70 (71) is the prayer of someone growing old who has trusted God since youth. Psalm 71 (72) pictures a just king to whom all nations bring gifts. Asaph envies the wicked until he enters God’s sanctuary.
days.question: Looking back over your life, where can you see God was faithful?

days.title: Remember the Wonders of Old
days.intro: Psalm 74 (75) says God alone judges. Psalm 76 (77) sinks into distress until the psalmist remembers how God led his people through the sea. Psalm 77 (78) begins retelling Israel’s story, with manna, the bread of angels.
days.question: Which memory of God’s goodness could steady you in a hard season?

days.title: Restore Us, O God
days.intro: Psalm 77 (78) continues: Israel keeps forgetting, yet God keeps forgiving and finally chooses David to shepherd his people. Psalm 78 (79) mourns Jerusalem in ruins, and Psalm 79 (80) begs the Shepherd of Israel to restore his vine.
days.question: Where do you see a pattern of forgetting God in your own story?

days.title: How Lovely Is Your Dwelling
days.intro: God judges unjust rulers in Psalm 81 (82). Psalm 83 (84) loves God’s house: one day in his courts is better than a thousand elsewhere. In Psalm 84 (85) mercy and truth meet, and justice and peace kiss.
days.question: Where do you feel most at home with God?

days.title: Teach Us to Number Our Days
days.intro: Psalm 87 (88) is the darkest psalm, ending in darkness, yet it is still a prayer. Psalm 88 (89) holds God to his promise to David. Psalm 89 (90), a prayer of Moses, sets our brief lives against God’s eternity.
days.question: If you numbered your days honestly, what would you spend them on?

days.title: Under His Wings
days.intro: Psalm 90 (91), prayed at Night Prayer, promises God’s shelter and his angels’ care. Psalms 91 to 93 (92 to 94) praise the Lord who reigns. Psalm 94 (95) warns, “Today if you hear his voice, harden not your hearts.”
days.question: Is there a place where you are hardening your heart against God’s voice?

days.title: Bless the Lord, My Soul
days.intro: Psalms 96 to 99 (97 to 100) call all the earth to rejoice in the Lord who reigns. Psalm 101 (102) is a lament of fading days. Psalm 102 (103) blesses God, who removes our sins as far as east is from west.
days.question: Which of God’s benefits to you could you name and thank him for today?

days.title: Send Forth Your Spirit
days.intro: Psalm 103 (104) celebrates creation: the sea, the beasts, the wine that gladdens the heart, and all life depending on God’s breath. The Church sings it at Pentecost. Psalm 104 (105) retells God’s faithfulness from Abraham to the Exodus.
days.question: Where in creation have you sensed God’s breath giving life?

days.title: His Mercy Endures
days.intro: Psalm 105 (106) honestly confesses Israel’s sins, from the golden calf onward, and God’s mercy each time. Psalm 106 (107) tells of wanderers, prisoners, the sick and sailors in a storm, all rescued when they cried to the Lord.
days.question: Which of the rescued in Psalm 106 (107) looks most like you?

days.title: A Priest Forever
days.intro: Psalm 108 (109) asks God to judge a false accuser. Psalm 109 (110), quoted often in the New Testament, calls the king a priest forever like Melchizedek. Psalms 110 to 112 (111 to 113) praise God who lifts up the poor.
days.question: How does knowing Christ is your high priest change the way you pray?

days.title: This Is the Day
days.intro: Israel goes out of Egypt and the sea flees. “Not to us, O Lord, but to your name give glory.” The psalmist lifts the cup of salvation. Psalm 117 (118) sings of the rejected stone that became the cornerstone.
days.question: What would it mean to treat today as the day the Lord has made?

days.title: Your Word Is My Delight
days.intro: Psalm 118 (119) is the longest psalm, an alphabet poem with an eight-verse stanza for each Hebrew letter. Nearly every verse praises God’s law, word or commands. Watch for how the psalmist turns love of the law into prayer.
days.question: Which line in today’s verses could you carry with you as a prayer?

days.title: A Lamp to My Feet
days.intro: Psalm 118 (119) closes: “Your word is a lamp to my feet.” The psalmist praises God seven times a day, a verse behind the Church’s hours of prayer, and ends like a lost sheep asking the Shepherd to come and find him.
days.question: What step ahead of you needs the lamp of God’s word?

days.title: Songs on the Way Up
days.intro: Psalms 119 to 130 (120 to 131) are Songs of Ascents, sung by pilgrims climbing to Jerusalem. Listen for the Lord who keeps you, the joy of going to his house, the cry from the depths, and a child resting with its mother.
days.question: What would it look like to rest in God like a weaned child?

days.title: By the Rivers of Babylon
days.intro: Psalm 131 (132) recalls David’s vow to find a home for the ark. Psalm 132 (133) praises brothers living in unity. Psalm 135 (136) repeats “his mercy endures forever,” and Psalm 136 (137) weeps in exile by Babylon’s rivers.
days.question: Where do you feel like an exile, and how do you still sing to God there?

days.title: You Have Searched Me
days.intro: Psalm 138 (139) marvels that God knows us completely and formed us in the womb. Psalm 140 (141) asks that prayer rise like incense. Psalm 141 (142) is prayed from a cave, and Psalm 142 (143) asks to be taught God’s will.
days.question: How does it feel to be fully known by God, and still loved?

days.title: Let Everything Praise the Lord
days.intro: The Psalter ends in a crescendo of praise. Psalm 144 (145) says the eyes of all look to God for food. The psalmist trusts God, not princes. Sun, moon, sea creatures and kings join in, and Psalm 150 calls every breath to praise.
days.question: What could you praise God for right now, out loud?

courses.title: Acts and the Early Church
courses.summary: Acts in 28 days, with the Fathers who knew the apostles
courses.intro: The Acts of the Apostles tells how the Church began: Pentecost, Peter and the Twelve in Jerusalem, Stephen the first martyr, and Paul's journeys to Rome. Read one chapter a day. Along the way Pax points you to the first generation after the apostles, Clement of Rome, Ignatius of Antioch and Polycarp, whose writings are in the Library.

days.title: The Ascension and Matthias
days.intro: Luke picks up where his Gospel ended. The risen Jesus promises the Holy Spirit and sends his followers to the ends of the earth, then ascends. The apostles pray with Mary and choose Matthias to replace Judas.
days.question: Where is God sending you to be his witness right now?

days.title: The Spirit at Pentecost
days.intro: Wind and tongues of fire fill the upper room, and the apostles speak in many languages. Peter preaches the risen Christ, about three thousand are baptized, and the first believers devote themselves to teaching, breaking bread and prayer.
days.question: Which part of the first believers’ life do you most want in yours?

days.title: In the Name of Jesus
days.intro: At the Temple gate a man lame from birth asks for money. Peter says he has no silver or gold, but heals him in the name of Jesus. Then Peter calls the astonished crowd to repent.
days.question: What do you have to give that is worth more than money?

days.title: We Cannot Stop Speaking
days.intro: Peter and John are arrested and stand before the council. Peter declares there is salvation in no other name, and they refuse to stop preaching. The believers pray for courage and share everything they own.
days.question: What keeps you from speaking about Jesus, and what would give you courage?

days.title: Obey God Rather Than Men
days.intro: Ananias and Sapphira lie about their gift and fall dead. The apostles work many healings and are jailed, but an angel frees them. Gamaliel urges caution, and the beaten apostles rejoice to suffer for Jesus’ name.
days.question: When has honesty before God cost you something?

days.title: Seven Chosen to Serve
days.intro: Greek-speaking widows are being overlooked, so the apostles have seven men chosen, Stephen and Philip among them, and lay hands on them. Stephen works wonders, faces false charges, and his face shines like an angel’s.
days.question: Who in your community is being overlooked, and how could you serve them?

days.title: Stephen, the First Martyr
days.intro: Stephen retells Israel’s story from Abraham through Moses and charges the council with resisting the Holy Spirit. He sees Jesus standing at God’s right hand. As he is stoned, he forgives his killers, and a young man named Saul approves.
days.question: Whom do you need to forgive, as Stephen forgave?

days.title: Philip and the Ethiopian
days.intro: Persecution scatters the Church. Philip preaches in Samaria, where Simon the magician tries to buy the gift of the Spirit. Then Philip meets an Ethiopian official reading Isaiah, explains the passage, and baptizes him beside the road.
days.question: Who has helped you understand the Scriptures, and whom might you help?

days.title: Saul Meets the Risen Lord
days.intro: On the road to Damascus a light strikes Saul down and Jesus asks why he is persecuting him. Blind, Saul is healed and baptized by Ananias and starts preaching. Peter heals Aeneas and raises Tabitha at Joppa.
days.question: Where has God interrupted your plans to turn you toward him?

days.title: Peter and Cornelius
days.intro: A Roman centurion named Cornelius is told by an angel to send for Peter. Peter sees a vision of unclean animals: what God has cleansed is not unclean. As Peter preaches, the Spirit falls on these Gentiles and they are baptized.
days.question: Whom might God be asking you to welcome that you have kept at a distance?

days.title: First Called Christians
days.intro: Peter explains to the Jerusalem church why he baptized Gentiles, and they praise God. In Antioch many Greeks believe. Barnabas comes, brings Saul from Tarsus, and there the disciples are first called Christians.
days.question: What would make someone call you a Christian just by watching you?

days.title: Peter Freed From Prison
days.intro: King Herod kills James, the brother of John, and jails Peter. While the church prays, an angel leads Peter out past the guards. He knocks at Mary’s house, where Rhoda is too excited to open the door. Later Herod himself is struck down.
days.question: Whom could you pray for today who is held captive in some way?

days.title: Barnabas and Saul Sent Out
days.intro: The Spirit sets apart Barnabas and Saul, now called Paul, for mission. On Cyprus a sorcerer is struck blind and the governor believes. At Antioch in Pisidia Paul preaches in the synagogue, and many Gentiles rejoice.
days.question: What might the Holy Spirit be setting you apart to do?

days.title: Hailed as Gods, Then Stoned
days.intro: In Iconium and Lystra Paul heals a man lame from birth, and the crowd calls Barnabas Jupiter and Paul Mercury. Then Paul is stoned and left for dead. He gets up, and they appoint elders and return to Antioch.
days.question: How do you respond when praise turns to rejection?

days.title: The Council of Jerusalem
days.intro: Must Gentile believers be circumcised and keep the Law of Moses? The apostles and elders meet. Peter and James speak, and a letter is sent with their decision. Afterward Paul and Barnabas part ways over John Mark.
days.question: How do you handle disagreement with fellow believers?

days.title: The Call to Macedonia
days.intro: Timothy joins Paul. A vision calls them to Macedonia, where Lydia and her household are baptized at Philippi. Paul and Silas are beaten and jailed, sing at midnight, and after an earthquake baptize the jailer and his family.
days.question: Could you praise God in your own midnight hour?

days.title: The Unknown God
days.intro: Paul’s preaching stirs up a riot in Thessalonica, while the Bereans search the Scriptures daily. In Athens Paul speaks on the Areopagus about an altar to an unknown god, the God in whom we live and move and have our being.
days.question: Where in your culture do you see people searching for an unknown God?

days.title: Paul in Corinth
days.intro: Paul works as a tentmaker with Aquila and Priscilla and spends a year and a half in Corinth after the Lord tells him in a vision not to be afraid. Later Priscilla and Aquila teach the eloquent Apollos the way of God more accurately.
days.question: Who has patiently taught you the faith more fully?

days.title: The Riot at Ephesus
days.intro: At Ephesus Paul lays hands on disciples who receive the Spirit, and people burn their books of magic. Demetrius the silversmith, fearing for the idol trade, stirs a crowd to shout, “Great is Diana of the Ephesians!”
days.question: What might you need to burn or give up to follow Christ more fully?

days.title: Farewell at Miletus
days.intro: At Troas, during Paul’s long talk at the breaking of bread, Eutychus falls from a window and is restored. At Miletus Paul bids farewell to the Ephesian elders, charging them to guard the flock the Holy Spirit placed in their care.
days.question: What flock has God placed in your care, at home or at work?

days.title: Arrested in the Temple
days.intro: Friends and the prophet Agabus warn Paul that chains await him in Jerusalem, but he is ready to die for Jesus. In the Temple a mob seizes him, and Roman soldiers carry him away. Paul asks to address the crowd.
days.question: What are you willing to suffer for the sake of Jesus’ name?

days.title: Paul Tells His Story
days.intro: Speaking in Hebrew, Paul tells the crowd about his zeal as a persecutor, the light on the Damascus road, and his call to the Gentiles. The crowd erupts. About to be flogged, Paul reveals he is a Roman citizen.
days.question: How would you tell the story of how you came to know Jesus?

days.title: Take Courage
days.intro: Before the council Paul divides Pharisees and Sadducees over the resurrection. That night the Lord stands by him and promises he will witness in Rome. Paul’s nephew uncovers a murder plot, and soldiers take Paul to Caesarea.
days.question: Where do you need to hear Jesus say, “Take courage”?

days.title: Paul Before Felix
days.intro: Accused of stirring up riots, Paul calmly defends himself before the governor Felix and confesses his hope in the resurrection. When Paul speaks of justice, self-control and judgment, Felix grows afraid and keeps him in prison two years.
days.question: Is there a hard truth you keep postponing until a convenient time?

days.title: I Appeal to Caesar
days.intro: The new governor Festus hears the case. To avoid a trial in Jerusalem, Paul appeals to Caesar. King Agrippa and Bernice arrive, and Festus explains the dispute over a dead man named Jesus, whom Paul says is alive.
days.question: How do you explain to others that Jesus is alive?

days.title: Almost a Christian
days.intro: Paul tells King Agrippa of his life as a Pharisee, his persecution of believers, and his call to open the eyes of the Gentiles. Festus calls him mad. Agrippa answers that Paul almost persuades him to become a Christian.
days.question: What keeps you from being fully persuaded rather than almost?

days.title: Storm and Shipwreck
days.intro: Sailing for Rome as a prisoner, Paul warns of danger but is ignored. A violent storm batters the ship for two weeks. An angel promises everyone will live, Paul gives thanks and breaks bread, and all 276 people reach shore.
days.question: How might God use you to bring hope to others in a storm?

days.title: Rome at Last
days.intro: On Malta a viper bites Paul without harm, and he heals many. He finally reaches Rome, meets the Jewish leaders, and for two years welcomes all who come, proclaiming the kingdom of God boldly and without hindrance.
days.question: How will you carry on the story of Acts in your own life?
